verses.translation_literal: Blessednesses of the complete of way, the ones walking in the Torah of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Oh, the happiness of those whose road is whole, who walk step by step in the teaching of the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The longest poem in the Bible opens with a cry, not a statement: 'ashrei' is an exclamation, plural and breathless, 'the blessednesses of...'. Play it as someone who has glimpsed a way of life and is pointing at it. Note what 'blessed' is not: not 'holy' and not 'passive'. The word describes the fortunate state of people who are on the right road, and the road is moving: 'walking' is a participle, an ongoing habit.

The KJV's 'undefiled' makes the first adjective a matter of ritual cleanness, a sense that tamim does not carry. It means complete, intact, without a missing piece, the word used of an unblemished sacrificial animal. 'Torah' is here broader than the Pentateuch: it is 'instruction', the teaching a father gives a child. This is the first of a set of terms the psalm cycles through for God's word across its 176 verses. The commentators count the set differently: Radak lists eleven (derekh, torah, edot, piqqudim, mitzvah, imrah, dabar, mishpat, tzedek, emunah, chuqqim), Meiri twelve ('twelve words revolve in it'). On why the psalm gives each letter eight verses, Meiri says plainly 'we do not know the intention of the count', and Radak offers an argument from eight ways of acquiring wisdom ('corresponding to the eight ways'). Neither ties the eight verses to a count of terms.

philological_notes.note: A plural construct exclamation, 'oh the blessednesses of'. It declares a state of fortune; it does not confer a blessing as the verb ברך does (compare v.12).
'Complete, whole, intact'. Used of sacrificial animals without defect; here a person whose conduct has nothing missing. KJV 'undefiled' narrows it to purity.
From a root meaning to throw, point, direct: 'instruction, direction'. Radak on Psalm 119:1 reads it as the shape of how commandments are done.

verses.translation_literal: Blessednesses of the keepers of his testimonies; with all heart they seek him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Happy are those who guard his testimonies like something precious, who go looking for him with the whole heart.
verses.directors_commentary:
Same exclamation, second voice: the speaker is piling up examples. The verb 'keep' (natsar) is the language of a watchman or of someone guarding a vineyard, not merely of obeying; the commandments are treasure. The 'testimonies' are what God has borne witness to, a word the KJV renders accurately and the BBE flattens to 'unchanging word'.

The second half moves from things to a person: they do not seek the rules, they seek him, with the suffix 'hu'. 'With all heart' is not about emotion. In Hebrew the lev is the seat of intention and thought, so the whole mind and will are in it. The line shifts mid-verse from participles to a finite verb, 'they seek', which makes the seeking sound like the real heart of the matter.

philological_notes.note: To guard, watch over, preserve; the language of watchmen and keepers. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'keepers'.

'His testimonies': what God has solemnly witnessed to. Malbim on Psalm 119:2 reads them as the narratives that testify to creation and providence; Metzudat Zion as the commandments that witness to creation, such as the Sabbath.

verses.translation_literal: Also they have not done injustice; in his ways they have walked.
verses.translation_dramatic: They have done no wrong, not once. They have simply walked in his ways.
verses.directors_commentary:
A quiet verse with a small particle doing heavy work. 'Af' means 'also, even, moreover', and the commentators split on how it joins the two halves: Metzudat David reads it as 'it is not enough to avoid wrong; they also walked in his ways', Ibn Ezra and Radak as 'and even more'. Both are in play, so deliver the line plainly and let the listener hear the extra step.

The verbs are past ('have not done', 'have walked'), as if the speaker were looking at finished lives. The KJV's 'they also do no iniquity' puts it in the present, softening the sense of a record. 'Avlah' is not 'iniquity' in the general sense but crookedness, injustice, a distortion of what is straight. The speaker is setting two roads side by side: the one that bends and the one he calls 'his ways'.

philological_notes.note: Injustice, crookedness, wrong. Malbim on Psalm 119:11 separates it from 'sin' (chet): the source of 'avlah' lies in the paths of understanding, sin in a swerve from wisdom.

'They have done, been busy at'. Malbim on Psalm 119:3 says pa'al is engaging in a matter, distinct from ma'aseh, the finished deed: they do not even engage in what holds injustice, though they might not complete it.
'Also, even, moreover'. Metzudat David: it is not enough to refrain from wrong; they also walked in his ways. Radak records other readings.

verses.translation_literal: You, you have commanded your precepts, to keep, exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: You, and you alone, laid your precepts down, to be kept, and kept with everything in us.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm turns for the first time from 'they' to 'you'. The pronoun 'attah' is stressed because Hebrew does not need it: 'You, you have commanded.' It is the moment the poem becomes a prayer, and the actors should shift to addressing God directly for the rest of the psalm.

The KJV's 'commanded us' adds a pronoun the Hebrew does not have, and BBE 'put your orders into our hearts' goes further: the verse has no 'hearts', though BBE echoes Ibn Ezra's gloss on 'your precepts', 'they are in the heart'. 'Piqqudim' is one of the psalm's recurring terms and comes from the root of 'entrust, deposit, appoint': precepts are things deposited with you. Malbim hears in it the sense of something stored for safekeeping, which fits the verb 'to keep'. 'Me'od' ends the line and lands as a drumbeat that returns in v.8; Meiri and Metzudat David both read the verse as if it said 'you commanded that they be kept exceedingly'. The Hebrew has no 'us' at all; KJV, YLT and ASV supply it.

philological_notes.note: 'Your precepts', from the root of visiting, appointing, entrusting. Malbim on Psalm 119:4 hears 'deposits': things stored for safekeeping.
'Exceedingly, very much'. Here it follows 'to keep'; Radak on Psalm 119:8 ties the same word in v.8 to the verb 'keep' too.

verses.translation_literal: Would that my ways be steadied to keep your statutes!
verses.translation_dramatic: If only my ways would hold steady, set firm, so that I could keep your statutes.
verses.directors_commentary:
From here the speaker steps out of the crowd. Verses 1 to 4 were about others; verse 5 is the first 'my', a wish, and it admits that the road described in v.1 is not yet his. Play it as hope with a catch in the voice.

The verb 'yikkonu' is the root of 'be established, set firm': it is the word used for a building on its foundation. The speaker is not asking to be given rules but to have his own wandering ways made solid enough to carry him. 'Chuqqim' are statutes carved or inscribed, 'decrees': something engraved. The Hebrew particle 'achalai' is rare, found here and in 2 Kings 5:3, and there is no equivalent English word, hence KJV 'O that', which is adequate. Rashi, Radak and Meiri take it as a noun, 'my prayer', and so read the verse as 'my plea is that my ways be established'.

philological_notes.note: A wishing particle, 'would that'. Rashi (comparing 2 Kings 5:3) and Meiri take it as a noun, 'my prayers', from 'to entreat'; Ibn Ezra gives 'my wish and request'. I follow the optative sense.
Niphal of 'to be firm, established, set straight'. Used of foundations; here the speaker's own ways become reliable.
'Your statutes', from the root of engraving. Malbim on Psalm 119:5 takes them as the commands whose reasons are not given, and so the ones the inclination resists.

verses.translation_literal: Then I will not be ashamed, when I look at all your commandments.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then I will not blush, when I fix my eyes on every one of your commandments.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Then' (az) answers the wish of v.5: if the ways are steadied, then shame is gone. The scene to picture is a man looking down a list, expecting his own failures to leap out at him. Metzudat David says exactly this: the one who has not kept them is ashamed when he sees them written. Shame in this world is a public and bodily state, not a private feeling; the face falls.

The verb 'habbit' is a look with attention, a fixed gaze, not a glance. The KJV's 'have respect unto' is archaic: in 1611 it meant 'regard, look at', and today it reads as 'esteem'. The Hebrew is a literal look, and the key word is 'all': not the convenient ones. 'Mitzvah' is 'commandment', the most familiar of the eight synonyms, and the only one here with the sense of a direct order from a superior.

philological_notes.note: To be ashamed, disappointed; the sense of a hope that has failed. Meiri on Psalm 119:6: the one who has transgressed is ashamed before himself when he looks at the Torah's warning.
Hiphil infinitive of 'to look': a deliberate, attentive gaze. KJV 'have respect unto' preserves an old sense of 'regard' but now misleads.

verses.translation_literal: I will thank you in uprightness of heart, in my learning the judgments of your righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will give you thanks with a heart made straight, as I learn the judgments of your justice.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Odekha' is from the root that means both 'to thank' and 'to confess', and the English choice between 'praise' and 'give thanks' loses half of it. The KJV's 'praise' is acceptable, but the same verb in the same form means 'I will confess you' in many other psalms. The speaker will thank God publicly, the way a pupil thanks a teacher who has shown him something he could not see.

'Yosher levav' is 'straightness of heart': the heart is a road made level, an echo of the 'ways' of earlier verses. 'Mishpatim' are the 'judgments', decisions in court, and 'tzedeq' is justice or right. The KJV's 'righteous judgments' is fine, but the Hebrew has a noun with a suffix, 'judgments of your righteousness', which gives the sense that God's own rightness is the source of the rulings. Metzudat David and Radak read the learning as the cause of the thanks: the speaker cannot thank properly until he learns.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'to throw, cast': to thank or confess, a public acknowledgement. KJV and ASV differ ('praise', 'give thanks').
'Straightness of heart'. Malbim on Psalm 119:7 takes yosher as understanding, the heart's power to see through matters.

verses.translation_literal: [Obj] your statutes I will keep; do not forsake me up to exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your statutes I will keep. Only do not leave me. Not now, not utterly.
verses.directors_commentary:
The aleph stanza closes with a vow and, in the same breath, a plea. The two halves sit uneasily, and that is the point: 'I will keep' is promise, 'do not forsake me' is the admission that he cannot do it alone. Deliver the vow firmly and then let the voice drop for the second half.

'Ad me'od' is 'up to exceeding', and the commentators fight over where it belongs. Radak and Metzudat David attach it to 'I will keep' ('I will keep them exceedingly'), echoing v.4, while Ibn Ezra attaches it to 'forsake me', which is how the KJV and most others render it ('forsake me not utterly'). The verb 'azav' is the word for abandoning a person or a place, the opposite of 'stay by', so the line fears a gap in God's presence.

philological_notes.note: 'Up to exceeding', that is 'utterly'. Ibn Ezra attaches it to the plea, Radak and Metzudat David to the vow.
To leave, abandon. Jussive after 'al, a plea: do not.

verses.translation_literal: In what will a youth purify his path? By keeping, according to your word.
verses.translation_dramatic: How can a young man keep his path clean? By guarding it, by living by your word.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new letter, beth, and a new voice: a question. The speaker steps out of the prayer and asks as a teacher would ask a class. 'Na'ar' is a young man, not a child: someone at the age when roads are chosen. Meiri notes the word also means a servant, and also someone immature in understanding, and that David may be calling himself that.

The verb 'yezakkeh' is 'make clean, make pure', and it is the root of 'zakh', clear or pure. The KJV's 'cleanse his way' is fine, but 'taking heed thereto' obscures the answer: the Hebrew says simply 'to keep, according to your word', a bare infinitive. Malbim distinguishes 'derekh' (the main road) from 'orach' (the side track off it), which the KJV does not: the youth is asking about the small paths where there is no map.

philological_notes.note: Piel: 'to make clean, make pure'. The same root appears in 'zakh', clear or pure.
'His path'. Malbim on Psalm 119:9 distinguishes orach, a branch off the main derekh, from derekh itself.
A young man, or a servant. Meiri on Psalm 119:9 lists the uses (Joseph, Joshua, Gehazi) and takes David to be calling himself unfinished.

verses.translation_literal: With all my heart I have sought you; do not make me stray from your commandments.
verses.translation_dramatic: With my whole heart I have gone looking for you. Do not let me wander off from your commandments.
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer to v.9 becomes a prayer, and it echoes v.2 in the first person: 'with all heart they seek him' there, 'with all my heart I have sought you' here. The speaker claims the standing of the people he called happy, and in the next breath admits that he might still wander.

'Tashgeni' is a causative: 'do not make me err', not merely 'let me not err'. The KJV's 'let me not wander' softens a verb that asks God not to be the cause of the straying. Radak and Metzudat David both notice it: since God gives understanding, withholding it would be a way of letting a person go astray. The root 'shagah' is 'to go astray, to err', used of sheep and of unintentional sin, and Malbim on Psalm 119:10 distinguishes shegiah, a theoretical error, from shegagah, and reads the plea as 'do not let my zeal for inquiry lead me to set a commandment aside'.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil: 'cause me to err'. Radak on Psalm 119:10 and Metzudat David read it as 'do not leave me in error by withholding understanding'.
'I have sought you': to inquire, resort to. The same verb as 'they seek him' in v.2; the speaker puts himself among those happy people.

verses.translation_literal: In my heart I have hidden your saying, so that I will not sin against you.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have tucked your word away inside my heart, where no one can take it, so that I will not sin against you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The best-known verse of the stanza, and the KJV's 'hid' is a good rendering, with one problem: it can sound like hiding from something. The verb 'tzafan' is to store up, to treasure, to put in a secret place, the word used of hoarded wealth and of a treasure kept safe. The speaker is not concealing the word; he is keeping it where thieves and forgetting cannot reach it.

'Imrah', a spoken saying, is a new synonym for God's word. The purpose clause matters: not 'because I love the rules' but 'so that I will not sin against you'. The sin is relational, 'to you', a failure toward a person. Radak adds that forgetting is itself a way of sinning, and Meiri has the picture of a word engraved on the tablet of the heart. Malbim sets 'sin' (chet) apart from the 'injustice' of v.3: even a man who knows what is straight can still fall.

philological_notes.note: To store up, treasure, hide in a safe place. Metzudat Zion: 'putting away'. Rashi: 'I did not let it be forgotten.'
'Your saying, your promise': God's word as something spoken. Not the same as dabar (v.9).
To miss the mark, to sin. Malbim on Psalm 119:11 separates it from 'avlah' (v.3): even a man who understands what is just may still fail.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [are] you, YHWH; teach me your statutes.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed are you, O LORD. Blessed, and I say it with the word still warm inside my heart. Now teach me. Let your statutes be given to me, line by line, as to one who knows he has not yet learned them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse has two beats: a blessing, then a request. The speaker does not begin with a demand. He praises first, and then asks to be taught, and the order matters. Ancient Near Eastern petitions to a king or a god normally opened with praise, and a petitioner who came with empty hands and a complaint was a poor client. Here the praise is also gratitude for what is already given. Radak hears 'I bless and thank you for having taught me, and I ask that you teach me more', and Ibn Ezra reads the request itself as the reward the speaker seeks. Play it as one breath of worship that turns into asking, with no pause for a bargain.

The KJV's 'Blessed art thou, O Lord' archaizes the pronoun and supplies 'art' for a verbless clause, but it is sound. Two things are lost. First, the Hebrew has no verb, just 'blessed you, YHWH', which reads like a formula spoken aloud in the temple or at table, and the divine name is replaced by 'Lord'. Second, 'teach me' (lammedeni) is a Piel imperative of lamad, to learn, so it means 'make me a learner', 'cause me to learn'. BBE's 'give me knowledge of' flattens that into information transfer. The speaker asks for schooling, not a handout. The word for what he wants, chuqqim, comes from the root 'to carve, inscribe'. These are things cut into stone or ruled into a ledger, fixed and not up for negotiation. The verse ends on chuqqekha, 'your statutes', and the audience is left holding the word.

philological_notes.note: A passive participle, 'blessed', used of God as the one worthy of praise, not as the recipient of a gift. With no verb in the clause, it is a declaration, not a wish. The same root can mean 'knee', so some hear 'to kneel' behind it.

Piel imperative of lamad with a first-person suffix: 'teach me', literally 'make me learn'. The root also gives 'goad' (malmad), the stick that trains an ox, so teaching here carries a sense of being directed along a path.

From chaqaq, 'to engrave, cut in'. A chōq is a thing inscribed: a statute, a fixed portion. This is the first of many chuqqim in Psalm 119, which uses the word as one of its eight or so synonyms for the divine instruction.

verses.translation_literal: With my lips I have recounted all [the] judgments of your mouth.
verses.translation_dramatic: My lips have told it over, again and again, every judgment that has come out of your mouth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker turns outward. After the heart (v11) comes the mouth: the verse is a pair of mouths, "my lips" answering "your mouth". The Torah is treated as speech that is passed on by speech, which is how most of ancient Israel received it, since few could read and the law was rehearsed aloud in households, at the gate and in festival assemblies. Play it as recitation, not as a private whisper; Radak and Metzudat David both hear a teacher who tells the judgments to others.

The KJV's "declared" is acceptable but flat. סָפַר is the verb of telling and counting (the same root as "scribe" and "number"), so it means to go over item by item, as one counts coins. Malbim notes the difference from "declaring": a סיפור runs through details at length. The actor should enumerate. "The judgments of your mouth" is the Hebrew's own phrase, and it is startling: God's verdicts have a physical source. The KJV keeps it, but its "judgments" hides that these are the court's rulings, the precedents of a divine judge.

philological_notes.note: Piel, 'I have recounted, told in full'. The root covers both counting and narrating; the verb suggests going through the judgments one by one, not a single proclamation.

'The judgments of your mouth': rulings as spoken verdicts. The mouth is the organ of God's legal speech, balancing the speaker's lips. Malbim reads the lips, mouth and tongue as three levels of knowledge (lips for knowing, mouth for wisdom, tongue for understanding), so 'judgments of your mouth' are those built on wisdom.

verses.translation_literal: In [the] way of your testimonies I have exulted, as over all wealth.
verses.translation_dramatic: On the road of your testimonies I have rejoiced, and not as a man rejoices who has stumbled on a fortune: more than that, as if every fortune there is were mine.
verses.directors_commentary:
The joy is measured in money, the only scale a hearer in the ancient world could feel. הוֹן is movable wealth: silver, flocks, stored grain. In an agrarian economy where a bad harvest could mean debt-slavery, to say "as over all wealth" is to claim the security of the richest man alive. Radak imagines a man who finds a treasure.

The verb שׂוּשׂ is a loud, bodily exulting, stronger than the KJV's mild "rejoiced". The comparison כְּעַל is also tricky: "as over" or "as upon", the particle of the thing you rejoice over. The KJV's "as much as in all riches" is a fair paraphrase but turns a poetic image into a comparison of degree. The "way" returns: the Psalm began with those who walk in the way of YHWH's Torah (v1), and the testimonies are a road, not a rule list. Malbim's distinction is helpful: the testimonies are the large road, the precepts (v15) its small paths.

philological_notes.note: Written with a mobile vav, an unusual spelling of 'testimonies'. Radak and Meiri note it as one of eight such places, with the mnemonic given in the Masorah.
Wealth, goods, property: a word from the world of trade and household capital, rare in poetry except Proverbs, where it is often set against wisdom.

verses.translation_literal: On your precepts I will meditate, and I will look at your paths.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will murmur over your precepts, and I will keep my eyes on your paths and not look away.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two verbs of attention, one for the voice and one for the eye. אָשִׂיחָה is audible muttering: the Hebrew meditation is done aloud, under the breath, like a man rehearsing a text he is memorizing. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as speech. So the KJV's "meditate" gives an English reader a silent, interior, almost monastic picture that the Hebrew does not hold. The actor should speak the line half-voiced.

אַבִּיטָה is to look steadily at something, as at the road ahead. The KJV's "have respect unto" is archaic: it means "look to, pay regard to", and the modern reader hears courtesy instead of attention. Metzudat David says the looking is with the heart's intent, to walk the paths and not only admire them. Note the cohortative endings, "let me" or "I will": it is resolution rather than report.

philological_notes.note: To speak, murmur, muse aloud. The same root is used of Isaac meditating in the field (Gen 24:63) and of complaint. The meditation is vocal.
Hiphil cohortative, 'let me look intently'. Not respect but sustained gaze at the way ahead.

verses.translation_literal: In your statutes I will delight myself; I will not forget your word.
verses.translation_dramatic: In your statutes I will play and take my joy. Your word I will not forget, not one syllable of it.
verses.directors_commentary:
אֶשְׁתַּעֲשָׁע is a word from the nursery: the root is used of a child dandled and played with (Isa 11:8, Jer 31:20, "a pleasant child"). The speaker delights in the statutes as a parent in a child, or as one plays. Rashi glosses it as busying oneself, citing Isaiah 17:7. The KJV's "delight myself" is correct but pale; the tone is of tender play, which in a verse devoted to חֻקּוֹת, the least explained commands, is audacious. Meiri says the speaker enjoys keeping them even where he does not know their reason.

The verse closes the Beth section. The pair "delight / not forget" reverses its opposite: you do not forget what you play with. The sibilants of אֶשְׁתַּעֲשָׁע and אֶשְׁכַּח are worth hearing.

philological_notes.note: Hithpalpel of שעע: to amuse oneself, delight, play. It is a reflexive of a verb used for dandling a child, so the delight is intimate and playful.

verses.translation_literal: Deal bountifully with your servant; I will live and I will keep your word.
verses.translation_dramatic: Be generous to your servant, and let me live, and I will keep your word.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new section opens, with gimel: the whole next eight verses begin with the letter, and the first word, גְּמֹל, even sounds like it. The speaker presents himself as עֶבֶד, a servant in a household whose standing depends wholly on the master's goodwill. גָּמַל is to repay or to deal with someone in a way that matches or exceeds what they have earned: here it is plain generosity, with no merit offered.

The Hebrew has two bare futures, "I will live and I will keep", with no "that" between them. The KJV ("that I may live, and keep") and ASV ("that I may live; so will I") supply a purpose clause; YLT keeps the Hebrew's flat "I live, and I keep". The flatness matters: the Psalmist asks for life only as the condition of obedience, and Radak and Metzudat David both stress that he does not ask for life for worldly pleasure. Malbim adds that the request is about the shortness of life, which blocks one from completing study.

philological_notes.note: Imperative: to do to someone, to deal with them well. Meiri notes that without an explicit payback it refers to the first act of kindness, not a reward.

verses.translation_literal: Uncover my eyes, and I will look at wonders from your Torah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Draw the veil from my eyes, and let me see the wonders hidden in your Torah.
verses.directors_commentary:
גַּל is the imperative of גלה, to uncover, strip, reveal: the verb for removing a covering or taking someone into exile. The picture is of eyes that are veiled, not just closed. The KJV's "open" is the right sense but loses the unveiling. The psalmist asks for what he cannot do for himself; this is the point where the Psalm admits that obedience requires illumination.

נִפְלָאוֹת are the "wonders", words normally used of God's acts in the Exodus. To apply it to the Torah is bold: law contains wonders. Rashi and Metzudat David read "hidden things", things concealed in the text and not stated outright. Ibn Ezra attaches "from your Torah" to the verb of looking, not to the wonders. Meiri reads the eyes as the eyes of the mind. Note that the same form גַּל will return in v22 from a different root, "roll away".

philological_notes.note: Uncover. Same spelling as the 'roll away' of v22 (root גלל); the repetition is probably deliberate wordplay across two petitions, one of uncovering and one of removal.
Wonders, things beyond ordinary understanding. Rashi takes them as the concealed matters of the Torah not spelled out in it.

verses.translation_literal: A sojourner am I in the land; do not hide your commandments from me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am only a sojourner in this land, a stranger passing through. Do not hide your commandments from me.
verses.directors_commentary:
גֵּר is a resident alien: someone who lives where he has no family, no land and no legal protection except the hospitality of others. In the ancient Near East such a person depended on local custom and was open to abuse, which is why Israel's law keeps reminding Israel to protect him. The speaker takes that status for himself: on earth, in the land, he is a dependent guest. For a guest, the host's rules are everything. A stranger does not know the local customs, and so asks not to have the rules concealed.

The KJV's "stranger" loses the legal term; "sojourner" (ASV, YLT) is better. בָאָרֶץ can mean "in the land" or "on the earth", and both fit. Radak, Metzudat David and Meiri read the verse as human mortality: we have no permanent standing here, so time to learn is short. Rashi simply says "few days". Malbim sees a soul from another world.

The verb הִסְתִּיר is the covering of the face; the opposite of the uncovering of v18.

philological_notes.note: Resident alien with no hereditary land. Used of Abraham (Gen 23:4) and of Israel in Egypt. Commentators read it as the transience of human life.
Hiphil jussive after אל: 'do not hide'. A prayer that God not conceal the commandments, a contrast to the uncovering requested in v18.

verses.translation_literal: My soul is crushed with longing for your judgments at every time.
verses.translation_dramatic: My very soul is ground down by its longing for your judgments, at every hour, without rest.
verses.directors_commentary:
גָּרְסָה is among the rarest and strongest verbs in the Psalm. It means to crush, grind, break into pieces: it is used of teeth broken on gravel (Lam 3:16) and gives its name to the crushed grain of Leviticus 2:14. Rashi connects it with that grain; Metzudat Zion with the gravel. Ibn Ezra derives it from the same גֶּרֶשׂ כַּרְמֶל but takes the sense as scorched, like parched grain: "burned up" with longing, not ground. The longing is so strong that it breaks the person. English cannot hide this behind "breaketh" (KJV, ASV), which sounds like an archaic way of saying "is bursting"; the original is a grinding, as of a millstone.

נֶפֶשׁ is the throat, the appetite, the whole needing self, not a disembodied "soul": a man with a dry throat and empty stomach longing for water. The wordplay is audible: תַּאֲבָה is a rare form of longing, the unusual noun matching the unusual verb. Radak: the longing continues even while busy with worldly affairs. בְכָל־עֵת, "at every time", is a crisp phrase: no moment is exempt.

philological_notes.note: To crush, break into bits. Rashi cites גֶּרֶשׂ (crushed grain, Lev 2:14) and Menachem's link of this verse with Amos 6:8; Metzudat Zion cites Lam 3:16. Ibn Ezra uses the same derivation from גרש כרמל but takes it as scorched, like parched grain ('burned and consumed'). I follow 'crushed'.
A rare noun of longing, an alternate form of תַּאֲוָה, with the same meaning of craving or intense desire.

verses.translation_literal: You rebuked [the] arrogant, [the] cursed, who stray from your commandments.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have rebuked the arrogant, the cursed ones, who wander off from your commandments.
verses.directors_commentary:
זֵדִים are the insolent, those who act presumptuously, who do not just fail but deliberately defy. The KJV's "proud" is weak; the word is closer to "insolent, willful" and names people who act with deliberate defiance. Radak reads them as those who idle away their time. The sound is a cluster of ר: אֲרוּרִים, the curse, is the same sound as the opposite of בָּרוּךְ, "blessed" (v12), which opened this chunk. The singer has just said "Blessed are you"; now come the cursed.

גָּעַר is to rebuke with a threat, the storm-god's roar at chaos (Ps 18:16, 104:7). The KJV's "rebuked" is accurate but mild. הַשֹּׁגִים is to go astray by error or slip, which Radak and Meiri note: the preposition מִן means "away from", they stray out of the commandments, not just err in them. The perfect tense: God has already rebuked. Radak reads it as a prophetic past for a future rebuke. Playing the verse, the actor can take it as a reminder to himself of what God did: the rebuke already happened.

philological_notes.note: Rebuke with force, the verb for the divine rebuke of the sea and of enemies. Radak takes the perfect as standing for a future, which is a grammatical possibility.
Those who go astray, wander. With מִן it means straying away from the commandments, not merely making errors within them.

verses.translation_literal: Roll away from upon me reproach and contempt, for your testimonies I have observed.
verses.translation_dramatic: Roll it off me, this reproach, this contempt, for I have held to your testimonies.
verses.directors_commentary:
גַּל is the imperative of גלל, to roll: the verb for the stone rolled from the well in Genesis 29:10, as Rashi cites. The shame is a weight lying on the speaker, a boulder that only God can heave off. KJV's "remove" flattens a physical image to an abstraction. Meiri notes that the form גַּל takes a patah where a holam might be expected, and the identical form גַּל of v18 ("uncover") comes from another root, a coincidence of sound that a hearer may take as a pun.

חֶרְפָּה is public insult, the sort that attacks a person's standing in a community where honor was the main social capital. בּוּז is contempt, the look down the nose. The two are paired because shame was public. The reasoning is judicial: "for I have observed", a plea based on the speaker's good conduct. The Hebrew perfect נָצָרְתִּי points to what he has already done, so the plea rests on a record, as the KJV's "have kept" shows. נָצַר is to guard, watch over, as one guards a vineyard.

philological_notes.note: Roll away. Rashi cites the stone rolled from the well (Gen 29:10). Meiri discusses the vowel and the competing derivation from גלה, and prefers גלל.
'Reproach and contempt': public insult and the scorn that goes with it, a pair for social disgrace. Metzudat Zion glosses בוז as 'disgrace'.

verses.translation_literal: Even [if] officials sit, against me they speak together; your servant meditates on your decrees.
verses.translation_dramatic: Though princes sit and talk together against me, your servant murmurs over your decrees.
verses.directors_commentary:
שָׂרִים are the officials of the court: ministers, commanders, nobles. They "sit", which can mean sitting in session, in the gate or the council, where decisions are made. Metzudat David reads it so: they sit as a standing practice (דרך קבע), not by chance. Radak pictures something looser, great men sitting at street corners and talking of the speaker with scorn. Either way, the sitting has the speaker as its subject. The KJV's "princes" suggests royal sons; "officials" or "rulers" is more accurate.

נִדְבָּרוּ is a Nifal, which Radak and Meiri read as persistent speaking (התמדת הדיבור); it also suits "they talk it over among themselves". In Hebrew, דבר with the preposition ב, as in Numbers 12:1 "Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses", carries the sense of speaking against. The KJV's "speak against" is therefore right, and BBE's "make evil designs" is a paraphrase.

Then the contrast: against the sitting, the servant. The same verb as in v15, יָשִׂיחַ, murmurs: while the great sit and talk, he sits alone and talks to the law. The two talkings are set against each other: their voices against him, his voice on the decrees. Radak and Malbim see the servant as one who does not answer but just keeps to the instruction.

philological_notes.note: Nifal of דבר: they speak among themselves, with ב, 'against me'. Meiri observes that דבר with ב usually signals disparagement (Num 12:1, Ps 78:19). Radak and Meiri: the Nifal marks persistent speaking.
He murmurs, muses aloud: the same verb as in v15. The contrast between the officials' talk and the servant's is intended.

verses.translation_literal: Even your testimonies [are] my delights, [the] men of my counsel.
verses.translation_dramatic: And your testimonies, they are my delight, they are my counselors, the men I sit with and take advice from.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here is the answer to the officials of v23. The great men sit in council against him; his own council is the testimonies. אַנְשֵׁי עֲצָתִי is literally "the men of my counsel", the people one consults, the king's advisors. The testimonies are personified as a privy council. Ibn Ezra reads an elided כ, comparing it to "wild ass" for "like a wild ass": they are "as" the men of my counsel. Meiri instead supplies a missing "they are": the testimonies are my counselors, because I take counsel from nothing else. Radak states it directly: they are my companions, not the officials.

שַׁעֲשֻׁעַי is the plural of delights: the word of v16 returns, from the nursery. So the same Torah is a child to play with and an advisor to consult. The KJV's "counsellors" is good, but its "also" (גַּם) is a link with v23: even as they plot against me, my own counsel sits elsewhere. Rashi's gloss, "my occupation", takes the delight as a pursuit.

This verse closes the Gimel section; the Daleth section begins in v25. English Bibles that print a letter heading after this verse are marking that boundary.

philological_notes.note: 'My delights', plural of intensity; related to the verb of v16. Rashi glosses it as 'my occupation'.
'Men of my counsel': the circle of advisors. The testimonies are personified as counselors. Ibn Ezra supplies an elided 'as' (כאנשי עצתי); Meiri supplies an elided 'they are'.

verses.translation_literal: It has clung to the dust, my soul; make me live according to your word.
verses.translation_dramatic: My whole self is pressed to the ground, my breath to the dust. I am down where the dead lie. Give me life, LORD, as you said you would.
verses.directors_commentary:
Open the stanza flat on the floor. With the letter dalet (ד) every one of the next eight verses begins with the same sound, and the first word is dalet's own cry: davekah, 'it has clung'. The word is the one used of a husband clinging to his wife (Gen 2:24); here it is the self clinging, helplessly, to the dirt. The dust is the grave, the ash of mourning and the bottom of humiliation at once, and the actor should not pick one. Nefesh, 'soul', is the throat and the breath, a living creature's whole self, not a ghost in a body; so the line says a living person is already close to the ground.

The KJV adds 'DALETH.' in front of the verse; the Hebrew does not. 'Quicken thou me' is archaic: ḥayyeni is simply 'make me live', 'bring me back to life', the same root as ḥayyim, 'life'. The prayer is a bargain with a promise: ki-dvarekha, 'according to your word', is the hook on which the whole psalm hangs. Rashi and Radak hear King David and Nathan's promise (2 Sam 7); the psalm itself names no occasion, and the director should leave the speaker anonymous.

philological_notes.note: To cling, stick, cleave; used of physical adhesion (tongue to the palate, Ps 22:16) and of loyal attachment (Gen 2:24). Here the self sticks to the dust and cannot lift itself. The same root returns in v. 31 for clinging to the testimonies, so the stanza moves from clinging to dust to clinging to God's word.
Piel imperative of 'live': make me live, restore me to life. The first of the repeated 'revive me' requests of the psalm (vv. 37, 40, 88...). The prayer asks for life, not merely survival.

verses.translation_literal: My ways I have recounted, and you answered me; teach me your decrees.
verses.translation_dramatic: I laid out my roads before you, one by one, the whole of them, and you answered me. Now teach me your statutes.
verses.directors_commentary:
A quiet verse after the floor of v. 25. The speaker has told God everything: sipparti is 'I counted out, recounted', the verb of a scribe or a man giving an account, not a vague 'declared'. 'My ways' are the roads he has walked, the choices and the plans. And God answered: the wayyiqtol is plain past, so this is a memory of prayers heard before, which is why he dares ask again. The KJV's 'thou heardest me' for vattaʿaneni softens: ʿanah is 'answer', not merely 'listen'. The trade here is cleanly made: I told you, you answered, now teach.

Ḥuqqim, 'decrees', are things cut or engraved into a stone, law with the edge of an inscription; the KJV's 'statutes' is fine but legal and cold. Radak and Metzudat David connect telling one's ways with David inquiring of the LORD (2 Sam 5); the Hebrew itself has no such setting.

philological_notes.note: Piel of 'count, recount, tell': to give a full account, in order. Close to a scribe's counting; the cognate noun sefer is 'book'. The speaker has given an itemised account of his ways.
From ḥaqaq, 'to cut in, engrave, inscribe'; a decree is something carved or prescribed. KJV 'statutes' renders it by the Latin legal word.

verses.translation_literal: [The] way of your precepts make me understand, and let me muse on your wonders.
verses.translation_dramatic: Show me the road your precepts run on, and let me understand it. Then I will turn over your wonders in my mind, and speak of them under my breath, again and again.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse opens on the word 'way', and the Dalet stanza keeps returning to it (vv.29, 30, 32). The singer does not ask only for the precepts but for their 'way': how they run, where they lead. Malbim sharpens this: the precepts themselves are understood, since they stand as reminders of the wonders the LORD did of old, such as the exodus from Egypt; what is not understood is the way of the precepts, because that miraculous way lies above human reason, and so he asks to be made to understand it and the secret of the wonders.

KJV says 'so shall I talk of', which adds a promise of result and makes 'wonders' into 'wondrous works'. The Hebrew is a plain wish, 'and let me muse' (a cohortative), and the verb שִׂיחַ covers quiet pondering, murmuring and speech alike; ASV and YLT 'meditate' keep the inward side, KJV and Webster 'talk' the spoken. Play it both ways: a man speaking to himself, half aloud.

philological_notes.note: The way of the precepts: the singer asks about the path the precepts form, not just their wording. Malbim on Ps 119:27 distinguishes the precepts, whose reasons are plain, from their miraculous way, which is not.
Cohortative 'let me muse/speak': the verb ranges from silent pondering to murmured speech. Metzudat David takes it as speaking to others, to teach the wonders.

verses.translation_literal: My soul has dripped from grief; raise me up according to your word.
verses.translation_dramatic: My soul is dripping away with grief, drop by drop, until there is little left of it. Lift me, as you said you would. Set me on my feet by your word.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb דָּלְפָה means to drip or leak, the sound of a roof that will not stop. Metzudat Zion ties it to the 'dripping' of a quarrelsome woman in Prov 27:15 (דֶּלֶף טוֹרֵד), and Metzudat David reads it as a soul that melts until it falls in drops. KJV 'melteth' is not far from this: Radak ('my soul is poured out') and Meiri ('melted and poured out, like a dripping of tears') take it that way too. What KJV loses is the root's concrete image, a slow leak, and the fact that the singer is not boiling over but running out. Radak also allows 'tears dripped'.

תּוּגָה is grief, heaviness; KJV 'heaviness' is old English for sorrow. קַיְּמֵנִי is 'make me stand, raise me up' from the root 'to rise', and 'strengthen' is an interpretation. Radak and Metzudat David both connect 'according to your word' with a promise given through Nathan the prophet, which is the commentators' reading of the psalm's speaker, not something the verse says.

philological_notes.note: To drip or leak; the same root as the 'constant dripping' of Prov 27:15. KJV 'melteth' agrees with Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David, but the root's concrete image is dripping.
Piel imperative 'make me stand/raise me up'. Meiri compares 'give me life according to your word' (חַיֵּנִי כִּדְבָרֶךָ), so he hears a plea for life.

verses.translation_literal: [The] way of falsehood remove from me, and [with] your torah be gracious to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Take the road of lies away from me; do not let it open under my feet. And in its place, be generous: give me your law as a gift.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the mirror of v.27: there a way to be understood, here a way to be removed. The pair 'way of falsehood' and 'your torah' sets two roads against each other, and v.30 will answer with the road chosen. KJV 'the way of lying' is acceptable, though sheker is not only spoken lies but anything false or deceptive; ASV and YLT 'falsehood' is closer.

The second half is the one KJV bends: 'and grant me thy law graciously' makes torah the thing given, and the verb חָנֵּנִי an adverb. The Hebrew verb is 'be gracious to me', and the torah comes in with a weak 'and [with]': be gracious to me with your torah. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'grant them favour', with the favour as the cause that the false road is put away; Radak takes the gift to be a heart that can understand and engage with it, and Metzudat David the grace to walk in it. Treat it as a plea for favour, not a request for a book.

philological_notes.note: Imperative 'be gracious to me'. The torah is what the grace is shown through, or the thing given; the Hebrew leaves the link open, and KJV 'grant me … graciously' chooses the second.
Falsehood, deceit; broader than a spoken lie. Malbim reads 'way of falsehood' as the path of those who would mislead one who studies the deep things of the torah.

verses.translation_literal: [The] way of faithfulness I have chosen; your judgments I have set.
verses.translation_dramatic: I chose the road of faithfulness. I did not drift onto it; I chose it. And your judgments, I set them level and in place, where I can see them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse has no petition, only a statement: here the singer stops asking and says what he has done. The two verbs, 'I have chosen' and 'I have set', are both perfects with no 'before me' in the Hebrew. KJV and Webster supply 'before me' (Webster at least brackets it), and ASV and BBE do the same, while YLT's 'compared' and Ibn Ezra's 'made level, even' follow a different sense of שׁוה, 'to be equal, to put on a par'. Meiri records both: some say 'I put them before me so as never to forget them', but he himself holds that 'I held them to be even and straight, without any crookedness'. Rashi simply has 'I put myself to your judgments'.

אֱמוּנָה is firmness, reliability, faithfulness; KJV 'truth' is the word אֱמֶת. Malbim reads the whole verse as a statement of belief in reward after death, which is his view, not the word's plain sense. The verb בָּחַר, 'choose', is the same word used for chosen things in Deuteronomy: a deliberate, costly choice.

philological_notes.note: Piel of 'to be level/equal': 'I set, I made level'. KJV and ASV 'laid/set before me' add words not in the Hebrew; YLT 'compared' follows the 'equal' sense.
Steadiness, reliability: the way that holds. KJV 'truth' collapses it into אֱמֶת, the word set against 'falsehood' in v.29.

verses.translation_literal: I have clung to your testimonies; YHWH, do not put me to shame.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have held on to your testimonies and not let go. O LORD, do not let me be shamed for it.
verses.directors_commentary:
דָּבַק is the verb of a body fastened to another: a man who 'clings to his wife' (Gen 2:24), Ruth who 'clung' to Naomi (Ruth 1:14). The picture is a grip. KJV 'stuck unto', YLT and Webster 'adhered' and ASV 'cleave unto' all keep it; only BBE, 'been true to', drops the image and keeps just the loyalty.

The petition 'do not put me to shame' is about reputation, not conscience. Metzudat David turns the verse into a cause and a plea: because I clung, do not bring me to shame. Radak: let me not fail to grasp them. Malbim hears shame before mockers who point to the singer's suffering in this world as proof that clinging to the testimonies does not pay. Play the verse tight and low, the grip first, then the plea.

philological_notes.note: To cling, stick: the verb of a physical bond (Gen 2:24; Ruth 1:14). KJV, YLT, ASV and Webster keep the image; BBE does not.
Hiphil of 'to be ashamed': 'make me ashamed, put me to shame'. Metzudat David reads it as a plea resting on the clinging.

verses.translation_literal: [The] way of your commandments I will run, for you enlarge my heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will run the road of your commands. I will run, because you have made room in my heart, and what was cramped has opened wide.
verses.directors_commentary:
With v.30, this is one of the two verses of the Dalet stanza (vv.25-32) without an imperative; the rest of the stanza begs, and here the singer promises, and runs. The promise has a ground: 'for you enlarge my heart'. KJV 'when thou shalt enlarge' makes the enlarging a future condition and the running the later result; the Hebrew כִּי is 'for, because' (YLT 'for Thou dost enlarge', BBE 'because you have given me a free heart'). On KJV's reading he runs once he is enlarged; on the Hebrew's, he runs because he is.

In Hebrew the heart is the seat of mind and will, and to 'enlarge' it is to give room: relief from tightness and distress. Meiri hears an enlarged mind that learns easily without toil, Malbim a heart freed from the enemies that press it, such as desire, anger and envy, and Radak a heart so wide that he runs without hindrance. Play it as breath returning.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'to be wide': to make room. Said of the heart, it is relief and capacity together; compare 'largeness of heart' in 1 Kgs 5:9 (Heb.).

'I run' or 'I will run': an imperfect, so habitual or future. Metzudat David: swiftly and eagerly. Malbim contrasts the broad 'way' (derekh), which he will run, with the narrow 'path' (netiv) of v.35.

verses.translation_literal: Teach me, YHWH, [the] way of your decrees, and I will observe it [to the] heel.
verses.translation_dramatic: Teach me, O LORD, the road your decrees lay down, and I will keep to it, keep to it all the way, heel to the end.
verses.directors_commentary:
From here each verse begins with the letter ה: the He stanza (vv.33-40). KJV and Webster print the letter as a heading. הוֹרֵנִי, 'teach me' (literally 'point me'), shares its root with תּוֹרָה, so the verse quietly says 'torah me'. Metzudat Zion cites Isa 28:9, 'whom will he teach (יוֹרֶה) knowledge?'.

The last word, עֵקֶב, is the verse's difficulty, and the versions split. It is 'heel' in Rashi, who has 'I will keep it in all its turns and the heels of its paths', 'end' in Radak ('all my days'), Meiri and Metzudat David, and 'reward' in Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion (as in Deut 7:12), because the reward comes at the end of the deed. KJV 'unto the end' chooses the middle one. The suffix of וְאֶצְּרֶנָּה points back to 'the way', which Hebrew can treat as feminine. Play it as a walk, step after step, with a heel as the last thing in the picture.

philological_notes.note: Heel; by extension end, outcome, reward. The same noun gives 'reward' in Deut 7:12. Commentators split: heel (Rashi), end (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David), reward (Ibn Ezra, Radak).
Hiphil imperative of 'to throw, point, direct'; the root behind torah. Metzudat Zion glosses it as teaching, citing Isa 28:9.

verses.translation_literal: Make me understand, and let me guard your torah, and let me keep it with all [my] heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give me understanding, and I will guard your law and keep it, keep it with my whole heart.
verses.directors_commentary:
Understanding first, then obedience: that is the order the verse insists on. Havineni is again 'make me discern' (see v. 27), and what follows are two verbs in the cohortative, ʾetzerah and ʾeshmerennah, 'let me guard, let me keep'. The KJV's 'I shall keep' and 'yea, I shall observe' flatten two verbs into near synonyms. Netzar, 'to guard', is what a watchman does with a treasure; shamar, 'to keep', is what one does with a command. Malbim draws the distinction: someone who does not understand a rule may keep from breaking it, but will not guard it as a precious thing.

The verse ends 'with all heart', bekhol lev. The Hebrew has no 'my', and the KJV, ASV and Webster add it. The heart in Hebrew is mind, will and desire together, so the phrase means 'with undivided attention', not 'with feeling'.

philological_notes.note: To guard, watch over, preserve like treasure; 'watch' in the sense of a watchman. Malbim reads it as stronger than shamar, 'keep'.
'With all heart': undivided, without 'my' in the Hebrew. The heart is the seat of mind and will.

verses.translation_literal: Make me tread in the path of your commandments, for in it I delight.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lead me, make my feet tread the narrow path of your commandments, because it is the thing I want.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the broad 'way' of v. 32 to the narrow nativ, the footpath worn by people walking, a trail rather than a highway. Malbim notes that derekh is the great road and nativ the small path for single walkers. Hadrikheni is from darakh, 'to tread, to bend the bow by stepping on it', and in the causative means 'make me walk it, make my foot fall on it'. The KJV's 'Make me to go' is bland and lets the sense of treading, even of treading a path down firmly with one's weight, slip away; BBE's 'make me go' is no better.

The reason clause matters: ḥafatzti is 'I delight, I want', the verb of desire, not of duty. The speaker is not forced onto the path; he asks for the means to walk what he already loves. KJV 'therein do I delight' is serviceable archaic English; the Hebrew is shorter and more direct: 'for in it I delight'. Metzudat David notes the Talmud's saying 'he who comes to purify himself is helped', which suits the structure: wish first, help second.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative of darakh: to tread, to cause to tread. The root is also the noun 'way'; the verb literally makes someone put their foot to the ground on that way.
A footpath, a track made by walking; narrower than derekh. Metzudat Zion: 'shevil umesilah', path and track.

verses.translation_literal: Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to profit.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bend my heart toward your testimonies, and away from profit, away from the pull of gain.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four verses of paths and walking end on the heart's tilt. Hat is 'bend, tilt, incline', the verb used of tilting an ear or turning aside, and the speaker asks God to tilt his heart as a weight is tilted, like a scale, not to wait for the heart to turn on its own. The KJV's 'Incline' is archaic but exact. The pair is blunt: 'to your testimonies, and not to ... '. Hebrew literally has 'and not to (it)', an elision that makes the refusal quick and hard.

The weight is on the last word. Betsa is 'profit, gain', often gain taken by force or by cutting a corner (Judah in Gen 37:26 asks 'What profit (betsa) is it if we kill our brother?'). The KJV's 'covetousness' turns a noun of gain into a vice of desire; YLT's 'dishonest gain' is the narrower reading; Radak and Meiri say simply 'love of money'. In the world of the psalm, when a household lives on a harvest that could fail and loans that could be called, profit is a daily temptation, and a courtroom, a merchant's weights and a creditor's contract all bend toward it. The testimonies have no price, as Ibn Ezra says: 'more precious than all wealth'.

philological_notes.note: Profit, gain, especially gain obtained by cutting or exploiting: Gen 37:26, Exod 18:21 ('men who hate betsa'). Radak: 'love of money'. KJV 'covetousness' recasts it as a desire; YLT 'dishonest gain' narrows it.
Imperative of natah: to stretch, tilt, bend. Used of an ear tilted to listen; here the heart is tilted by God like a balance.

verses.translation_literal: Make my eyes pass over from seeing emptiness; in your way give me life.
verses.translation_dramatic: Turn my eyes aside from empty things, so they do not rest on them. And on your road, give me life.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the fifth verse of the He stanza (vv.33-40), and like v.35, v.36 and the others it begins with ה: a double petition, 'make my eyes pass' and 'give me life', the first a negative and the second a positive. The eyes are the door the singer wants guarded; שָׁוְא is emptiness, the worthless, the thing with nothing in it. It follows v.36's 'unjust gain': Meiri and Malbim both hear it as the same emptiness of money and reward, and Radak as what the eyes go wandering after, since sin kills.

KJV 'vanity' is the usual old rendering of שָׁוְא and still fits; BBE 'what is false' narrows it. The verb הַעֲבֵר is 'make pass over, take away': ASV and KJV 'turn away', YLT 'remove'. The last word is the plea for life 'in your way', and the Hebrew writes בִּדְרָכֶךָ without the plural yod (Radak, Meiri), so the text can be heard as 'way' or 'ways'; ASV 'ways' and KJV 'way' each take one.

philological_notes.note: Emptiness, the worthless: what has nothing in it. Meiri and Malbim tie it to the money and reward of v.36; Radak to what the eyes chase.
Written without the plural yod; both Radak and Meiri note that the plural yod is missing, so it may be heard as 'way' or 'ways'.

verses.translation_literal: Make stand, for your servant, your word, which [is] for your fear.
verses.translation_dramatic: Raise it up, LORD, the word you spoke. Make it stand for your servant, the word that was given so that I might fear you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb הָקֵם is the language of making something stand upright, the same verb used of setting up a covenant, a tent pole or a dynasty. The speaker asks that a spoken promise be given legs. Rashi says the word is the one God promised him; Radak connects it to the promise to establish the kingdom for his sons after him, and Rashi to the condition 'if your sons keep their way' (1 Kings 2:4). The 'servant' is a legal status, not a flourish: a vassal who holds his land and his life from his lord and whose lord is bound by the treaty to protect him.

The last two words are hard, and English versions split. The KJV's 'who is devoted to thy fear' attaches the clause to the servant, which Meiri also does; YLT, ASV and BBE attach it either to the word or to the servant's heart. The Hebrew has no verb at all: אֲשֶׁר לְיִרְאָתֶךָ is 'which [is] for your fear'. Metzudat David hears it as the promise that is the gateway to the fear of the LORD. I have left the ambiguity open. Note that 'fear' (יִרְאָה) is not terror: it is the reverent loyalty that a vassal owes his sovereign.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative of 'to rise': 'make stand, establish, fulfil'. It is used for setting up an oath, a vow or a dynasty.

'Which [is] for your fear'. The relative has no verb, so it may attach to 'word' (the promise that leads to reverence) or to 'servant' (the one who is devoted to fear). The commentators divide on this.

verses.translation_literal: Make pass over my reproach which I dread, for your judgments [are] good.
verses.translation_dramatic: Take it from me, LORD, the shame I have been afraid of. Lift that reproach away. Your judgments are good. They have always been good.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the speaker asks God to remove חֶרְפָּה, public disgrace, and he says he dreads it. In a shame culture, reproach is not a bruised feeling but a social death: it can cost a man his standing, his marriage prospects, his place at the gate. The text does not say what the reproach is. Rashi hears an old sin that his enemies could throw at him; Radak a stain that might fall on his descendants; Malbim the taunt that the kingdom would be taken from him. The director should choose one and play it, but the verse itself holds it back.

The odd turn is the reason: 'for your judgments are good'. One would expect a man who dreads reproach to say that the judgments are terrible. Instead he says that they are good, which makes the dread itself the thing that needs explaining. Metzudat David resolves it: God's judgments are good because they are tempered with mercy. Radak says the same, that God does not judge a man by the full measure he deserves. The KJV's 'judgments' is fine, and BBE's 'decisions' is accurate, since מִשְׁפָּט is a ruling, a verdict; 'which I fear' in the KJV flattens יָגֹרְתִּי, a stronger word of dread, which Metzudat Zion compares with 'Moab was in dread' (Num 22:3).

philological_notes.note: 'I dread'; a rare verb meaning to be terrified of, not merely to fear. It is the verb used of Moab's dread of Israel.
'Reproach, disgrace, taunt'. It is a public shame, the opposite of honour, and it returns in verse 42 with the participle 'the one who taunts me'.

verses.translation_literal: Behold, I have longed for your precepts; in your righteousness make me live.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look. Look at me: I have been hungry for your precepts. Not for ease, not for a quiet name, but for the very words you gave. So by your righteousness, LORD, give me life. Give me back my breath.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the last line of the he stanza (vv.33-40), and it closes the circle. The stanza opened with הוֹרֵנִי, 'teach me' (v.33), and in v.37 it asked חַיֵּנִי, 'make me live'. The same imperative comes back here, now with the claim that the speaker has earned nothing and longs only for the precepts. Say הִנֵּה, 'behold', as an actor would turn a face toward the audience: it is an offering of evidence, not of merit.

The verb תָּאַבְתִּי, 'I have longed', is rare. It recurs in Ps 119:174 (תָּאַבְתִּי לִישׁוּעָתְךָ, 'I have longed for your salvation'), so the poet longs for the precepts and for the rescue they promise in the same word. The related root יאב appears in Ps 119:131, where it is the same longing in another dress; that link is my own reading. The KJV 'quicken me' is archaic: 'quicken' meant 'make alive', and the Hebrew is the plain 'make me live', a request for life itself. 'In your righteousness' is deliberately open. Radak hears 'lengthen my days so that I may keep the commandments'; Metzudat David hears 'count my good intention as a deed'; Malbim hears 'treat me by your own nature, not by my deserts'. The actor need not choose: the line asks for life on the basis of God's character, not the speaker's record.

philological_notes.note: 'I have longed': a perfect of a rare root for deep craving. It returns in Ps 119:174 with salvation as its object. Ibn Ezra glosses it with כליתי, 'I am spent', as the language of being consumed by love.

Piel imperative with suffix, 'make me live'. It is the refrain of the psalm; here it closes the he stanza after its first appearance in v.37. KJV 'quicken' is the older English for the same causative.

verses.translation_literal: And let them come to me, your covenant loyalties, YHWH, your salvation according to your word.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them come to me, LORD. Let your kindnesses come, one after another, to the door of the man who waits. Let your rescue come with them, just as you said it would.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new stanza begins with ו, and every verse from here to v.48 starts with the letter. Here it is a plain 'and', but it also gives the line the feel of a prayer already underway, continuing what v.40 asked.

The verb is a jussive, 'let them come', and the subject is plural: חֲסָדֶךָ, 'your covenant loyalties'. The plural is not visible in the spelling, because the word is written without its plural yod; Radak and Meiri both point this out. Ibn Ezra glosses the odd verb form ויבואוני as 'ויבואו אלי', 'may they come to me', which is just the same wish with the suffix spelled out. The KJV 'Let thy mercies come also unto me' adds 'also', which is not in the Hebrew, and 'mercies' blurs חֶסֶד, the loyalty that the stronger partner owes under a covenant. The poet is asking the king-like God to honour what he is bound to. 'Even thy salvation' in the KJV also makes salvation an explanation of the loyalties; the Hebrew simply sets תְּשׁוּעָתְךָ beside them, as a second subject.

כְּאִמְרָתֶךָ, 'according to your word', is the hinge. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it as 'as you promised me', and Metzudat David names Nathan the prophet's word to David. The line is therefore a claim on a promise, not a hope in the dark.

philological_notes.note: Plural, 'your covenant loyalties', written without the plural yod. Radak and Meiri note the defective spelling, which is why a plural verb sits next to a form that looks singular.
'According to your word', in the sense of 'as you have said'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as God's promise to the speaker.

token_glosses.gloss: and let them come to me

verses.translation_literal: And I will answer the one who taunts me a word, for I have trusted in your word.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then I will have something to say to the voice that mocks me. One word. Not a curse, not a boast: the word you gave me, because I leaned my whole weight on it, and it held.
verses.directors_commentary:
The stage has a second character now: the taunter, חֹרְפִי, 'the one who sharpens his tongue at me'. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri tell us what the taunt was: that there is no salvation for the speaker (Meiri cites Ps 3:3, 'there is no salvation for him in God'). So the answer is not an argument but a counter-testimony.

Two things here are easy to lose. First, the pun: דָּבָר, 'a word', is the thing he will answer, and the ground of the answer is בִּדְבָרֶךָ, 'your word'. The poet answers with the word he trusts. Second, the grammar of the first verb: it is a first-person imperfect, 'I will answer' or 'let me answer', and 'a word' is what is given back. The KJV 'So shall I have wherewith to answer' turns the verb into the possession of an answer, and adds a causal 'so shall' that depends on the previous verses. YLT keeps the simple verb.

Metzudat David reads 'a word' as 'words of taunt, as he spoke to me', so that the poet pays him back in kind. My reading is the other one, the one the other commentators share: the word is the answer, not a return jeer. The actor should play it calm. The taunter has been loud; the answer is short.

philological_notes.note: Participle, 'the one who taunts me'. The root is a sharp, cutting insult; the noun חרפה is 'reproach' in v.39. The taunt is quoted by the commentators as 'there is no salvation for him', echoing Ps 3:3.
'A word', repeated in the verse as בִּדְבָרֶךָ. The same noun is the answer and the ground of the trust. The English needs a repeated 'word' to keep the echo.

verses.translation_literal: And do not snatch away from my mouth a word of truth up to muchness, for I have hoped for your judgments.
verses.translation_dramatic: And do not tear the true word out of my mouth. Not now, not ever. I have hoped for your judgments, LORD; do not let me stand before the taunter with an empty mouth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has just promised to answer his mockers; now he fears he will be left with nothing to say. אַל־תַּצֵּל is a request addressed to God, and the verb is strong. נצל normally means 'to rescue' (to pull someone out of danger), and here it means 'to snatch away'. The commentators saw the oddness at once and reached for parallels. Rashi glosses it as 'do not separate', citing Gen 31:9, where God 'took away' (וַיַּצֵּל) the flock of the father. Meiri cites Gen 31:16, 'all the wealth which God took away from our father'. Metzudat Zion also points to Genesis 31. Ibn Ezra and Radak compare the stripping of Egypt (וינצלו את מצרים, Exod 12:36). The picture is of loot being taken out of someone's hands; the speaker asks not to be plundered of his truth.

The KJV 'take not the word of truth utterly out of my mouth' keeps this reasonably, and 'utterly' is its guess at עַד־מְאֹד, which is literally 'up to muchness'. 'Judgments' in the KJV is fine for מִשְׁפָּטִים, but note that the Hebrew has the singular 'your judgment' (written with the suffix on a singular form). Radak adds that if the speaker's mouth were closed it would be as if God had taken the word from it, because it is God who opens the mouth.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil jussive negated by אל, 'do not snatch away'. The root usually means 'rescue'; the sense here is the 'removal' that the commentators find in Gen 31. Rashi glosses it 'do not separate'.
'Up to muchness', an idiom for 'exceedingly'. Meiri takes it with the request: 'I ask this very much'. Rashi takes it as 'in all my teachings and judgments, that I not stumble in them'.

verses.translation_literal: And I will keep your torah continually, for ever and ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I will keep your teaching. Every day, every hour, without a gap in it. For ever, and then past ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
The vav stanza continues, and the line that closes this window is the vow behind everything asked so far. The verb וְאֶשְׁמְרָה carries a cohortative ending, which gives it the colour of resolve: 'let me keep'. The speaker is no longer asking for something; he is promising.

The KJV 'So shall I keep' makes the vav a consequence, 'if all this happens, then I will keep', and Ibn Ezra reads it exactly so (אז אשמרה, 'then I will keep'). YLT's 'And I keep' leaves the plain 'and', which is what the Hebrew says. Either way, the commentators take the line as the aim of all the requests of vv.41-43.

The triple of time words is the actor's cue to build. תָּמִיד is the daily, regular, 'continually' (the same word as the tamid offering). לְעוֹלָם וָעֶד is 'for ever and ever', literally 'to the age and onward'. Radak gives two readings: all the days of my life, or this world and the world to come, in which the keeping is kept for me; Meiri understands the second, Metzudat David the first. The plain sense is the first: until I die, and beyond.

philological_notes.note: 'Your torah', here not the book but the teaching. The root means 'to throw, to point', hence 'direction'. The word has the same sense as the other terms of the psalm (law, precepts, word).
'Continually': the word used for the daily offering. The speaker's keeping is meant to be as regular.

verses.translation_literal: And I will walk about in the broad place, for I have sought your precepts.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I will walk, and the walls will fall back, and there will be room to move. For I have gone looking for your precepts.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture is spatial and it is the opposite of a trap. In the Hebrew Bible, distress is narrowness, from the same root as 'Egypt' (מִצְרַיִם, the narrow place), and salvation is being brought out into a wide place. The speaker will walk about in a broad open area, בָרְחָבָה: the verb is the reflexive form, to stroll back and forth, a free man pacing his own ground. The KJV's 'at liberty' translates the picture into a political abstraction and loses the open space.

The reason is the odd part: 'for I have sought your precepts'. The verb דָרַשׁ is the verb for inquiring of God and studying a text, and it is a past action that grounds a future freedom. Radak says that the one who studies the law will not have his steps constrained in its path. Metzudat David says it is like a man walking on open ground who does not easily stumble. Rashi hears it as legal practice: 'a ruling spread open in Israel'. The point is that obedience is not the narrow road that people suppose; it is a wide field.

philological_notes.note: 'In the broad place, in open space'. The opposite of distress (narrowness). It is spatial, not an abstraction like 'liberty'.
'I have sought, inquired after'. The word for consulting God or searching a text. Rashi glosses it בִּקַּשְׁתִּי, 'I sought'.

verses.translation_literal: And I will speak in your testimonies before kings, and I will not be ashamed.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I will speak of your testimonies, aloud, in the presence of kings. And I will not blush. I will not look down.
verses.directors_commentary:
The earlier verses were private: the mouth, the eyes, the hands. Here the scene is the royal court, and the speaker will talk about God's testimonies, עֵדֹת, the covenant's witnesses, in front of men who hold the power of life and death. The ancient world's courts were full of other gods; to speak for the LORD in front of a king was to risk contempt, and shame (בּוֹשׁ) was the social punishment for being shown wrong in public. Ibn Ezra says people naturally fear kings. Meiri adds that the man who speaks his own inventions before the wise will be ashamed, but the man who speaks God's testimony speaks truth and will not be.

The KJV's 'also' is not in the Hebrew; it is another way the English version turns a flat list of resolutions into a staircase. The Hebrew is just 'and I will speak', with ו, and the beauty is its plainness. The preposition בְּ here is 'in/with' the testimonies, so the speaker speaks 'in' them, not merely about them, in the way a witness speaks in the words of a sworn statement. The verb אֵבוֹשׁ is future, but the force is a vow of steadiness: Radak says he knows he will win by his reply.

philological_notes.note: 'Your testimonies': the covenant's witnessing stipulations, the commandments seen as statements God has sworn to. A recurring word in the psalm.
'I will be ashamed, put to shame': public disgrace at being shown wrong. It is the opposite of the confident standing of the one who speaks truth.

verses.translation_literal: And I will delight myself in your commandments, which I have loved.
verses.translation_dramatic: And in your commandments I will take my pleasure, the way a child plays. I have loved them, and I will go on loving them.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the public scene before kings, the camera comes back indoors. Ibn Ezra's one-word comment is 'in secret', and Radak says that even alone the speaker will find more joy in them than others find in company. The verb אֶשְׁתַּעֲשַׁע is a reflexive of 'to play' (the noun is the word for a child's plaything or a parent's delight), so it is closer to 'I will play in your commandments' than to the dry 'delight myself' of the KJV. The commandments are not a load but a playground.

The final clause, 'which I have loved', is a past tense, a love that is already a fact. The speaker does not promise to learn to love the commandments; he says he has loved them, and the future delight grows out of that. The KJV, ASV and Webster all translate אֲשֶׁר as 'which', and so does the Hebrew; BBE's 'to which I have given my love' is an interpretation. Malbim says the delight has a counterpart in the next verse, because a person must not think that his play is only mental, with no labour of doing them.

philological_notes.note: Hithpalpel, 'I will play, delight myself': related to the noun for 'playthings, delights'. It suggests joyful, unhurried absorption, as a child plays.
'Your commandments': what has been enjoined. The speaker delights in what he is told to do.

verses.translation_literal: And I will lift up my palms to your commandments, which I have loved, and I will muse on your statutes.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I will lift my open hands toward your commandments, the ones I have loved. And I will whisper over your statutes, turning them over and over.
verses.directors_commentary:
The vav section ends with a gesture and a sound. Lifting the palms, כַּפַּיִם, is the posture of prayer and blessing and also of reverence for a greater person; Ibn Ezra says it is the way of honour and receiving, from love. It is directed here, oddly, not to God but 'to your commandments', as though they were a person to be greeted. Metzudat David says the speaker lifts them to take the commandments to himself and do them, and Malbim says the lifted hands stand for the doing of the commandments, with no hope of reward, from love.

The last verb, אָשִׂיחָה, is the sound half. שִׂיחַ is to talk to oneself, to murmur, to ponder aloud; the KJV's 'meditate' sounds like a silent mental exercise, but the Hebrew word is audible, a low muttering over the text. Metzudat David glosses it 'I will speak and learn in them', and Radak ties it to training the mouth. Malbim notes the word 'statutes' (חֻקִּים): the commandments whose reason is hidden. The speaker will muse over those too, even when he cannot see why. The BBE's 'stretched out to you' replaces 'to your commandments' with 'to you', which is a smoothing of the Hebrew's odd direction.

philological_notes.note: 'I will lift up my palms': the gesture of prayer or reverence. Here the object is the commandments themselves.
'I will muse, ponder aloud': to speak to oneself at length. It is audible, a murmur, so it differs from silent 'meditation'.
'Your statutes': from the root 'to engrave'. Malbim connects them with the commandments whose reason is hidden.

verses.translation_literal: Remember [the] word to your servant, on which you have made me hope.
verses.translation_dramatic: Remember, Lord. Remember the word you gave your servant, the very word on which you taught me to hang my hope.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens its zayin stanza with an imperative, and it is a bold one. Prayer in the Hebrew Bible regularly asks God to 'remember', which never means that God has forgotten; it means: act on what you promised. The speaker is not pleading for a new favour but calling in a debt of faithfulness, the kind owed by a king to a vassal who has served him.

The KJV is accurate here, but 'upon which thou hast caused me to hope' hides how odd the verb is. Hebrew says the LORD himself made the speaker hope: hope is something God plants, and so something God is bound to honour. Play the line as quiet confidence, not anxiety. Rashi and Malbim hear a particular promise, Nathan's oracle to David in 2 Samuel 7; the text does not name it.

philological_notes.note: Piel of 'to wait, to hope', with a first-person object: 'you made me hope'. Malbim distinguishes it from a vaguer 'expectation': it is hope resting on a clear promise.
'Remember' as covenant language: to remember is to act on a commitment.

verses.translation_literal: This [is] my comfort in my affliction: that your saying has kept me alive.
verses.translation_dramatic: This is what comforts me in my affliction: your word has kept me alive.
verses.directors_commentary:
'This' points at something just spoken of, the word and the hope of the last verse, and the line should come as a hand laid on the speaker's shoulder. The affliction (עֳנִי) is not mild sadness; it is the lowered, pressed-down condition of someone weak against stronger people, as the next verses show.

The KJV's 'quickened' is a fine Elizabethan word that modern readers hear as 'speeded up'. It meant 'made alive'. The verb is the Piel of חיה, and the Hebrew says the word kept him alive. Radak imagines an exile who would have died of grief without it; Malbim hears David on the run from Absalom.

philological_notes.note: Piel 'gave life, kept alive' with a suffix: the word is subject, not merely a comfort. 'Quickened' in the KJV means 'made alive'.
'Your saying, your utterance': a word of promise, as against דָּבָר, a general word or matter.

verses.translation_literal: [The] arrogant have mocked me up to muchness; from your law I have not turned aside.
verses.translation_dramatic: The arrogant have laughed at me, laughed hard and long. And still I have not stepped off the road of your teaching.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'arrogant' (זֵדִים) are not just proud; they are people who act with presumption, as if no one is above them. Their weapon is mockery, and in a shame-and-honour society ridicule is a serious attack: it tries to make loyalty to the Torah look foolish. Radak and Metzudat David take the mockery to be aimed at the speaker's constant study.

The KJV 'had me greatly in derision' is accurate if stiff; 'declined' means 'turned aside', which the Hebrew נָטִיתִי says (the verb of leaving a path). The two halves are set side by side with no 'but': mockery at full strength, steadiness unmoved. Play the second half flat, almost mild.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of לוץ 'to scoff, mock'. Metzudat Zion links it to לץ, 'scoffer'.
'I have turned aside' from a path, the same picture as the 'way' language elsewhere in the psalm.
