verses.translation_literal: I remember your judgments from long ago, YHWH, and I comfort myself.
verses.translation_dramatic: I remember, LORD, how you have judged since the world was young, and in remembering, I find comfort.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker's comfort comes from an odd place: not from a gentle promise but from God's judgments. In the Hebrew Bible God's mishpatim are his acts of setting things right, and the old ones are evidence that wrongs do not stand forever. Metzudat David reads them as judgments on the wicked; Radak as judgments that fell on good people and were followed by good.

The KJV says 'of old' and 'comforted myself'; both are right. The last verb, וָאֶתְנֶחָם, is reflexive: the speaker does the comforting, by calling the past to mind. It echoes the comfort (נֶחָמָה) of verse 50, so the thread is kept: comfort in the word, comfort in the record.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael of נחם: 'I comforted myself'. The same root as נֶחָמָה in verse 50. Rashi reads the comfort as coming from knowing God punishes and then relents.
'From of old, from long ago': time out of mind, not necessarily 'forever'.

verses.translation_literal: Scorching rage has seized me from [the] wicked, [those who] forsake your law.
verses.translation_dramatic: A scorching fury has taken hold of me. It comes from the wicked, from those who walk away from your law.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the comfort is broken by anger, and the verse turns on one rare noun. זַלְעָפָה occurs only a few times, in Psalm 11:6 for the scorching wind sent on the wicked and in Lamentations 5:10 for fever-heat. It is a burning, parching word. The KJV's 'horror' and the 'trembling' of Radak and Meiri take it as fear; ASV and BBE take it as rage. The picture is of heat, so a hot anger is the safer reading, and the verse can be played as shaking with indignation.

The preposition מִן, 'from', is the other key: the burning comes from the wicked, not just 'because of' them as in the KJV. The wicked here are specific: people who have walked off from the law (עֹזְבֵי), the exact opposite of the speaker in verse 51.

philological_notes.note: A rare word for scorching heat, used in Psalm 11:6 ('a scorching wind') and Lamentations 5:10. Here it can mean burning indignation or shuddering dread; Metzudat Zion relates it to the verse in Psalm 11.

verses.translation_literal: Songs your statutes have been to me, in [the] house of my sojournings.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your statutes have become my songs, wherever I make my temporary home.
verses.directors_commentary:
Hebrew sets 'songs' first: the surprise is that rules could be sung at all. In a world where law was learned by memory and recited aloud, setting it to a tune is how you carry it on the road. The speaker is a גָּר-type figure, living as a sojourner without land or rights, and for such a person a portable song is the only property.

The KJV's 'house of my pilgrimage' is lovely but misleading: 'pilgrimage' suggests a holy journey, while the Hebrew is the place where one lives as a resident outsider. Radak reads exile; Metzudat David and Malbim, simply the places he lived. Meiri notes a second possibility, 'terror', from the root מגור, but 'sojourning' is the plain sense.

philological_notes.note: 'My sojournings', the places where one lives as a resident alien; the same word is used for the patriarchs' stay in Canaan. Meiri also mentions a link to 'terror'.
'Songs, melodies' (sung or played). The word comes first in the Hebrew, and it is for emphasis.

verses.translation_literal: I have remembered in the night your name, YHWH, and I have kept your law.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the night I remember your name, LORD. In the dark, with nothing else to hold, I say it. And I keep your law.
verses.directors_commentary: Night in the ancient world is not a blank. Without street lamps, the dark is long, quiet and a little dangerous, and it is when a person lies awake with their own thoughts. The singer fills it with a name. The Hebrew places 'in the night' before 'your name', so the night comes first and the name arrives into it; the KJV's 'thy name, O Lord, in the night' reshuffles that into a smoother English order and loses the way the dark opens the line. 'Your name' is not a label. In the ancient Near East a name carried a person's character and reputation, and to remember YHWH's name is to call to mind who he has shown himself to be. The KJV also writes 'the Lord' for the divine name; the Hebrew has the four-letter name itself, which the psalm uses as an address, a person speaking to a person. The second half turns remembrance into conduct: remembering and keeping are paired, as often in Hebrew, where to remember is to act on what one knows. Radak hears solitude in it, the speaker alone at night with his thoughts; Rashi hears a time of trouble and darkness. Both fit an actor who plays this quietly, in a low voice, at a bed or a doorway.

philological_notes.note: To remember, in Hebrew, is not only to recall but to bring to mind in a way that moves the will. The verb opens the verse and sets the night scene.

A vav with a first-person form carrying the cohortative ending. It can read as 'and so I kept' or as 'and I would keep'. The literal layer takes it as a plain report of keeping that follows from remembering.

verses.translation_literal: This has become mine, that I have observed your precepts.
verses.translation_dramatic: This has become mine: I have guarded your precepts.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse ends the zayin stanza on a riddle: what is 'this'? The Hebrew leaves it open, and the commentators split. Rashi hears a crown that sets the speaker's seed on the throne, as the Sages read it. Radak takes it as the knowledge and care God gave in reward for keeping the commands. Metzudat David and Meiri point to the greatness or deliverance that he now enjoys.

The KJV 'This I had, because I kept' makes the cause plain, but כִּי can also mean 'that' or 'namely': it may be that keeping the precepts is itself what has become his. The effect is dignified understatement. Say it softly. The speaker has not been given a prize; he has been given a character.

philological_notes.note: 'I have guarded, observed': to keep as one keeps a treasure or a city. The psalm uses a ring of such verbs (שמר, נצר), each with a nuance.
'Because' or 'that/namely'. The choice changes whether keeping is the cause or the content of 'this'.

verses.translation_literal: My portion [is] YHWH — I have said — to keep your words.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is my portion. That is what I have said, and what I have said I will do: to keep your words.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new stanza opens (ḥet) with the psalm's most land-based image. 'Portion' (חֵלֶק) is the share of land a family was allotted when Israel settled; the Levites alone had none, because the LORD was their portion (Num 18:20, Deut 10:9). To say the LORD is my portion is to say: I have staked my whole livelihood on him. Radak and Malbim contrast this with those who choose wealth or fields.

The KJV adds 'Thou art', turning a statement into an address, and 'that I would keep', which smooths the sentence. The Hebrew is more broken and more urgent: 'My portion: YHWH. I have said. To keep your words.' The speaker puts it on oath, in public.

philological_notes.note: 'My portion, my allotted share', as in the division of the land among the tribes; it recalls the Levites' status. Malbim cites 'I am your portion and your inheritance'.

verses.translation_literal: I have softened your face with [my] whole heart; show me favour according to your saying.
verses.translation_dramatic: With all my heart I have sought your face. Be gracious to me, as you have said you would be.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Face' is the face of a king, whose expression tells the petitioner whether he will live. To 'soften' it (חִלִּיתִי, the idiom behind 'entreat') is to plead until the face turns kind. The Hebrew uses it of Moses at Sinai (Exod 32:11), as Metzudat Zion notes.

The KJV 'thy favour' replaces the 'face' with an abstraction, and BBE's 'given my mind to do your pleasure' reverses the direction: the speaker asks, he does not offer. The next word, חָנֵּנִי, is of the same family as 'grace': 'show me favour'. The petition has a limit and a basis: 'according to your saying', the promise from verse 49. The speaker asks for no more than he has been told to expect.

philological_notes.note: An idiom: 'to entreat the face', literally 'to soften' it. Metzudat Zion compares 'and Moses besought' in Exodus 32.
'Show me favour, be gracious': the request of someone with no claim except God's promise.

verses.translation_literal: I have reckoned my ways, and I have turned back my feet to your testimonies.
verses.translation_dramatic: I took stock of my ways, weighed each one, and then I turned my feet around and set them toward your testimonies.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb חָשַׁב is bookkeeping: it means to calculate, to count the cost. Rashi and Radak take it just so, as weighing the loss of a commandment against its reward and the reward of a sin against its loss. The speaker is not lurching into repentance; he does the sums and walks.

The KJV's 'thought on my ways' is vague, and YLT's 'reckoned' is better. The second verb is וָאָשִׁיבָה, a Hiphil of שׁוּב, 'to turn back': he makes his own feet return, which is the Hebrew word for repentance in action. It is a body image: feet, the part that actually takes the road. Play it as a decision with some weight, not a sudden conversion.

philological_notes.note: 'I reckoned, I calculated'. Rashi and Radak read a weighing of gain against loss.
Hiphil of 'to return': 'I made [my feet] turn back'. The root is the Bible's word for repentance.

verses.translation_literal: I have hurried and have not lingered to keep your commandments.
verses.translation_dramatic: I hurried. I did not linger, did not hesitate: I went to keep your commandments.
verses.directors_commentary:
The stanza closes at a run. After the sober reckoning of verse 59 comes speed: the speaker states the same thing twice, first positively (חַשְׁתִּי, 'I hurried'), then negatively (לֹא הִתְמַהְמָהְתִּי, 'I did not dawdle'). The second verb is itself a stretched-out word, a drawn-out stammer that sounds like what it says, so say it slowly, then cut it off.

The KJV is accurate here ('made haste, and delayed not'). The point is cultural: delay was the risk, since a good intention left until tomorrow often dies. Ibn Ezra cites the saying that the eager hasten to do a commandment. Meiri and Malbim both stress doing it at once, without waiting.

philological_notes.note: Hithpalpel of מהה, 'to linger, hesitate'; the reduplication makes the word itself sound slow. Metzudat Zion compares Habakkuk 2:3.

verses.translation_literal: Ropes of wicked [men] have circled me; your torah I have not forgotten.
verses.translation_dramatic: The ropes of the wicked are drawn around me, loop upon loop, and I stand inside their tightening ring. Yet one thing they have not pulled from me. Your Torah, LORD. I have not let it slip.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play the first half as physical pressure, the second as a held breath. The Hebrew picture is of a net or snare: חֶבֶל is a rope, and the same word can mean a gang or band of people (1 Samuel 10:5, 'a company of prophets') and the pangs of a trapped animal. Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion take it as 'bands of the wicked', a company; Rashi gives 'troops'. The audience would hear all three: ropes, gangs, and pain. Do not choose.

KJV 'have robbed me' follows the old derivation of עִוְּדוּנִי from the 'plunder' in Genesis 49:27 (Menahem, Rashi, Radak, Meiri), but the other reading, 'surrounded', as in YLT and ASV, sits better with ropes. Rashi himself offers a second sense, 'they have multiplied against me'. The line ends on the contrast: ropes around the body, Torah still in the mind. 'Forgotten' in Hebrew memory is about practice as well as recall: to forget the Torah is to stop living by it.

philological_notes.note: Rope, cord; also a band of people and a pang or pain. All three senses are in play. KJV 'bands' keeps the ambiguity partly; BBE 'cords' loses the people.
Probably a Piel from עוד, 'to encircle, surround' (so STEPBible, YLT, ASV). Menahem and Rashi derive it instead from עַד 'prey' (Genesis 49:27) and read 'robbed', which is where KJV gets its word.

verses.translation_literal: [At the] middle of [the] night I rise to give thanks to you, over [the] judgments of your righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: At the very middle of the night, when the world is dark and deaf, I rise. Not from fear. To give you thanks, for your judgments, and for the justice in every one.
verses.directors_commentary:
The actor rises from sleep, not from a bed of fear but of gratitude, and the stage is silent. חֲצוֹת לַיְלָה, 'midnight' or the middle of the night, is the hour of the Exodus (Exodus 12:29) and of Boaz's night (Ruth 3:8); Malbim ties it to the plague of the firstborn, the hour in which the LORD judged. In an age without clocks the night was divided into watches, so 'the middle' marks the very depth of it, the hour when a worker most needs sleep. KJV 'I will rise' makes this a resolution; the Hebrew is simply 'I rise', a habit.

KJV 'righteous judgments' flattens a construct chain: 'judgments of your righteousness', your verdicts of justice. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read them as the verdicts on the wicked, which fits the verse before it; Radak and Meiri read them as the Torah's own rulings. Let the ambiguity sit, because the man gives thanks that the world has a judge.

philological_notes.note: 'Half of the night', a poetic form of חֲצִי. The hour carries the weight of the Exodus night in Malbim's reading.
Hiphil of ידה: 'to give thanks, to confess, to praise', with the hand-gesture sense of the root. 'Thanks' is the English that fits עַל, 'for', that follows.

verses.translation_literal: A companion [am] I to all who fear you, and to those who keep your precepts.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am a companion to every soul that fears you, and to everyone who keeps your charge. Their company is mine.
verses.directors_commentary: After the ropes of the wicked in verse 61 and the lonely midnight thanks of verse 62, the singer says where he belongs. In a village society a person's identity was his circle: kin, fellows, the ones who sit with him at the gate and the table. To be a 'companion' (חָבֵר) is to be bound to others by shared purpose, a partner or associate, and here the circle is defined not by blood but by what its members do and revere. Note the two descriptions: those who 'fear' YHWH, which in biblical Hebrew means reverent loyalty rather than terror, and those who 'keep' his precepts, one an inner attitude and one a practice. The KJV's 'I am a companion of all them that fear thee' is faithful and barely needs mending, though 'of' hides the Hebrew's lamed, 'to, for', which makes the singer's companionship something offered to them. The BBE's 'worshippers' narrows 'those who fear' to cult, and 'who have your orders in their memory' swaps keeping for remembering. Radak takes the line as the counterpart of hating the wicked; Meiri notes that the singer deals with them as a fellow rather than as a superior. Play it warmly and without ceremony. Of my own ear: 'companion' (חָבֵר) and the 'ropes' (חֶבֶל) of verse 61 sound alike, and a hearer may catch the echo of bound-to-the-wicked against bound-to-the-faithful, but the Hebrew does not put the two words on one root.

philological_notes.note: Companion, partner, associate. The word echoes the sound of חֶבֶל, 'rope', in verse 61, and the verses can be heard as a pair, the bond of the wicked set against the company of the faithful. That is a reading of the sound only; the two words are different lemmas.
'Fear' here is reverent loyalty toward YHWH, the posture of those who take him seriously, and is paired with the practice of keeping his precepts.

verses.translation_literal: Your steadfast love, YHWH, the earth is full [of]; your statutes teach me.
verses.translation_dramatic: The whole earth is full of your steadfast love, LORD. Fill me as well: teach me your statutes.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is a hinge. The first half is a wide shot, the whole earth full of YHWH's חֶסֶד, his covenant loyalty; the second half is a close-up on one voice asking for a lesson. The Hebrew opens with 'your steadfast love' and leaves the verb 'is full' to follow, so the sentence leans on the gift before it says what it does, and the earth is the container: 'the earth is full', with love as that of which it is full. A line that says love fills the earth is not the same as one that says the earth is full of love, and the Hebrew gives the second. The KJV's 'the earth, O Lord, is full of thy mercy' is therefore close in structure but reorders it, and 'mercy' is too narrow: חֶסֶד is the faithfulness of one party to a bond, and no single English word carries it. For ancient hearers, the land's rains, harvests and survival were the visible proof of this loyalty, which is why a farming people could speak of the earth as full of it. Ibn Ezra and Radak read the second half as a petition that the same loyalty extend to the singer, as teaching; Metzudat David puts it more sharply, that of all the kindnesses this is the one asked for. The plea 'teach me' (לַמְּדֵנִי) returns in verse 66 and again in verse 68, where 'your statutes' (חֻקֶּיךָ) returns with it, as the strand of the Teth section that asks for instruction. Deliver the first half broad and slow, the second quiet and near.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, steadfast love, the faithfulness proper to a bond. It stands first in the line for emphasis, and KJV 'mercy' narrows it.
Imperative of the intensive stem, 'teach me', with the pronoun suffix. It recurs in verses 66 and 68, and verse 68 pairs it again with 'your statutes'.

verses.translation_literal: Good you have done with your servant, YHWH, according to your word.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have dealt well with your servant, LORD. Good, and good again, just as you said you would.
verses.directors_commentary:
This opens the Teth stanza, and every line of the next eight verses begins with the letter ט, whose first word is טוֹב, 'good'. The verse sets the key: the first word in the line is 'Good'. KJV and its relatives smooth it to 'thou hast dealt well', losing that opening sound; the Hebrew puts 'good' first so the stanza begins with the very word it will repeat.

עֶבֶד, 'servant', is a status word: a person bound to a master's household and under his protection. To be God's servant is to claim both obligation and a claim on his care. כִּדְבָרֶךָ, 'according to your word', is the promise kept: Metzudat David says that no word of his fell to the ground. Radak notes the unusual accent on עַבְדְּךָ and the vocative 'LORD' as a call, which gives the line a breath before the end. Read it as quiet vindication.

philological_notes.note: 'Servant', a dependent in a patron's household, often also used of those who serve a king. The psalmist's claim on God's 'word' rests on that bond.

verses.translation_literal: Goodness of discernment and knowledge teach me, for in your commandments I have trusted.
verses.translation_dramatic: Teach me the goodness of discernment, and of knowledge. For I have put my trust in your commandments.
verses.directors_commentary: The Hebrew begins with the object, 'goodness of discernment and knowledge', and only then the plea, 'teach me', so the singer first names what he wants and then asks for it. The word טַעַם means literally 'taste', the sensation on the tongue, and from there judgment, discernment and, in later Hebrew, the reason behind a thing. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all take it as the rationale of the commandments: the singer already obeys, and now asks to understand why. The sensory point is my own reading: the psalm asks to taste, not only to be told, the way one tastes food to know whether it is good. The KJV's 'good judgment and knowledge' turns 'goodness of' into an adjective, 'good', and so loses the construct chain that makes 'goodness' the thing taught; the YLT keeps it. The second half, 'I have trusted in your commandments', uses the verb behind 'amen' (הֶאֱמָנְתִּי): to trust, to treat as firm. The KJV and ASV's 'believed' is acceptable, but the sense is trust that acts, here that the commandments will hold. In a society where law came as the king's or god's word, and not as something a person argued toward, to ask for the reasons is a bold step, and the psalm makes it from inside loyalty, not from doubt: I trust, and so I want to understand. Meiri says as much: although the singer has already kept them without knowing why, he asks to know. Say it as a request from someone who has already given his trust.

philological_notes.note: Taste of food, then discernment, judgment, reason. The sensory sense is why the literal rendering keeps 'goodness of' with a word that means taste in other contexts; later Hebrew uses it for the reason behind a commandment.
The causative stem of the root behind 'amen' and 'firm'; to hold something as reliable, to trust. The preposition 'in' marks what is trusted: the commandments.

verses.translation_literal: Before I was afflicted I [was] going astray, and now your saying I keep.
verses.translation_dramatic: Before the weight came down on me, I was wandering, off the road and not knowing it. Now I keep your word.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the confession at the centre of the stanza, a plain before-and-after. טֶרֶם אֶעֱנֶה, 'before I was afflicted', uses the verb that returns in verse 71 (עֻנֵּיתִי): the man says the affliction itself was what taught him, and the repeated root makes the two verses a frame. KJV 'I went astray' reads like a single act; the Hebrew has a participle, שֹׁגֵג, 'going astray', a state, wandering without knowing.

The verb is the old crux. Rashi, Radak and Meiri hear אֶעֱנֶה as 'answer, speak, recite' (as in Job's 'answered', Malachi 2:12's 'one who wakes and one who answers'): before I studied aloud in the house of study I was erring. The reading adopted here is 'afflicted', the one the English versions share and the one the repeated root in verse 71 and the theme of the section favour.

Note also אִמְרָה, 'saying' or 'utterance', another of the Torah's names; 'I keep' is the guarding verb שמר.

philological_notes.note: Two roots are possible. ענה II: 'to be afflicted, bowed down' (so the English versions and STEPBible), the same root as עֻנֵּיתִי in verse 71. ענה I: 'to answer, speak, recite', the reading of Rashi, Radak and Meiri's first reading.
To err unwittingly, to stray without intending to. The noun שְׁגָגָה is the technical term for an unintentional offense in Leviticus. Not rebellion but ignorance.

verses.translation_literal: Good [are] you, and doing good; teach me your statutes.
verses.translation_dramatic: You are good, and what you do is good. Teach me your statutes.
verses.directors_commentary:
Short and plain, with two words from the same root. טוֹב אַתָּה, 'you are good', says what God is; וּמֵטִיב, 'and doing good', a Hiphil participle, says what God keeps doing. KJV 'doest good' catches that; BBE 'your works are good' turns the verb into a noun. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David divide the two halves neatly: good without being asked, and doing good to the one who asks. That makes the closing 'teach me your statutes' a prayer that rests on character rather than on merit.

The stanza keeps its refrain here: in verse 64 the same request, חֻקֶּיךָ לַמְּדֵנִי, closed the previous stanza; now it recurs as the answer to the goodness just named. Play it slowly, almost a whisper after verse 67's confession.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil participle of יטב, 'to be good': 'one who does good, makes well'. The Hebrew sets 'good' (טוֹב) and 'doing good' side by side, a being and a deed.

verses.translation_literal: They have smeared falsehood on me, the arrogant; I with all [my] heart guard your precepts.
verses.translation_dramatic: The proud have smeared me with a lie, thick and sticky, and it clings. But I guard your precepts with all my heart.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb טָפְלוּ is the picture: to smear, to plaster on. Rashi and Metzudat Zion link it to Job 14:17, 'you sew up (or smear over) my iniquity', and read 'they have joined, patched together a lie against me'; Metzudat David pushes the image into slander, a false claim that I am not what I seem. KJV 'have forged a lie' keeps the sense of manufacturing but loses the smear. Picture plaster applied to a wall: the lie covers the man's reputation like a coating.

זֵדִים, the 'arrogant', are not merely proud but insolent, people who act against God and others with presumption. The speaker is smeared in public, and his answer is not argument but fidelity: the verb אֶצֹּר means to guard or treasure, to keep as a thing to protect. The pronoun אֲנִי, 'I', stands first in the second half in contrast to 'they'. 'With all heart' is the wholehearted undivided loyalty that Deuteronomy asks for.

philological_notes.note: To smear, plaster over; by extension to attach, patch together a falsehood. Rashi and Metzudat Zion compare Job 14:17, and read it as 'join, compose' against me.
Arrogant, insolent people, those who boil over with presumption against God's order; stronger than ordinary pride.

verses.translation_literal: It has grown thick like the fat, their heart; I — [in] your law I have delighted.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their hearts have thickened over, sealed in fat, dull as a slab of tallow, and nothing gets in. But I, I take my delight in your teaching.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker draws a hard contrast, and the first half is physical. In the Hebrew world fat (חֵלֶב) is the rich, choice part: the portion offered to God, the best of the animal. It is also, as in Isa 6:10 ('make the heart of this people fat'), the image of a heart so coated that nothing reaches it. Metzudat Zion ties the verb טָפַשׁ to exactly that sense, and the Aramaic Targum renders it with the same root. So the 'proud' of the previous verse are not wicked in a cartoon way; they are insensible, stuffed with comfort. Play the line without relish: a contemptuous diagnosis, not a sneer. The KJV's 'as fat as grease' makes the image comic and loses that this is a verb of becoming, 'has grown thick', a slow process. The rare verb occurs only here in the Bible.

Then the pivot: אֲנִי, 'I', stands first in its clause, hard against 'their heart'. Their heart is thick with fat; his delight is in the law. Hebrew puts 'your law' before the verb with no 'in', and English needs one; Radak and Meiri both note the missing ב. The verb שִׁעֲשָׁעְתִּי is a reduplicated form of the root שׁעע, 'to play, delight', the word for a child's fondling, a pleasure that is lively rather than solemn. The KJV's 'I delight in' is fair but flat; this is a man who plays with the law as the others feed on their ease. Radak and Metzudat David read the contrast as one of mind: they cannot understand, but he does.

philological_notes.note: A verb found only here. It means 'to be thick, gross, unfeeling', as fat is thick; the same root gives later Hebrew and Aramaic 'fool' (טפש). Metzudat Zion links it to Isa 6:10, where the people's heart is made fat (הַשְׁמֵן).

A reduplicated (pilpel-type) form of 'to play, to take delight'. Here it is intensive and takes 'your law' directly; English supplies 'in'. Meiri reads it as equal to the reflexive 'I have delighted myself' and Radak notes that תורתך stands for בתורתך.

verses.translation_literal: Good for me that I was afflicted, so that I may learn your statutes.
verses.translation_dramatic: It was good for me, good, that I was brought low. For that is how I learn your statutes.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn of the whole stanza, and one of the hardest lines in the Psalm. 'Good' (טוֹב) is back at the head, and the affliction of verse 67 returns as עֻנֵּיתִי, a Pual: 'I was afflicted', something done to me. So the confession in 67 becomes a thanksgiving. The Hebrew says 'that', not 'because': it is good for me that I was afflicted, with the purpose clause לְמַעַן, 'so that I might learn'. KJV 'that I might learn' keeps both, and the translation is sound; the difficulty is not the grammar but the idea that suffering is a teacher.

The classical commentators divide on what the affliction is. Rashi: the discipline God sent to turn him back. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David: the self-denial of study itself, the effort and toil that wearies the body. Ibn Ezra, more conditionally: if hardships come that make me learn, then they are good. The reading that fits the context is plain: suffering broke his complacency, and the loss became a lesson. Do not play it as a lesson he enjoyed. Play it as a conclusion he arrived at.

philological_notes.note: Pual of ענה II, 'to be afflicted, humbled'. The same root as אֶעֱנֶה in verse 67, which sets 'before affliction' and 'because of affliction' in a frame. Radak and Metzudat David take it of self-affliction in study.

verses.translation_literal: Good for me [is] the torah of your mouth, more than thousands of gold and silver.
verses.translation_dramatic: The Torah from your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold, thousands of silver, heaped and counted.
verses.directors_commentary:
The stanza ends in a sum. תּוֹרַת־פִּיךָ, 'the torah of your mouth', is something spoken: instruction that came out of God's mouth, not a document. KJV 'the law of thy mouth' keeps the phrase, and 'better unto me' keeps the stanza's key word, though it translates טוֹב as 'better' only because of the comparative מִן that follows.

The price is stated in the unit an ancient listener would feel: אַלְפֵי זָהָב וָכָסֶף, 'thousands of gold and silver', counted in shekels or talents, not coins; the Hebrew leaves the unit unsaid, and the cheap mind fills it in with whatever it wants most. Ibn Ezra notes that people afflict themselves for wealth, and so this man, who afflicted himself for Torah (verse 71), has made the better trade. Metzudat David draws the same argument: if people wear themselves out for wealth, how much more should one for Torah.

philological_notes.note: 'Torah of your mouth': instruction spoken by God; the noun תּוֹרָה comes from ירה, 'to throw, to point out, to teach'. Here the Torah is received by ear.
'Thousands of', a bare number with no unit; the Hebrew gives no weight or coin. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read the verse as a contrast with people who afflict themselves for gain.

verses.translation_literal: Your hands made me and established me; give me understanding, and let me learn your commandments.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your hands made me. Your hands set me upright and made me firm. So now give me understanding, and let me learn what you command.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new stanza opens (Yod, the letter that begins ‘your hands’, yadeikha, the first word) and the first word is a body part, the hands of God as a craftsman. The picture is a potter or a builder: ʿasah, ‘make’, then kun, ‘set firmly in place’, as one sets a foundation or a stand. The speaker argues from design: you made me with a mind, so finish the work and let that mind be taught.

KJV ‘fashioned’ is fair for kun but loses the sense of making something stand upright and stable. The Hebrew grammar carries the logic: ‘give me understanding’ is an imperative, and ‘let me learn’ is a cohortative, a wish that follows from the request, so ‘that I may learn’ is right. Radak reads the verse as a whole anatomy of understanding: heart, brain, lungs, tongue and lips, built to receive wisdom. Play the line as a plea from a creature to its maker, not as a boast.

philological_notes.note: Polel of kun: to set something up so that it stands firm, as a foundation or a throne is established. The partner of ‘made me’: made, then settled in place. Ibn Ezra reads it as ‘prepared me to receive understanding’.
Hiphil imperative: cause me to discern. The request is for the ability to see into the commandments, not just to know the list.

verses.translation_literal: Those who fear you, let them see me and let them rejoice, for for your word I have waited.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let those who revere you look at me and be glad. Let them see a man who waited for your word, and did not wait in vain.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has just asked for understanding and now imagines an audience: ‘those who fear you’, the loyal community, whose gladness would confirm that waiting on God pays. The verse is a prayer for vindication seen in public. Ancient honour culture is the background: a person’s fortune was read by neighbours as a verdict on his piety.

There is sound play in the first two words, yereʾeikha yirʾuni, ‘your fearers—may they see me’, two roots (yrʾ ‘fear’ and rʾh ‘see’) that sound almost alike. Fear and sight lock together, and reading aloud should let the echo show. KJV turns the wish into a prediction (‘will be glad when they see me’) and hides that both verbs are wishes. It also renders yiḥalti as ‘hoped in’; the Hebrew has lamed, ‘for/toward’ your word, and the verb is waiting with tension, a rope pulled tight. Rashi’s reading is a mutual one: they are glad because I am like them, one who fears and waits.

philological_notes.note: To wait expectantly, to hope. Refrain word of the psalm (compare 119:81, where it repeats in the next stanza). Metzudat Zion glosses it as qiviti, ‘I have waited’.
A participle used as a noun: ‘your fearers’, the standing label of the pious in the Psalms, a community and not just individuals.

verses.translation_literal: I have known, YHWH, that righteousness are your judgments, and [in] faithfulness you have afflicted me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I know it, LORD. I know your judgments are right, and I know that even this, even the weight of your hand on me, you laid on me in faithfulness.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the heart of the stanza, and the actor should not rush the first two words. יָדַעְתִּי יְהוָה: 'I know, YHWH', a knowledge reached through suffering, not offered as a theory. Radak says he understood it from the law and then confirmed it by looking back over what he had endured: God is a God of faithfulness without wrong. The tone is neither bitter nor sweet; it is acceptance with open eyes.

The Hebrew puts 'righteousness' (צֶדֶק) first, as a bare noun predicate: 'righteousness are your judgments', not 'your judgments are righteous' as the KJV, ASV and YLT have it, and certainly not 'are right' (KJV, Webster), which pales into mere correctness. A מִשְׁפָּט is a verdict, a legal ruling, so the speaker is conceding the case before the court of God. The second clause has the word 'faithfulness' with no preposition: וֶאֱמוּנָה עִנִּיתָנִי. English needs 'in', and Radak and Meiri both note the missing ב. The KJV does supply it ('in faithfulness'), and this is a place where it is right to; BBE's 'unchanging faith' is a loose gloss that turns אֱמוּנָה (steadiness, reliability) into a creed.

The verb עִנִּיתָנִי is the same root as 'I was afflicted' in verse 71, the same hand and the same word. Rashi's short comment, בְּדִין, 'justly', gives the plainest reading: the affliction was lawful and in order. Malbim goes further and reads it as a purposeful refining of the speaker, but that is his interpretation, not the text's. Ibn Ezra adds the observation that it happened many times.

philological_notes.note: 'Righteousness', in the sense of what is lawful, in order, right in a court. As predicate it is placed before the subject, so it carries the stress: 'righteousness are your judgments'. Not just 'correct'.

'And faithfulness', reliability, steadiness. It stands without a preposition where English needs 'in'; Radak glosses it 'as if באמונה' and Meiri says the ב is missing. The sense is adverbial: God afflicted him faithfully, in keeping with his own character.
'You have afflicted me': the piel of ענה, to bring low, humble, oppress; the same root as 'ʿunneiti' in verse 71. The same word stands for both the experience and the God who sent it.

verses.translation_literal: Let your covenant loyalty be, please, to comfort me, according to your word to your servant.
verses.translation_dramatic: Now, I beg you, let your steadfast love be my comfort, as you promised your servant.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the confession of 119:75 comes the request, and the little word naʾ, ‘please’, turns a demand into a plea. ‘Let your ḥesed be’: ḥesed is covenant loyalty, the commitment of the stronger party who has bound himself, which is why KJV ‘merciful kindness’ is soft and Latinate where the Hebrew is about faithfulness to a bond. It is the second half of the pair: you were faithful in affliction (emunah), now be loyal in comfort (ḥesed).

The verb naḥam, ‘comfort’, can also mean to be moved to relent; the speaker asks for both consolation and a change in what God is doing. ‘According to your word’ anchors it in a promise already made. Metzudat David connects the promise to David and Nathan; that reading is his, and the Hebrew itself says only ‘to your servant’.

philological_notes.note: Loyalty owed within a bond, kindness that keeps a promise. Not generic mercy: it presupposes a covenant. See HALOT.
Piel infinitive: to comfort me. Radak ties it to the affliction of the previous verse (‘from my suffering’).

verses.translation_literal: Let your compassions come to me, and I will live, for your torah [is] my delights.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let your compassion come to me, and I shall live. Your torah is my delight, the thing I play with and love.
verses.directors_commentary:
Raḥamim, ‘compassions’, is a plural built on reḥem, the womb. The picture is a mother’s gut-level care for her child, which is why KJV ‘tender mercies’ is better than most renderings; it keeps the tenderness, though the womb is gone. The speaker’s need is stated plainly: ‘and I will live’. He does not mean only escape from death. After the affliction he is hollowed out, and only this will restore him.

The verse ends with an unusual plural, shaʿashuʿai, ‘my delights’. The root is the one used of a child dandled and played with (Jer 31:20 calls Ephraim a yeled shaʿashuʿim, a darling child). So the torah is not a burden or a legal code to him, but something he plays with. KJV ‘my delight’ flattens the plural. ‘Tender mercies’ and ‘delights’ answer each other: God’s tenderness toward him, his tenderness toward God’s torah.

philological_notes.note: Plural of intensity from reḥem, the womb; compassion of the kind a mother feels. KJV ‘tender mercies’ has the right feel.
Plural noun: delights, things one plays with and enjoys. The root is used of a child at play (Isa 11:8, Jer 31:20). Radak and Ibn Ezra stress that the torah is the one delight he has.

verses.translation_literal: Let the insolent be ashamed, for [with] falsehood they have twisted me; I, I will meditate on your precepts.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the proud be put to shame. They bent me out of shape with lies. But I, as for me, I will turn your precepts over in my mind and say them quietly to myself.
verses.directors_commentary:
The stanza turns on a hard contrast: the insolent (zedim, those who boil over in arrogance) and ‘I’. The pronoun is stated, ʾani, though the verb would carry it, so play it with weight: as for me. The insolent ‘twisted’ the speaker (ʿivvetuni, from ʿavat, to bend crooked, as of a crooked scale or a perverted verdict). It is a legal image: they have bent his case with sheker, a lie. KJV ‘without a cause’ turns the lie into something vaguer, and ASV ‘overthrown’ and BBE ‘given decision against’ pick different halves of a picture of a case judged crookedly.

Rashi reads this through a Talmudic story (Sanhedrin 107a) about David and a trick question put to him by flatterers, with adultery as its subject; I report it and do not rely on it. The answer to lies is not a counter-attack but sicha, ‘meditation’, a word that really means to speak, murmur and talk over, so the speaker mutters the precepts under his breath. Note the repeated root of shame: yevoshu now and ʾevosh in 119:80, the shame he pushes onto them and refuses for himself.

philological_notes.note: Piel of ʿavat: to bend, make crooked, pervert. Used of perverting justice. Metzudat Zion connects it to ʿavon, ‘iniquity’, which is a different reading: they charged me with guilt. I keep ‘twisted’.
To muse, talk to oneself, murmur; the same root gives the noun for a complaint or musing. ‘Meditate’ is a little too quiet: it is aloud, under the breath.
The insolent: those who seethe and act in defiance. KJV ‘proud’ is right but lighter than the Hebrew.

verses.translation_literal: Let those who fear you turn to me, and the knowers of your testimonies.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let those who revere you come back to me, those who know what you have testified.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has lost his standing: the pious have withdrawn from him while the insolent slandered him. Yashuvu li, ‘let them turn to me’, is a plea that they come back, that they take his side again. Both Rashi and Radak report a rabbinic tradition of the great court (Sanhedrin) leaving David after his sin with Bathsheba, and read the verse as his request for them to return. That is a later reading of the verse, not something the Hebrew says.

Two groups are named, the God-fearers (a name for the loyal community) and ‘the knowers of your testimonies’, the learned. The text is a plain wish with no ‘and they shall know’ conditional. KJV ‘those that have known’ turns the participle into a past tense, and ASV ‘and they shall know’ follows the written text (Ketiv), a verb rather than a participle. Our reading follows the traditional reading (Qere). The ‘testimonies’ (ʿedot) are the stipulations of the covenant that witness against and for its parties.

philological_notes.note: Written ידעו, ‘and they know’, but read as a participle ‘and the knowers of’ (Qere). The Qere is followed here; ASV renders the written text.
‘Your testimonies’: the covenant stipulations that stand as witness.

verses.translation_literal: May my heart be whole in your statutes, so that I will not be ashamed.
verses.translation_dramatic: May my heart be whole in your statutes, without crack or flaw, so that I am never put to shame.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last verse of the Yod stanza closes the circle with shame. In 119:78 the speaker asked that the insolent be ashamed (yevoshu); here he asks that he himself not be (ʾevosh). The same root, the same stakes. In this world shame is public failure, exposure that your trust was misplaced.

Tamim, ‘whole’, is the word for an animal fit for the altar, without blemish, and for a person undivided in loyalty. KJV ‘sound’ is acceptable but loses the sacrificial colour. ‘Heart’ is the whole inner person, mind and will, not the feelings. The statutes (ḥuqqim) are the ‘engraved’ ones, rulings that have no explanation attached; Malbim says that is exactly where a divided heart would hesitate and then be embarrassed before the nations, so a whole heart is the answer. That is his reading. ASV has the next letter’s heading ‘KAPH’ glued to the end of this verse; it is not part of the text.

philological_notes.note: Complete, whole, without defect: the word for an unblemished sacrificial animal and for a person of undivided integrity.
Statutes, from ‘to engrave, to prescribe’. Malbim stresses that these are the laws whose reason is not given.

verses.translation_literal: My soul is spent for your salvation; for your word I have waited.
verses.translation_dramatic: My soul is worn to nothing, straining after your rescue. And still I wait for your word.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new stanza (Kaph): every verse from here begins with kaf, and this one begins with kalta, ‘it is finished, used up’. The verb is kalah, to come to an end, and the mood is exhausted longing. It is the verb of a throat that has called until there is no voice left and of eyes that have strained until they fail (119:82). KJV ‘fainteth’ is warm but modern readers hear a swoon; the Hebrew is closer to ‘is used up’, ‘is spent’. Rashi and Meiri gloss it as longing, like Ps 84:3.

Nefesh, ‘soul’, is literally throat, appetite, the self that needs; it is the hunger of a person starving for rescue. The second line is the pivot: ‘but’ is not in the Hebrew, the two clauses sit side by side. Spent and waiting go together. Yiḥalti repeats from 119:74 and points back to the Yod stanza’s hope.

philological_notes.note: To be finished, spent, to pine away. Rashi and Metzudat Zion gloss it as longing (iwwta, taʾawah); the repetition of the verb in the next verse makes a chain.
Throat, appetite, self; the speaker’s whole needy being.

verses.translation_literal: My eyes are spent for your word, saying: When will you comfort me?
verses.translation_dramatic: My eyes grow weary looking for your promise. And all the while I ask, how long? When will you comfort me?
verses.directors_commentary:
The same verb opens the verse: kalu, ‘they are spent’. In 119:81 it was the soul; now it is the eyes. The listener hears the exhaustion move from the unseen to the visible, as Ibn Ezra notes. Eyes that strain for rescue, scanning the horizon, were an idiom: ‘eyes that fail’ (Deut 28:32, as Metzudat Zion notes). It is the posture of a watchman, a sick man or someone waiting at a door.

ʾImrah is a spoken word, a saying, a promise, a different word from dabar in 119:81; KJV and the rest render both ‘word’, which hides the shift. Then the speaker turns the sentence into direct speech: lemor, ‘saying’, and the question matay, ‘when?’, the cry of the lament psalms. No answer is given. Leave the silence after it. The question comes back in 119:84.

philological_notes.note: ‘My eyes are spent’: the idiom of eyes that fail from looking and waiting too long. Metzudat Zion cites Deut 28:32.
‘For your saying’: a spoken promise. Ibn Ezra glosses it as gezeratkha, your decree; Radak and Meiri read it as hatavatkha, your promise.

verses.translation_literal: For I have become like a wineskin in smoke; your decrees I have not forgotten.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have hung so long in the smoke that I am cured like leather, blackened, shrunken, hard. And still your decrees have not slipped from me.
verses.directors_commentary:
A נֹאד is a skin bag, usually goatskin, that held wine or water; hung in a tent or house, it sat near the cooking fire, and the smoke dried it, blackened it and wrinkled it. Rashi says exactly this: a leather skin that dries out in smoke. Ibn Ezra and Radak apply the picture to the speaker's own skin, shrivelled and dry; Meiri adds that it is 'from the weight of his troubles'. Play it as a body worn down, not as a man who has lost his mind. The word קִיטוֹר is smoke or vapour, as in the smoke of the furnace over Sodom (Gen 19:28), which Metzudat Zion cites.

The KJV says 'bottle', which a modern reader hears as glass; the Hebrew is a skin. The KJV also puts 'yet do I not forget' as a concession; the Hebrew has just a flat verb, 'your decrees I have not forgotten', with the object placed first for emphasis. The decrees are what he holds on to while everything else shrinks.

philological_notes.note: A skin container for liquids, wine or water. Its shrinking in smoke is the image: it loses its suppleness and shape.
Smoke, vapour that rises from burning; the same word as in Gen 19:28. The root is קטר, 'to go up in smoke'.

verses.translation_literal: How many [are] the days of your servant? When will you do, against my pursuers, judgment?
verses.translation_dramatic: How many days does your servant have left? How many? And when, LORD, when will you bring justice down on the men who hunt me?
verses.directors_commentary:
Two questions, with no answer between them. The first is a lament about time: kamah yemei, ‘how many are the days’, meaning how few. It is the arithmetic of a man who thinks his life is running out before the verdict comes. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as fear that he will die before he sees justice; Meiri reads it as: my time is short, so act now. Malbim hears the opposite edge: surely you must judge while I am alive.

Then ‘when?’ again (matay, as in 119:82). The speaker asks God to ‘do judgment’ (ʿasah mishpat), the same noun mishpat that was ‘your judgments’ in 119:75, so what he asked as a believer (your judgments are right) he now asks as a victim: let them be carried out on those who chase me. Rodfai, ‘my pursuers’, is a hunting word. KJV ‘persecute’ is a church word: the Hebrew is the chase of an animal. A cry like this belongs to the oppressed, not to a man wanting revenge for its own sake: in a world with no police, God is the only court of appeal.

philological_notes.note: ‘How many are the days of your servant?’ A rhetorical question about how short a life is. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as a fear of dying before justice arrives.
‘Those who chase me’: a participle of radaf, to pursue, as a hunter or a soldier does. The preposition be- gives ‘upon’ or ‘against’.

verses.translation_literal: They have dug for me, the arrogant, pits, which are not according to your law.
verses.translation_dramatic: The proud have been digging, digging for me, and what they dig is deep, and the law you gave has no place in it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The pit is the hunter's trap: a hole dug in the path and covered, to catch an animal or a man. 'Dug for me' means it is prepared for one man in particular. Radak and Meiri read it as a figure for counsel and schemes against him, plots laid with no justice in them; Metzudat David says the same, 'they planned evil plans against me'. The arrogant, זֵדִים, are not mere bullies but people who act as though no law binds them.

The word שִׁיחוֹת is spelled with a yod; Meiri and Radak explain it as a by-form of שׁוּחוֹת, 'pits', which Metzudat Zion glosses as 'holes' and ties to Psalm 57:7. The final clause, אֲשֶׁר לֹא כְתוֹרָתֶךָ, is terse: 'which are not like your Torah'. The KJV's 'which are not after thy law' is faithful in sense; note that the relative clause may attach to the pits or to the men, and Ibn Ezra and Radak connect it to what the Torah forbids: shedding innocent blood.

philological_notes.note: A by-form of שׁוּחוֹת, 'pits', from the root שׁוח, 'to sink, to dig down'. The yod spelling is explained by Radak and Meiri.
The arrogant: those who act presumptuously, boiling over against law and against others.

verses.translation_literal: All your commandments are faithfulness; with falsehood they have pursued me; help me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Everything you have commanded can be trusted. They hunt me with a lie. Help me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse has three beats, and the last is a single word: עָזְרֵנִי, 'help me', the one-word prayer. Everything before it is argument; this is the cry. Play the first clause calm and the last as a breaking of the voice.

On the middle clause the commentators split. Rashi and Radak take שֶׁקֶר as 'in vain, for nothing', that is, my enemies pursue me without cause. Metzudat David says they claim zeal for God's commandments but their real purpose is falsehood against him. The pursuit (רָדַף) is the verb of a hunter after prey, and also of an army after a fleeing enemy.

The KJV 'faithful' turns a noun into an adjective; the Hebrew says the commandments are אֱמוּנָה, 'faithfulness' itself, not merely reliable. The KJV also has 'wrongfully', which flattens שֶׁקֶר, 'a lie', into an adverb of unfairness.

philological_notes.note: Firmness, reliability, faithfulness; the commandments are not just trustworthy but made of it. The same word returns in verse 90 for God's own faithfulness.
Falsehood, a lie, also 'for nothing, without cause'. It is placed first in its clause, so the stress falls on the lie.

verses.translation_literal: Like a little, they had finished me on the earth; and I, I did not forsake your precepts.
verses.translation_dramatic: A breath more, a hair's breadth, and they would have ended me, here on the earth. But I did not let go of your precepts. Not even then.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Like a little' (kim'at) is the Hebrew way of saying 'within a little' or 'almost': the gap between life and death is measured by something very small. The KJV 'They had almost consumed me' reads well, but 'consumed' is too decorative; the verb kalah is the plain word for finishing, using something up, bringing it to an end. 'On the earth' matters too: it is not the grave that is in view but the ordinary stage of ordinary life, the only place a person can keep a precept. The second half turns on a pronoun: 'and I' stands alone, and the speaker's refusal is placed against the opponents' near success. Radak and Meiri hear a stronger claim in the last clause: he could have taken revenge and did not, because the precepts forbade shedding blood. That is an interpretation, not something the Hebrew says. In a world with no police and no court of appeal, a man who has been hunted for years would normally strike first.

philological_notes.note: 'Almost, within a little'; literally 'like a little'. The idiom makes the escape very narrow.
'Your precepts'; the word is used only in the Psalms and belongs to the vocabulary of this chapter's eight synonyms for torah. The spelling here has a vav as a vowel letter.

verses.translation_literal: According to your covenant loyalty make me live, and let me keep the testimony of your mouth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give me life, as your faithful love has always given it, and I will keep what your own mouth has spoken.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the close of the kaf stanza and it is a petition, not a bargain. The measure of the request is chesed, covenant loyalty, which is a word of relationship, not of feeling: it is what a party to a covenant owes the other. The KJV 'Quicken me after thy lovingkindness' is a fine English of 1611, but 'quicken' now means speed up, not give life, and 'lovingkindness' is Coverdale's coinage, not a plain Hebrew idea. The verb is the causative 'make me live', in the sense of preserve and revive someone who is nearly dead (see the previous verse). The vow that follows is a wish, a cohortative: 'and let me keep'. It is not a condition (KJV 'so shall I'); life is asked for in order that obedience may continue. 'The testimony of your mouth' is the commandment as spoken, with the word 'mouth' keeping it an oral, personal thing rather than a written code. Metzudat David notes that the request does not rest on merit.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, faithful love. A duty of relationship that God freely takes on; hence the request is made on his character, not on the speaker's merit.
'The testimony of your mouth': what God has solemnly declared, spoken rather than only written.

verses.translation_literal: Forever, YHWH, your word stands firm in the heavens.
verses.translation_dramatic: Forever, O LORD. Your word is fixed in the heavens, planted there like a pillar that no one can move.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new letter, lamed, and a new scale: the poet lifts his eyes from his enemies to the sky. The verse begins with לְעוֹלָם, 'forever', before the divine name, so that the first sound is duration. נִצָּב is the Niphal of the root for standing: a thing set upright and left there, as a standing pillar or a garrison posted at a post.

Ibn Ezra reads it plainly: 'your decrees stand in heaven'. Metzudat David adds a point about astrology: even if the courses of the heavens and the constellations point to evil or good, the decree of God's word stands in the heavens and cancels what they indicate. That would be a pointed thing to say in a world where Babylonian and Greek astrologers read fate in the stars. Radak links the 'word' to the creative command, 'the word you spoke for the heavens to be'.

The KJV 'settled' is a gentle, domestic word for a verb that means 'set upright and fixed'; BBE's 'fixed' is closer. Note the divine name is placed between 'forever' and 'your word', so the line is almost addressed in two breaths.

philological_notes.note: Niphal participle of נצב, 'to be set up, to stand upright'. A standing thing, fixed in place.
'Your word', which Radak reads as the creative command by which the heavens came to be.

verses.translation_literal: To generation and generation [is] your faithfulness; you set the earth firm, and it stands.
verses.translation_dramatic: From one generation to the next, your faithfulness. You set the earth in its place, and it stands.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two verbs frame אֶרֶץ: כּוֹנַנְתָּ before it, וַתַּעֲמֹד after it. You set it; it stands. The earth is the proof of the claim in the first half: what God established, endures, with nothing holding it up but his act. Say 'earth' in the middle with weight.

The idiom לְדֹר וָדֹר, 'to generation and generation', is Hebrew's way of saying 'without end'; it is not a count. אֱמוּנָתְךָ takes up אֱמוּנָה of verse 86 and now it belongs to God himself. Metzudat David notes that this faithfulness holds 'even though the course of the heavens indicate change', continuing the point of verse 89.

The KJV 'abideth' is archaic; the verb is simply 'stands', as in verse 91 where the same root עמד is used of the creatures who 'stand' ready. Ibn Ezra adds a cosmological note, that the earth is the central point of the sphere; I leave that to the reader as one medieval reading.

philological_notes.note: Polel of כון, 'to establish, make firm'; the verb of founding the earth, often used of God's creation.
'And it stands': the earth takes the stance God gave it. The same root returns in verse 91.

verses.translation_literal: For your judgments they stand this day, for the whole [is] your servants.
verses.translation_dramatic: Today, still, they stand at their posts to carry out your judgments, for everything that is serves you.
verses.directors_commentary: 'They' is not named, and the sentence is built on that silence. Because it follows two verses about heavens and earth, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read it as the heavens and the earth, standing like servants awaiting orders; Malbim hears a challenge in it: if heaven and earth are ready now, why does God wait to judge the wicked? The KJV 'They continue this day according to thine ordinances' turns a posture into an abstract continuing. The verb is 'stand', the same as in the last verse ('it stands'), and this repeated root is the thread of the stanza: things stand because he stands behind them. 'This day' (hayom) is not 'today' in a vague sense; it is the day of speaking, the present, and the same word the psalmist uses elsewhere for the day when God's voice is heard. 'The whole' (hakol) is a bold word: all that exists is one household of servants, an image from the world of kings and their courts, where a servant stood to attention and waited for the command. In a culture where servants belonged to a master, to call all things God's servants is to say that nothing is outside his rule.

philological_notes.note: 'They stand'; the posture of a servant awaiting orders. It repeats the root of ותעמד in verse 90.
'The whole, everything'; the unnamed subject of the verse is all creation.

verses.translation_literal: Had your law not been my delights, then I would have perished in my affliction.
verses.translation_dramatic: If your law had not been my delight, I would have gone under then, in the depths of my affliction.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a contrary-to-fact sentence: לוּלֵי, 'if not', then אָז אָבַדְתִּי, 'then I would have perished'. The poet speaks from the far side of the danger. The plural שַׁעֲשֻׁעַי is intense: not 'my delight' but 'my delights', the thing he plays with and is amused by; the word is used elsewhere of a beloved child (Jer 31:20) and of wisdom's joy at creation (Prov 8:30). Whether the Hebrew is meant to carry that sense here is my reading. The Targum has פִּרְנוּקֵי, which I read as 'my delight, my pampering'; it is not evidence for a child image.

The KJV 'delights' keeps the plural, which is good. But 'I should then have perished' is heavy and archaic. עֳנִי is 'affliction, poverty, humiliation'. Radak says the law comforted him so he did not perish of grief; Metzudat David asks how the law, which might seem to tire a man, could strengthen one caught in poverty's ropes, and answers that only the word of the King overrides nature.

philological_notes.note: Plural of a reduplicated noun, 'delights, amusements'; it expresses play and tenderness, not duty.
Affliction, poverty, humbling. The same root as the 'afflicted' of this psalm.

verses.translation_literal: For ever I will not forget your precepts, for by them you have made me live.
verses.translation_dramatic: Never will I forget your precepts. They are how you gave me life.
verses.directors_commentary: The reason clause says it all: 'for by them you have made me live'. This links the verse to verse 88, where he asked for life, and to verse 92, where he said he would have perished. In Hebrew the key verb is the same, chayah, the causative 'make alive'. Here it is a completed act, a perfect: it has already happened. The KJV 'quickened' is an obsolete word and has the problem noted earlier. 'Forget' in biblical Hebrew means to cease to act on something, not only to lose it from memory, so the vow is a vow of loyalty and practice: 'I will never put them aside'. Radak and Meiri read the verse as an answer to 'then I would have perished': because the precepts saved me, I will never let go of them.

philological_notes.note: 'I will forget'; in biblical idiom, to forget is to neglect, to stop acting on. So the vow is about practice, not memory.

verses.translation_literal: Yours [am] I; save me, for your precepts I have sought.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am yours. Save me. I have gone looking for your precepts all my days.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two words לְךָ־אֲנִי are joined by a maqqef and mean 'to you [belong] I': a claim of ownership, the language of a servant to his master. Radak says it directly: 'your servant', and a master saves his own servant, as one who owns a man protects what is his. Metzudat David turns the line to the poet's gaze: his eyes hang on God to save him.

The plea is short, three beats: I am yours; save me; here is why. The reason is not merit but pursuit: דָּרַשׁ means to seek out, to inquire, the verb of one who goes to a prophet or an oracle for an answer. He has sought the precepts as one would seek a ruling.

The KJV 'I am thine' reads well and is accurate; it loses only the word order, in which 'yours' comes first, stressing whose he is. הוֹשִׁיעֵנִי is the Hiphil of יָשַׁע, from which the name Joshua comes.

philological_notes.note: 'I have sought, inquired after': seeking out with effort, as one consults an oracle or studies a text.
Hiphil imperative of ישע, 'to save, to deliver'; the root of the name Yeshua/Joshua.

verses.translation_literal: For me the wicked have waited, to destroy me; your testimonies I will consider carefully.
verses.translation_dramatic: The wicked are lying in wait for me, ready to destroy me. And I? I turn my mind to your testimonies, and I weigh them.
verses.directors_commentary: The grammar sets two actors facing each other. 'For me' stands first: the wicked wait for him specifically. The verb qiwu is the verb of hope, the same root as 'those who wait for the LORD' (Isa 40:31), twisted here to mean the hope of the wicked, who wait for his fall as one waits for a rain or a harvest. The KJV 'waited for me' hides this reversal. Their purpose is 'to destroy me', which links to the verb 'perished' in verse 92 and puts the two verses side by side: he nearly perished; they wanted him to. In reply, the speaker does not act against them. He will 'consider carefully' (etbonan, from binah, discernment) the testimonies. This is a decision to think rather than to strike back, and it is a contrast between active waiting and wise reflection. The same word 'testimonies' recalls verse 88, 'the testimony of your mouth'. Meiri and Metzudat David add that the plot was also to keep him from study.

philological_notes.note: 'They have waited, hoped'; the usual word for hope in God, used ironically of the wicked who await the speaker's ruin.
'I will consider carefully'; a reflexive stem of binah, discernment. It means to study something attentively, not only to look at it.

verses.translation_literal: To every perfection I have seen an end; broad [is] your commandment, exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have walked to the edge of everything that calls itself perfect, and I have seen where it stops. Every one of them has a rim, a last wall. But your commandment? It stretches out wide, wide beyond my seeing.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker sets two measures side by side: things that have a limit, and a commandment that has none. Say it as a discovery, not a boast. He has tested every claim to completeness and found its edge, and now he turns, almost surprised, to something he cannot reach the edge of. In the stanza that precedes this (vv.85-87), the proud dig pits and pursue him because 'all your commandments are faithful'; Malbim reads this verse as the answer to that charge, so the 'broad' commandment is also a defence.

The KJV's 'an end of all perfection' is close, but 'perfection' hides how odd the Hebrew is. Tiklâ occurs only here, and the old readers disagree on it: Meiri takes it as 'longing, desire' and hears a verse about every desire being satisfied and finally ending, while Rashi and Radak hear 'completion, limit' (Radak: the extent to which I have grasped their purpose). Qēṣ, 'end', can be the start or the finish of a span, as Ibn Ezra notes with 'from the end (miqqēṣ) of seven years'. The commandment is 'broad' (rĕḥābâ), a word for open space, as for a wide field or a street. For the ancient listener, a wide place is room to move without being hemmed in; the commandment is not a narrow ledge.

philological_notes.note: A word found only here. Read as 'completion, perfection, limit' (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat David) or as 'longing' (Meiri, comparing 2 Sam 13:39 wayĕkal Dāwid, 'David longed'). The KJV 'perfection' picks the first sense without saying there is a choice.
'Broad, spacious', said of the singular commandment (miṣwâ). Radak says the singular is a collective for all the commandments together.

verses.translation_literal: How I have loved your torah! All the day it [is] my meditation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Oh, how I love your teaching! It never leaves me. All day long it is on my lips and in my mind, the thing I turn over and speak of aloud.
verses.directors_commentary: The Mem stanza opens on a cry rather than a claim: māh is an exclamation, "how!", and the actor should let it break out before the sentence settles. The KJV's "O how love I" is a fair echo of the Hebrew's inverted order, but "meditation" has since become a word for silent, seated stillness. Śîḥâ is nearer to murmured speech, musing aloud, even complaint (the same root is used for Hannah's praying and for a person's chatter). The speaker is not sitting in a quiet corner; the torah is going round and round in their mouth all day, which is how ancient readers learned a text by heart. Malbim presses the point: even idle talk, he says, is only about torah. Note that "all the day" (kol-hayyôm) is a plain Hebrew idiom for "constantly", not a literal twelve hours.

philological_notes.note: 'Meditation' here is audible musing, talk turned over and over; the root can also mean complaint or conversation. It returns in verse 99, tying the two verses together.

verses.translation_literal: More than my enemies it makes me wise, your commandments, for to forever it [belongs] to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: My enemies are clever. But your commandments make me wiser than they are, and no one can take that wisdom from me, for it is mine for ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
He is not boasting of his own brains. The enemies of this psalm are the proud who dig pits for him (v.85), and he says the commandments, not his wit, put him ahead of them. Play the line quiet and settled: the argument is not yet over, but he knows how it ends.

The grammar is the interesting part. The verb is feminine singular, 'it makes me wise', yet its subject, 'your commandments', is plural and arrives after the verb. The verb leads, and the plural noun follows it like a name added to a pronoun. The KJV and ASV smooth this over to 'thou through thy commandments hast made me wiser' and 'they are ever with me', so the second clause becomes a plural 'they' where the Hebrew says a singular 'it', hî. The sages do not agree on what the singular means: Ibn Ezra and Meiri say 'each one of your commandments', as the plural 'foal of she-asses' names a single colt in Zech 9:9 (Meiri's example; Ibn Ezra's is 'daughters stepped over the wall', Gen 49:22); Radak says the whole body of the commandments. Rashi, citing the Talmud (Sotah 21a), hears Doeg and Ahithophel, two wise men whose learning the law outstripped. 'For ever' (lĕʿôlām) gives the second clause its point: enemies come and go, but the commandment is his possession for good, as Malbim also says.

philological_notes.note: A feminine singular verb with a plural subject that follows it. The Piel of ḥākam is causative, 'makes me wise'. Ibn Ezra and Meiri read the verb as agreeing with 'each one' of the commandments.

verses.translation_literal: More than all my teachers I have gained insight, for your testimonies [are] a meditation to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have learned more than all those who taught me, and why? Because your testimonies are what I turn over in my mind, again and again.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse is easy to play as arrogance, and that would be wrong. The reason follows at once: his teachers gave him what they had, and the testimonies, which he mutters over day and night, taught him the rest. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David both say he learned from all of them, and that it was through their teaching that he came to speak the testimonies, so the verse is gratitude as well as boast.

The KJV 'I have more understanding than all my teachers' is a fair sense, but it turns the verb into a possession ('I have more'). The Hebrew is a comparison of action, 'from all my teachers I have gained insight', and Meiri hears 'from each one of them I learned'. Śîḥâ ('meditation') is murmured, half-spoken thought; he does not read the testimonies silently but talks them over. The ancient school was oral, and a student who 'had' the text was one who could say it.

philological_notes.note: The plural of ʿēdût, 'testimony', from the root ʿwd 'to bear witness, to repeat'; here the written form carries the vav that marks the long vowel. It is a different noun from ʿēdâ, 'assembly', which has the root יעד.
Hiphil of śākal, 'to gain insight, to act with understanding'. The sense is of insight that results in good conduct, which is why Ibn Ezra links it to his constant study.

verses.translation_literal: More than elders I understand, for your precepts I have kept.
verses.translation_dramatic: Even the old and grey I outstrip in understanding. For your precepts are what I have kept, guarded like a flame.
verses.directors_commentary: The third boast, and the boldest: elders were the ancient world's archive of wisdom, and to claim understanding beyond theirs is to say the torah is a deeper well than experience. The KJV's "ancients" is a dated English word for the old; the Hebrew zĕqēnîm are simply "elders", the men who sat at the gate and decided cases. The speaker's reason is a kept commandment, not a clever mind: the verb nāṣar means to guard, to keep watch over (the same root is used of a fortress or a vineyard watchman), so the line has a protective, almost military tone. Radak makes a neat distinction: the speaker kept the precepts first as inherited tradition and then through study. Malbim points out that even elders, with all their experience, cannot reach certainty about the past without the precepts. Notice the shift of tense: "I understand" is an imperfect verb, and "I have kept" a perfect: the understanding is ongoing and rests on obedience already done.

philological_notes.note: To guard, watch over, protect (as of a city or vine). The image is of keeping something safe, not merely obeying it.
The hithpolel of bîn, 'to show oneself discerning, to gain understanding by looking closely'. It returns in verse 104.

verses.translation_literal: From every evil path I have restrained my feet, so that I may keep your word.
verses.translation_dramatic: I held my feet back. From every road that bends toward harm, I held them back, so that I could keep your word.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image is physical: he locks his own feet away from certain roads. The verb kālāʾ means to shut up, to hold in prison, and the feet are the prisoner. It is the same verb used when the rain was 'restrained' in Genesis 8:2, as Metzudat Zion notes, and when Abigail hears David say that God had 'restrained' him from shedding blood (1 Sam 25:33), the parallel Rashi cites. The KJV's 'refrained my feet' is a good sense, but it lets the prison language go; 'refrained' sounds like a choice not to walk, while the Hebrew pictures a lock.

The KJV also renders ʾōraḥ ('path') as 'way', the same word it uses for derek, so the English reader cannot see that this psalm uses two words. Malbim says ʾōraḥ is the narrower word, a footpath smaller than a road: he does not only avoid the main road of evil, but even the small, private paths. Ibn Ezra and Radak add that his motive was not fear of consequences but 'to keep your word'. The purpose clause (lĕmaʿan, 'so that') makes that motive explicit: he restrains his feet for the sake of the keeping.

philological_notes.note: 'I shut up, restrained'; the same verb as 'the rain was restrained' (Gen 8:2). The sense is of confinement, not mere abstention.
'Path'. In this verse it is absolute and takes the adjective rāʿ, 'evil'; in v.104 it is construct, 'path of falsehood'. Malbim reads it as a smaller track than derek.

verses.translation_literal: From your judgments I have not turned aside, for you, you have taught me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have not turned away from your judgments, not once. You yourself were the one who taught me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reason he gives is not 'I am loyal' but 'you taught me'. The emphasis falls on the pronoun: 'for you, you' (kî-ʾattâ). Say it with the weight on the teacher. He does not claim to have found the path by his own wit; the one he is accountable to is the one who showed it.

The verb hôrētānî comes from yārâ, the same root as tôrâ, 'instruction'. The pun is not carried in English: 'you have taught me' hides that he is saying 'you have 'torah-ed' me'. The KJV 'for thou hast taught me' is sound, and the Hebrew perfect fits it; the ASV and YLT also keep the perfect. Radak offers a second sense, 'you helped me keep them' (by opening the way), and Metzudat Zion simply glosses it as 'teaching'.

Malbim reads the verse as a claim about law. Though the judgments are rational ordinances, and a person might sometimes think he could judge a matter by his own reasoning, the speaker says he did not turn aside to judge by anything but the law of the Torah, because God was his teacher and no one comes after the wisdom of God and his teaching.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of yārâ, 'to teach, direct', the root behind tôrâ. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'teaching'; Radak also allows 'you helped me'.

verses.translation_literal: How smooth [they are] to my palate, your saying, more than honey to my mouth!
verses.translation_dramatic: How sweet it is on my tongue, your saying! Sweeter than honey in my mouth.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the taste verse: palate (ḥēk) and mouth (peh) in two halves, and honey as the standard of sweetness. Let the actor linger on the mouth words. The audience should feel the sensation before they hear the claim.

The verb is a rarity. Nimlĕṣû occurs only here (my own reading), and its sense is argued. Rashi glosses it 'were sweetened'. Radak and Metzudat Zion link it to mĕlîṣâ, 'eloquent saying', so that God's words are 'smooth' as fine speech is smooth; Ibn Ezra rejects that link explicitly, since mĕlîṣ and mĕlîṣâ take the mem as a prefix, not a root letter, and so offers only 'were sweet'. I give 'smooth' in the literal, which keeps both options open, and 'sweet' in the dramatic.

The KJV 'How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey' makes the verse plural and adds two things the Hebrew does not have. The noun ʾimrâ is singular, 'your saying', and the plural 'words' erases that; Radak says the singular means 'each one of the sayings of the LORD'. The 'yea' is also an addition: the Hebrew just sets 'more than honey' beside the first clause, with no extra marker. And 'sweeter than honey' is the KJV's gloss for min dĕbaš, 'from honey', which the Hebrew says more briefly.

philological_notes.note: A Niphal form found only here. Rashi: 'were sweetened'. Radak and Metzudat Zion derive it from the root of mĕlîṣâ, 'eloquent speech'; Ibn Ezra rejects that derivation and understands it simply as 'were sweet'.
'Your saying', singular. Radak says it stands for each of the LORD's sayings; the KJV makes it plural.

verses.translation_literal: From your precepts I gain understanding; upon so I hate every path of falsehood.
verses.translation_dramatic: Out of your precepts I draw understanding, and that is why I hate every road of lies.
verses.directors_commentary: The Mem stanza ends where it began, in the speaker's own feelings, but now the love of verse 97 has a mirror image: hatred. The KJV's "get understanding" is slightly commercial; 'etbônān is the same reflexive verb as in verse 100 and is better rendered "I gain understanding by looking closely". The word for hate, śānē', is the strong one, and the object is "every path of lies", again 'ōraḥ, the small footpath of verse 101: "evil" there, "falsehood" here. The effect is a frame: the speaker shut their feet away from the evil path, and now hates the false one. Metzudat David and Malbim read the connection as cause and effect: understanding leads straight to hatred of falsehood, not as a matter of temperament but as a consequence of seeing clearly. The KJV renders ʿal-kēn "therefore", which is accurate; the English reader should hear it as a small hinge. The letter-heading "NUN" that interrupts some printed texts at this verse is a later labeling device, not part of the Hebrew verse.

philological_notes.note: Falsehood, deceit, what is untrue to its own claim. The commentators read it as false opinions and false ways of life alike.
A fixed idiom, 'therefore', literally 'upon thus'. It sets the hatred as a consequence of the understanding.

verses.translation_literal: A lamp to my foot [is] your word, and a light to my path.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your word is a lamp at my feet, and a light on the road ahead of me.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the best-known line of the psalm, and the KJV is nearly the Hebrew, so there is little to correct. It says 'feet' and 'my path', where the Hebrew has 'foot' (singular, collective) and 'pathway'; a minor loss. What a modern audience misses is the lamp.
