It was a small clay dish of olive oil with a wick, lit by hand, giving a circle of light barely a stride across. Nobody carried one to see a distant horizon; it showed the next step. A person on a night road carried it at the foot, and the line is about guidance step by step rather than a view of the whole way.

The two halves are a parallel pair, and Metzudat David notes simply that the second repeats the first. Meiri and Malbim go further and hear a difference: nēr, the lamp, is the small light, and ʾôr, the light, the larger one. Malbim says the traveller needs both, a small lamp at the foot so as not to tread on thorns and stones, and a large light to see the path ahead. In the Nun stanza that starts here, after the Mem stanza's teaching and study, the word becomes a thing used at night on a road.

philological_notes.note: A lamp, the small oil lamp of the home. Meiri and Malbim read it as the smaller light, set against the larger ʾôr of the second half.
'To my pathway'; Metzudat Zion glosses it as a track and a trodden road. Tied to the root of nĕtîb, 'a path'.

verses.translation_literal: I have sworn, and I have confirmed [it], to keep the judgments of your righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: I swore it, and I have stood by the oath: to keep your righteous judgments.
verses.directors_commentary:
An oath, then a confirmation. He swore to keep the judgments, and he stood up to hold the oath. Play the first word as a vow made aloud, with all the weight an oath has in a world where speech is binding, and the second as the quiet of someone who has kept it.

The grammar here decides the sense. Wāʾăqayyēmâ is a waw-consecutive form of the first person with a paragogic -â, an ending that adds emphasis, not futurity. It reads as a completed act, 'and I have confirmed [it]', which is how the ASV, YLT and BBE render it, and Metzudat David glosses 'I fulfilled the oath'. The KJV 'and I will perform it' turns a past act into a future promise. Malbim does read it as a future ('I will also fulfil my oath'), and that is a defensible alternative, but the plain form of the verb is the past. Ibn Ezra preserves a third, mixed view: the oath 'was then in potential, and is now in act'.

Note that the oath is the object of the verb that follows, 'to keep' (lišmōr), so what he swore and what he confirmed are the same thing: keeping 'the judgments of your righteousness', which the KJV's 'righteous judgments' compresses from a construct chain.

philological_notes.note: A first-person form with waw-consecutive and a paragogic -â: 'and I have confirmed [it]'. Malbim reads a future; Metzudat David gives 'I fulfilled the oath'.

verses.translation_literal: I have been afflicted up to muchness; YHWH, make me live according to your word.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have been brought low, very low. O LORD, give me life, as you have promised.
verses.directors_commentary: After the oath, the weight falls: the stanza closes on suffering. The KJV's "afflicted very much" is accurate but flat; nǎʿănêtî is a niphal of ʿānâ, "to be bowed down, humbled", and Rashi hears in it the very word for "poor" (ʿānî): the speaker has been made poor and low. ʿAd mĕʾōd, "up to muchness", is a Hebrew way of saying "to the limit", and Radak and Meiri read it as near to death. That explains the request. Ḥayyēnî is a piel imperative of ḥāyâ, "to live": "make me live", which is why the KJV's "quicken" is so archaic that readers now take it to mean speed up, when it means "bring to life". The measure is "according to your word", which could be the promise to revive the lowly (Meiri) or the word of a given verse (Radak says there are those who read it as the promise that one who keeps the laws lives by them). Whichever it is, the speaker has just sworn an oath and now asks God to give them breath enough to keep it.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of ʿānâ, 'to be bowed down, humbled, afflicted'. Rashi links it to ʿānî, 'poor, lowly'.
Piel imperative of ḥāyâ: 'make me live, revive me'. KJV 'quicken' means this in older English.

verses.translation_literal: The freewill offerings of my mouth, accept, please, YHWH, and your judgments teach me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Take what my mouth offers you freely, O LORD, these words no one demanded of me. Take them gladly, and then teach me your judgments.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse opens with the thing offered, "the freewill offerings of my mouth", and only then the plea, so the speaker sets the gift down before asking for anything. A nedavah was the offering a worshipper brought unprompted, over and above what the law required (Lev 7:16; 22:18-23). Here the gift is speech: praise, prayer and this very psalm. Rashi reads it as "a pleasing thing that my mouth gives freely", noting that every nedavah has the sense of willingness; Radak has the prayers and praises said "with a generous spirit"; Malbim, more narrowly, has the vow to keep the judgments. The KJV's "Accept, I beseech thee" moves the verb to the front and archaizes the small particle na ("please"), which is soft and polite, not a cry. The Hebrew keeps the offering first, as the ASV and YLT, which follow the order, show.

The second half asks for the same thing the whole psalm asks: teach me. Radak says that is what most of his prayer is about; Meiri takes it as help to succeed in study until he knows them. The verse stands in the Nun stanza (vv.105-112).

philological_notes.note: A nedavah is a gift made out of willingness, the opposite of an obligation. The plural "freewill offerings" is put on the lips: words offered as a sacrifice would be offered at the altar. The root also gives "noble, generous" (nadiv).
Retzeh is the verb for God's acceptance of an offering; its noun ratzon is the "favour" that makes a sacrifice valid. The particle na makes the imperative a request.

verses.translation_literal: My life [is] in my palm continually, and your law I have not forgotten.
verses.translation_dramatic: My life lies in my open hand, every hour of every day, and I could lose it in a breath. Yet your law I have never forgotten.
verses.directors_commentary:
"Life in the palm" is an idiom for deliberately risking death: Jonathan "put his life in his palm" against the Philistine (1 Sam 19:5, with Judg 12:3 and Job 13:14), and Ibn Ezra cites exactly that. Metzudat David gives the picture: something held in an open hand can fall the moment the hand moves. Rashi takes it as living near death through many dangers; Meiri and Malbim tie it to war and enemies. The verse itself names no enemy; the wicked appear only in the next verse, with their snare, so the danger is felt before it is explained.

The KJV's "My soul is continually in my hand" keeps the idiom but "soul" is misleading to a modern ear: nefesh is the life that breathes, not a separate spiritual part. The BBE's "ever in danger" explains the sense and loses the hand. The pair of lines turns on "yet": the Hebrew has a plain waw, and the contrast is carried by the placing of "your law" ahead of the verb. The perfect "I have not forgotten" is the claim of a whole life, not a single moment. Say the first line fast and the second slowly.

philological_notes.note: An idiom for living at risk of death. Kaf is the palm or hollow of the hand, not the fist: the life is held open and could drop.
In Hebrew thought "forget" is also "neglect, stop acting on"; not forgetting the law means keeping it in practice, as Malbim's "I am occupied with it always" has it.

verses.translation_literal: The wicked have set a snare for me, and from your precepts I have not strayed.
verses.translation_dramatic: The wicked have laid a snare across my path, hidden and patient. I have walked on, and I have not wandered from your precepts by a single step.
verses.directors_commentary:
פַּח is a bird-trap: a net or spring-loaded noose hidden on the ground where the bird lands, and the psalms use it constantly for the schemes of enemies (Ps 91:3; 124:7; 140:6). The speaker is the bird that does not land. Metzudat David and Radak read the snares as set in his way; Malbim reads them as lures to pull him from the straight path, so the temptation and the threat are one.

The KJV 'erred' is archaic, and BBE's 'was true to your orders' loses the image of travelling. תָּעָה is to wander off course like a lost animal, the opposite of keeping the road. Note פִּקּוּדִים, 'precepts': a word found only in the Psalms, from the root of 'appoint, oversee', so God's instructions are assignments given to one who is posted. Verse 109 and this verse form a pair: the danger is real, and the speaker does not move from the path.

philological_notes.note: A fowler's snare, not a trap in general. The image is a bird caught by something it could not see; Metzudat Zion glosses it as the net that catches.
To wander, to go out of the way; Metzudat Zion defines it as leaving the straight road for another. The KJV 'erred' hides the travel picture.

verses.translation_literal: I have inherited your testimonies for ever, for the joy of my heart [are] they.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your testimonies are my inheritance, and no one can take it from me, for ever. They are the joy of my heart, every one.
verses.directors_commentary:
נָחַלְתִּי is a legal and family word: to take possession of a נַחֲלָה, the ancestral land allotment that kept a household alive and could not be sold away from the clan (Num 36; 1 Kgs 21:3, Naboth). For a man under threat, whose life is 'in his palm', this is a pointed claim: his true property is not land, which enemies can seize, but the testimonies. Meiri compares it to a man who holds an ancient family estate; Radak adds that he will not leave it for a single hour.

The KJV 'taken as an heritage' adds 'taken as' and turns a plain verb into a comparison; the Hebrew says 'I have inherited'. The Hebrew stresses the heart's joy with a doubled sound, שְׂשׂוֹן, a word for festive rejoicing, the kind heard at harvest and wedding. Ibn Ezra hears the testimonies as the wonders of God's past deeds, which the singer enjoys as if he had been there himself.

philological_notes.note: To receive as an inheritance or hereditary holding. The word frames the testimonies as family land that outlasts the singer.
Exultant, festive joy; the doubled sibilant sounds like laughter. Radak links it to Ps 19:9 'the precepts of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart'.

verses.translation_literal: I have inclined my heart to do your decrees, for ever, [to the] end.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have bent my heart, turned it like a hand turned toward a door, to do what you have decreed. For ever I will keep to it, to the very end.
verses.directors_commentary:
Natiti libbi is "I turned my heart": the verb is transitive (Ibn Ezra and Meiri both say so, comparing "stretch out your hand"), so the speaker is the one who bends it. Radak says that if the heart was leaning toward worldly things, the poet turned it aside; Metzudat David says he turned it from the pleasures of the age. It is an act of will, not a feeling, which suits a psalm full of words for doing and keeping.

The last two words are the hard part: le'olam ekev. The KJV's "alway, even unto the end" reads ekev as "end" and makes the two nouns a pair: Radak, "always I will do them, to the end of my days"; Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion say the same and call the pair synonyms, as in the Hebrew of Daniel 12:2, and ekev is the heel as the end of the body. Rashi reads ekev instead as "upon their tracks and their paths", a footprint sense, from the heel that leaves them. Ibn Ezra and Meiri add "reward", from the other sense of ekev (Ps 19:12), so that le'olam would mean "for the sake of the world to come". The KJV has chosen the first, which fits the plain context best. The ASV prints the Samekh heading after this verse, but in the Hebrew the Samekh lines begin at the next one.

philological_notes.note: To stretch or bend; with "heart" as object, to incline it deliberately. The verb is transitive, so the heart is acted upon by the speaker.

Heel, then what follows the heel: the end, the track, and (in some verses) the consequence or reward. Here it is read "end" by Radak and Metzudat David, as "paths" by Rashi, and as "reward" by Ibn Ezra and Meiri.

verses.translation_literal: Divided ones I have hated, and your law I have loved.
verses.translation_dramatic: The double-minded I hate. Your law I love.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Samekh stanza opens with a rare word, se'afim, built on the root of se'ifim, "branches" or "divisions", the same word as in Elijah's challenge, "How long will you limp between two se'ifim?" (1 Kgs 18:21). Rashi hears a wordplay: se'ifim is the name of the thought, se'afim the people who think those thoughts (Job 4:13 "se'ifim of the visions of the night" is the related noun; Job 20:2 has "my thoughts"). So the first reading takes the word as persons: Ibn Ezra, "those who have thoughts" (the adjective form, like "I praised the dead"), and Meiri, the perplexed, those who swing between two options. The second reading takes it as the thoughts themselves: Radak (a noun, not an adjective, "all the other thoughts I hated"), Metzudat David, and Metzudat Zion ("the sense of thought").

The KJV chose the thoughts ("vain thoughts"); the ASV and BBE chose the people. We follow the people: a plural beside "I hate" and a person's "law I love" makes a clean pair of opposites, and it echoes the divided people of 1 Kings 18. The verb "hate" in the Psalter is the opposite of "love", a position taken, not temper.

philological_notes.note: A hapax built on the root of se'ifim "branches, divisions, divided positions" (1 Kgs 18:21). Read as persons (the divided, the double-minded) by Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Meiri, or as a noun for thoughts by Radak, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion.

verses.translation_literal: My hiding place and my shield [are] you; for your word I have waited.
verses.translation_dramatic: You are the place where I hide, you are the shield in front of me. For your word I wait, and I go on waiting.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two military images: סֵתֶר is cover, a place to vanish from sight, and מָגֵן is the small round shield carried to stop blows face to face. Malbim reads them as complementary: God hides him from the enemy so that he is not seen, and if they come near, God stands as a shield. The word-order puts the nouns first and 'you' after them, so the verse sounds like an answer to the danger of verses 109-110.

The verb יָחַל is waiting with expectation, a hope that stretches over time; the KJV 'I hope in thy word' is acceptable, but English 'hope' can sound vague. Meiri and Radak understand 'word' (דָּבָר) as God's promise. YLT's 'For Thy word I have hoped' keeps the preposition ל, 'for, toward'. BBE's 'secret place' for סֵתֶר is nearer the Hebrew than KJV's 'hiding place' is, in a sense; BBE's 'breastplate' for מָגֵן is not: the Hebrew shield is held in the hand.

philological_notes.note: To wait expectantly, to hope. The perfect here speaks of a hope already long held. Meiri and Radak read the 'word' as the promise.

verses.translation_literal: Turn aside from me, evildoers, and let me keep the commandments of my God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Away from me, you who do evil! Leave me, so that I may keep the commandments of my God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker suddenly turns from God to the people around him and speaks to them directly, a sharp break in a psalm that has addressed only God. The verb סוּר is an order to leave the road: 'turn off'. The KJV 'Depart from me, ye evildoers: for I will keep' reads the second clause as a reason; the Hebrew has a cohortative, וְאֶצְּרָה, 'and let me keep', a wish, a purpose. ASV 'That I may keep' gets that right. Radak and Meiri say the sense is 'do not distract me'; Malbim says battle makes keeping the commandments impossible.

מְרֵעִים are those who do harm, the same root as 'evil' and 'bad': the term is about action. Note 'my God' (אֱלֹהָי): the only place in the stanza where the speaker claims the relationship in personal terms, as a reason to refuse company.

philological_notes.note: Cohortative of 'to guard, keep': 'let me keep' or 'that I may keep'. It expresses purpose or wish, not simple future as in KJV.

verses.translation_literal: Sustain me according to your saying, and I will live; and do not shame me from my hope.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hold me up, as you have said you would, and I will live. Do not let me be put to shame over the hope I have kept.
verses.directors_commentary:
סָמַךְ is to lean on something, to prop or brace; the prayer asks God to be the support under a falling man, which fits the 'life in my palm' of verse 109. כְּאִמְרָתְךָ, 'according to your saying', points back to a promise; Radak connects it to Lev 18:5, 'which if a man do, he shall live in them'. The 'and I will live' is a consequence: if you hold me, I live.

The second line uses shame as an honour-and-shame term. In the ancient world to be 'ashamed' (בּוֹשׁ) is public humiliation, to be shown wrong in front of others. The KJV 'ashamed of my hope' reads like an inner embarrassment; the Hebrew has מִן, 'from/because of', that is, 'do not let my hope lead to my disgrace'. Metzudat David says that one whose hope is frustrated is shamed. שֵׂבֶר 'hope' is a rare word, from the verb 'to look, expect' (Ps 146:5).

philological_notes.note: 'My hope', from a root meaning to look expectantly (not the common שבר 'break'). Metzudat Zion ties it to Ps 146:5.
'Do not put me to shame': public disgrace when hope proves empty, not mere embarrassment.

verses.translation_literal: Support me, and let me be saved, and let me look to your decrees continually.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hold me up, and I will be saved; and I will keep my eyes on your decrees, always.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two verbs of rescue lead and one of regard follows. The pair se'adeni and ivasha'ah is a rising request: Malbim says se'ad, a prop under the weight, is more than semikhah, a hand that steadies (v.116), and that "saved" is complete. The last verb, ve'esh'ah, is a near-echo of ivasha'ah, a sound play in which the deliverance (yasha) is answered by the gaze (sha'ah): saved, then "looking to".

The meaning of esh'ah is disputed. Rashi gives "be occupied with" (as in Exod 5:9, "let them not give heed to false words") and, alternatively, speaking and repeating. Ibn Ezra reports a Targum reading "I will tell" but prefers "delight", from sha'ashu'im, with the word doubled. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion compare vayispor and ve-ishtaʿi, "recount"; Radak gives "delight" as the other option. The Targum printed here has "I will delight" (agaʿgeʿa), close to the "delight" reading and the BBE. The KJV's "have respect unto" is a stiff, archaic way of saying "look at with regard", which keeps the shared verb "sha'ah"; it gives neither delight nor recounting. We keep the gaze so the verb stays visible against the rescue.

philological_notes.note: Disputed: "I will look to, be occupied with" (Rashi; Exod 5:9), "I will recount" (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion, by comparison with ve-ishtaʿi), or "I will delight" from sha'ashu'im (Ibn Ezra, Radak's second option; the Targum here has agaʿgeʿa). The sound echoes ivasha'ah.
To prop up, to support with food or strength; Malbim says it is stronger than semikhah in v.116.

verses.translation_literal: You have spurned all who stray from your decrees, for their deceit [is] falsehood.
verses.translation_dramatic: You cast aside, like refuse underfoot, every one who strays from your decrees. For their cunning is a lie, and a lie cannot stand.
verses.directors_commentary:
סָלָה is rare: to toss aside, to trample as worthless. It appears in Lam 1:15, 'the Lord has trampled (סִלָּה) all my mighty men', which Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all cite. The KJV 'trodden down' is a good rendering; ASV 'set at nought' is weaker; STEPBible's 'reject' also loses the force of being trampled. The perfect tense expresses what God does as a rule, a general truth, and the singer says it to explain why he trusts God.

שׁוֹגִים are those who 'go astray', from the root of 'inadvertent error' (שְׁגָגָה). Metzudat David and Radak note the irony: the straying call it a mistake, but 'their deceit is falsehood' says it is deliberate. The pair שֶׁקֶר and תַּרְמִית ('lie' and 'deceit') are heaped together; the KJV puts them in a nearly circular sentence, 'their deceit is falsehood', which is accurate. Malbim reads שגיאה as intellectual error, a view the Hebrew allows.

philological_notes.note: To trample, to treat as worthless. The only other occurrence of this verb is Lam 1:15.
Deceit, treachery; Metzudat Zion links it to Jer 14:14 'the deceit of their heart'.

verses.translation_literal: Dross you have made cease, all [the] wicked of [the] earth; therefore I love your testimonies.
verses.translation_dramatic: All the wicked of the earth you sweep away like slag from the silver. And so I love your testimonies.
verses.directors_commentary:
סִיג is dross: the grey waste that floats to the top when silver is smelted and must be skimmed away so that the pure metal remains. The prophets use the same picture (Isa 1:22, 25; Prov 25:4). The Hebrew puts 'dross' first, with no 'like', so the wicked simply are the dross; KJV and ASV add 'like', which is a fair gloss but softens a harder metaphor. YLT 'Dross!' keeps the abruptness. Malbim and Metzudat David draw out the refiner's furnace.

הִשְׁבַּתָּ is a causative of 'to stop, to cease' (Sabbath's verb), which gives 'you have made cease'; KJV 'puttest away' is vague and BBE 'waste metal in your eyes' invents. Radak notes that 'all' (כָּל) is not strictly universal, as in 'all the earth came to Egypt' (Gen 41:57). The conclusion, 'therefore I love', makes justice the reason for love.

philological_notes.note: Dross, the waste skimmed from smelted silver; a metaphor for the morally worthless. Used in Isa 1:25 and Prov 25:4.
Hiphil: to cause to stop, to bring to an end. Meiri glosses 'you have annulled'.

verses.translation_literal: My flesh has bristled from dread of you, and of your judgments I am afraid.
verses.translation_dramatic: My flesh shudders at the dread of you, every hair standing up. And your judgments, I fear them.
verses.directors_commentary:
סָמַר is the physical shiver of terror: hair standing stiff, skin tightening. Rashi cites Job 4:15, 'the hair of my flesh stood up' (תְּסַמֵּר שַׂעֲרַת בְּשָׂרִי), and gives the Old French word for bristling; Metzudat Zion and Radak link it to מַסְמֵר, 'nail', for the hair stands up stiff like nails. The KJV 'trembleth' is too general: the Hebrew is a specific picture of goosebumps and standing hair.

The verse follows verse 119 closely. The God who sweeps away the wicked must be feared even by the one who loves him: love and awe are not set against one another. Ibn Ezra says that when the speaker recalls the judgments done to the wicked, fear seizes him. פַּחַד is sudden dread, not 'fear of God' in the calm sense (יִרְאָה); the verse uses both words, one for the body and one for the mind. Verse 120 closes the Samekh strophe.

philological_notes.note: To bristle, to stand stiff (of hair or skin) from fear. Related to מַסְמֵר 'nail'. Same verb in Job 4:15.
Dread, a sudden terror felt in the body, as distinct from יִרְאָה 'reverent fear' in the second half.

verses.translation_literal: I have done justice and righteousness; do not leave me to my oppressors.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have done what is just. I have done what is right. Now do not hand me over, LORD, do not set me down and walk away, and leave me in the grip of those who press upon me.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new stanza opens with the letter ayin, and its first word, 'asiti, 'I have done', is also the letter's sound; the verse is a plea built on a claim. The speaker does not ask for mercy but for what is owed: in the ancient Near East a king or judge was above all the defender of the weak against the strong, and the petitioner here stands as one who has kept the contract, 'justice and righteousness' being the royal programme in miniature. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri all read it that way: I have wronged no one, so do not give me to those who wrong me.

The verb is blunter than the KJV's 'leave me not'. Hiphil of nuach is 'set down, let rest, abandon', as one leaves a load or a prisoner where they lie; Metzudat David glosses it 'be delivered into the hand of'. The oppressors are 'osheqai, those who extort or defraud, the vocabulary of the strong cheating the dependent (Lev 19:13); not enemies on a battlefield but creditors and officials. The KJV's 'mine oppressors' is archaic; the Hebrew simply has 'to my oppressors'.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of nuach: 'cause to rest, set down, leave behind'. The plea is not 'forgive' but 'do not abandon me where I stand, in their hands'.
Participle of 'ashaq, 'to oppress, extort, defraud', economic as much as physical wrong. Metzudat Zion ties it to 'osheq and gezel, 'extortion and robbery'.

verses.translation_literal: Stand surety for your servant for good; let not the arrogant oppress me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Be my pledge, LORD. Stand as guarantor for your servant, and let the outcome be good. Do not let the proud close their hands on me.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the language of the marketplace and the debtor's court. 'Arov is 'to give a pledge', as Judah did for Benjamin (Gen 43:9) and as Hezekiah asks in Isaiah 38:14 ('I am oppressed; be my surety'); the same two roots, 'ashaq and 'arav, turn up there, and the Hebrew commentators (Meiri, Metzudat Zion) point to that verse. The speaker asks God to put his own name on the loan: if the proud demand payment, they must reckon with the guarantor. Malbim draws out exactly this: the 'good' that is the servant's lot is held in trust, and God, as surety, must restore whatever is seized.

The KJV, ASV and Webster keep 'be surety', but the older Hebrew exegetes (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David) took 'arov instead as a transitive form of 'arev, 'to be sweet': 'make your servant's lot pleasant'. That is why BBE and some others render it so loosely. 'Zedim', 'the arrogant', are those who boil over, who act in presumption; the KJV's 'the proud' is accurate but weaker than the Hebrew, which implies defiance rather than mere pride.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of 'arav, 'to pledge, stand surety' (Gen 43:9; Prov 6:1). Rashi glosses it as hatzalah, 'rescue', 'be guarantor on my behalf against the evil'. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion take it as a causative of 'arev, 'pleasant', 'make good'; the same ambiguity sits behind Isaiah 38:14.
'The arrogant, the presumptuous', from zid, 'to seethe, act insolently'. Elsewhere in this psalm they are the people who mock and dig pits (vv. 21, 51, 69, 78, 85).

verses.translation_literal: My eyes have failed for your deliverance and for the word of your righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: My eyes are spent with watching. They have strained toward your rescue until nothing is left in them, toward the word you spoke, and the righteousness that word promises.
verses.directors_commentary:
The eyes 'fail' because they have been fixed on the horizon too long. Deuteronomy 28:32 and 28:65 use the same image, kilyon einayim, 'failing of the eyes', for hopeless watching, and Meiri cites the Deuteronomy expression; Metzudat Zion calls it a desire that is delayed. Here it is not despair but the exhaustion of waiting, as a sentry's eyes tire before dawn. The actor should play it with a raw, dry-eyed stillness rather than tears.

There are two objects: yeshu'ah, 'deliverance', the act; and imrat tzidqekha, 'the word of your righteousness', God's own promise. Rashi and Radak read the second as the specific promise God made; Ibn Ezra reads it as his righteous decrees. The KJV's 'salvation' carries too much later theological weight; the Hebrew word is the rescue of someone at the brink, here from oppressors (v. 121-122). KJV's 'the word of thy righteousness' is literal and good; ASV 'thy righteous word' loses the genitive.

philological_notes.note: Perfect of kalah, 'to come to an end, be used up'. With eyes it is 'to pine, grow dim with watching', as in Deuteronomy 28:32 and Lamentations 2:11.
'The utterance of your righteousness'. Imrah is the Psalm 119 word for God's promise, spoken and reliable; Rashi: 'the promise you promised me'.

verses.translation_literal: Do with your servant according to your covenant loyalty, and teach me your statutes.
verses.translation_dramatic: Deal with your servant as your own steadfast love would deal. Not by what I have earned, but by who you are. And teach me your statutes.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker asked for justice in verse 121; now he swaps the register entirely. Chesed is not 'mercy' (KJV), which suggests pity from a superior, but covenant loyalty, the faithful commitment of a party bound by an oath. Metzudat David says it plainly: 'according to your chesed, and not according to my deeds'. Malbim sets the verses side by side: teaching the hidden statutes is beyond what justice owes, so it can only be asked as an act of chesed.

The verb is the plainest in the language, 'ase, 'do', which the speaker has just used of his own conduct (v. 121 'asiti). The KJV 'deal with' is fine; BBE's 'be good to' adds more than the Hebrew has. 'Chuqqim' are things engraved or fixed, hence statutes; the KJV 'statutes' stands.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, steadfast love: a loyalty owed within a bond and freely kept. 'Mercy' (KJV) is too soft and pity-centred; Metzudat David: 'and not by my deeds'.

verses.translation_literal: Your servant am I; give me understanding, and let me know your testimonies.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am your servant. Give me understanding, and I will know what your testimonies say.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Servant' here is a status, not a metaphor: an 'eved belongs to a household and owes its master obedience, and in return can expect the master's protection and instruction. The speaker puts the claim first in the Hebrew, 'your servant, I' (the pronoun is emphatic and the word order front-loads the relationship), and then asks for what a master owes his servant, to be told what he is meant to do. Malbim notes the contrast with the previous verse: teaching the statutes needed chesed; teaching the testimonies is a right of a servant.

The form 'give me understanding' is the Hiphil of bin; 'ede'ah, 'and let me know', is a cohortative of purpose, so the sense is 'give me understanding so that I may know', as the KJV and ASV have it ('that I may'). 'Edot', 'testimonies', are the covenant's witnessing documents; the KJV's 'testimonies' is right and the BBE's 'unchanging word' is a paraphrase.

philological_notes.note: 'Your testimonies', the commandments seen as witnesses to the covenant. Related to 'ed, 'witness'.

verses.translation_literal: A time to act for YHWH: they have broken your law.
verses.translation_dramatic: It is time, LORD. It is time for you to act. They have broken your law.
verses.directors_commentary: Five words in Hebrew, and nothing wasted: a time, to act, for YHWH, they have broken, your law. Play it short and low, like someone who has stopped arguing and now simply states the hour. The line holds two meanings at once and the Hebrew does not choose. 'A time to act for YHWH' can be the psalmist urging God to move against those who break his law (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David and Malbim read it so, pointing to a fixed time for judgment); or it can mean 'a time for [us] to act for YHWH', that the faithful must now stand firm because the law is being undone (Radak's second reading, and Meiri). The rabbis took it as an emergency licence: one may bend one law to save the whole, citing Elijah on Carmel, who offered at a forbidden high place (Rashi, citing b. Berakhot 63a). The KJV, 'It is time for thee, Lord, to work', commits to the first reading and adds 'thee', which is not in the Hebrew. 'Time' (עֵת) is an appointed moment rather than clock time; in the ancient world a verdict, a harvest or a festival has its own 'et', and the speaker is saying the hour has come due. 'Have broken' (הֵפֵרוּ) is the word for annulling a covenant or vow, a legal act, not an accident.

philological_notes.note: 'To act' with no object: God, or the faithful, must do something. The bare verb is why the line splits two ways. Metzudat David reads it as 'to carry out judgment on the wicked'.
Hiphil of פרר, to break or annul, the verb used for breaking a covenant. It carries legal weight: they have not stumbled but cancelled.

verses.translation_literal: Therefore I love your commandments more than gold, and more than fine gold.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so I love your commandments. I love them more than gold, more than the purest gold there is.
verses.directors_commentary: The 'therefore' is the actor's problem: it points back, but the commentators disagree where. Radak hears it as contrast with the people just named: they have broken your law and chase profit, their whole bustle is to acquire money, so I love your commandments, to teach them, do them and busy myself in them, more than the gold and fine gold they scramble for. Malbim and Metzudat David hear it as consequence: because I know a time of judgment is coming, I love the commandments, since wealth cannot rescue anyone on that day. Ibn Ezra ties it back to 'I am your servant': I will not ask for a reward in gold or fine gold. Play it as conviction, not boast. The KJV's 'above gold; yea, above fine gold' is sound; 'yea' is its own addition, the Hebrew simply repeats 'more than'. Pāz (פָּז) is refined, high-purity gold, a word the Psalter uses for the best that money buys (Ps 19:10); Metzudat Zion defines it as 'the good gold'. In a world where gold was the one store of value that did not rot, rust or lose face, saying you prefer a command to it is saying you prefer it to security.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'upon so'. Rashi notes it often means 'because' rather than 'therefore', citing Gen 33:10, Num 10:31 and Isa 15:7. Read that way, the verse says 'because I love'. The causal arrow runs either direction.
Refined gold, set against plain זָהָב as the finest grade; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'the good gold'. The pair builds a climax: gold, and then better than gold.

verses.translation_literal: Therefore all the precepts of everything I have pronounced upright; every path of falsehood I have hated.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so every precept of yours, on every matter, I call straight. And every road of lies, I hate.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hardest line in the stanza, and the stage direction is: do not smooth it. The Hebrew says 'all the precepts of all' (כָּל־פִּקּוּדֵי כֹל), a doubled 'all' that no one has fully explained. The KJV, 'all thy precepts concerning all things', picks one reading and inserts 'thy' and 'things', neither of which is in the Hebrew, and renders the verb as 'esteem' where it says 'I have made straight, I have declared upright'. Ibn Ezra reads the verb as a variant of אשר, to call blessed, the yod standing for an alef, as in Leah's 'for the daughters will call me blessed' (Gen 30:13); on this reading the speaker 'pronounces blessed' the precepts. He reads the doubled 'all' as all-inclusive, covering every person of heart. Radak says the repeated 'kol' means both the written precepts and the unwritten customs of Israel, every one of which has a reason that the mind can see, and that the speaker 'makes them straight' before those who sneer at them. Meiri reads the precepts as the universal truths that even outside thinkers affirm, in which they agree with us, and 'every path of falsehood' as what they hold beyond that. Take the verb as a verdict, not a mood: the psalmist stands up and declares the law straight in public, and in the same breath names its opposite. The pairing of straight and false is a road image, 'path' (אֹרַח) against the straight way.

philological_notes.note: A Piel perfect, 'I have made straight' or 'I have declared straight'; Rashi glosses it as 'they were upright in my eyes, and I said of them: they are upright'. Ibn Ezra instead derives it from אשר with a yod for alef, 'I have pronounced blessed', comparing Gen 30:13 ('the daughters will call me blessed'). His grammar, not mine.

'All the precepts of everything': the doubled 'all' is unexplained. Ibn Ezra: it includes every man of heart; Radak: the written and unwritten precepts; Meiri: the universal precepts reason itself confirms.
'Path of falsehood': the road image runs through the whole psalm (vv.9, 101, 104). Verse 104 uses the same phrase, which Malbim cites.

verses.translation_literal: Wonders [are] your testimonies; therefore my soul has kept them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Wonders, every one. Your testimonies are wonders, and so my soul has held to them, kept them close, guarded them.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new stanza opens with the letter pe, and its first word is pela'ot, 'wonders', a root used for God's miraculous acts (Ex 15:11; Ps 77:15). Applied to testimonies, the word says they are not merely hard but beyond ordinary grasp. Rashi and Metzudat David say 'hidden and marvellous'; Malbim, 'secret and concealed'. The Hebrew phrase puts the predicate first, 'wonders, your testimonies', which the KJV smooths to 'Thy testimonies are wonderful', losing the drumbeat.

The soul keeps them: nefesh is not an immaterial spirit but the whole living self, throat and breath and appetite. The verb natzar means to guard as one guards a vineyard or city, a heavier word than 'keep'. Rashi on 'therefore': the speaker keeps all of them because he does not know which one will earn the reward (Eccl 11:6).

philological_notes.note: 'Wonders, marvels': in Exodus 15:11 and Psalm 77:15 God's own deeds. Metzudat Zion links it to Judges 13:18 ('it is wonderful', covered, incomprehensible).
'Guarded them', with the verb in the feminine singular because nefesh is feminine. Radak also hears 'fixed her gaze on them', 'to examine'.

verses.translation_literal: The opening of your words gives light, giving understanding to the simple.
verses.translation_dramatic: The moment your words open, light comes in. And the simple, who knew nothing, begin to understand.
verses.directors_commentary:
Petach is a doorway, an opening; the KJV 'entrance' is a fair choice, and BBE and ASV 'opening' is closer to the single image. Hearers in the ancient world would picture a one-room house with a single door: when the door is opened, light falls in. The Hebrew commentators read it differently: for Rashi, the 'opening' is the beginning of the revelation, 'I am the LORD your God who brought you out' (Ex 20:2) or, in another reading, 'Let there be light' (Gen 1:3); Radak, 'when a person begins to contemplate them, his eyes are enlightened'.

The 'simple', pethayim, are not stupid but untrained, open to being shaped, for good or ill (Prov 1:22; 9:4). The KJV's 'simple' is right. The final clause is a participle with no subject, 'one giving understanding': Meiri and Radak understand it as God, so the verse may be addressed to him, 'you are the one who gives understanding'.

philological_notes.note: 'Opening, doorway, unfolding'. Ibn Ezra relates it to pitchon peh, 'opening of the mouth'; Rashi reads it as the beginning of God's speech.
'The simple, the naive': people open and easily led. Metzudat Zion glosses 'fools', but in Proverbs the pethi is teachable.

verses.translation_literal: My mouth I opened wide, and I panted, for for your commandments I longed.
verses.translation_dramatic: I opened my mouth wide and gasped like one who is starving for air, because I was longing, longing for your commandments.
verses.directors_commentary:
An image from the body: a mouth gaping wide, a chest heaving. Pa'ar is to open wide, as of a gaping mouth (Isa 5:14, of Sheol); sha'af is to gasp or snuff up air, as a wild donkey in the wind (Jer 2:24, cited by Rashi and Metzudat Zion). The speaker is an animal at the end of a long run, mouth open, drawing in what it craves. Radak adds a better picture: a hungry man whose food is being brought opens his mouth before it arrives.

The last verb, ya'avti, occurs only here in the Bible. Ibn Ezra says it 'has no equal in Scripture'; Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as the same as ta'avti, 'I longed'. The KJV and ASV 'longed' follow the same sense, and 'panted' is the right verb for the previous one. Malbim: the commandments are not bread but air: a man can live a few days without food, not a moment without breath.

philological_notes.note: 'And I panted, gasped, snuffed up'. Jeremiah 2:24 uses the same verb for a wild donkey sniffing the wind in heat; Rashi cites it for 'swallowing'.
A hapax legomenon, here only. Ibn Ezra: 'it has no companion in Scripture'; Radak and Metzudat Zion equate it with ta'avti, 'I longed, craved'.

verses.translation_literal: Turn to me and be gracious to me, according to the custom for those who love your name.
verses.translation_dramatic: Turn your face to me, LORD, and be gracious. Do for me what you always do for the ones who love your name.
verses.directors_commentary:
Panah elai, 'turn to me': God's face is turned toward someone to see them, and turned away to ignore them; the plea is for his attention before his gift. 'Channeni', 'be gracious to me', is from chen, favour freely given, the opposite of what is owed. Malbim sets the contrast with the last words: 'mishpat' is what is due, 'chaninah' a free gift, and the speaker asks that what is due to those who love God's name be extended to him as grace even if he does not yet deserve it.

Mishpat here is not 'justice' but 'the customary way, the usual practice', as in Genesis 40:13 ('after the former manner'); Radak compares 'kemishpat habanot', 'as is the custom for daughters' (Ex 21:9). The KJV 'as thou usest to do' gets this exactly; BBE's 'as it is right' loses the habitual sense. 'Name' stands for the person, known and invoked.

philological_notes.note: 'According to the custom, the usual way', rather than 'according to judgment'. Radak compares Exodus 21:9, 'kemishpat habanot'.
'Be gracious to me': chen is favour given freely, unearned. Malbim sets it against mishpat, what is due.

verses.translation_literal: My footsteps establish by your word, and may not any wickedness have power over me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Set my steps firm in your word. And let no wrong take hold of me and rule.
verses.directors_commentary: The Pe stanza runs 129-136, and this verse opens its second half. Each of its eight verses begins with the letter פ, and here the voice shifts from admiration to petition: the first half says what the word is, the second asks what it will do. 'Footsteps' (פְּעָמַי) is a rarer word for steps than the usual 'derekh', a body word: the beat of the foot on the ground. 'Establish' (הָכֵן) is the verb for setting a thing on a firm base, as one sets a pillar. So the picture is of feet planted on the word as on rock. The second clause asks that wickedness not 'have power' (תַּשְׁלֶט) over him, the verb of a ruler, and with 'any' (כָל) it reaches even the smallest fault: Radak says 'any' means even a light transgression. The KJV, 'Order my steps in thy word', is archaic: 'order' in 1611 meant arrange or direct, and a reader today hears command. 'Iniquity' for אָוֶן is fair, but the Targum has 'falsehood', and Metzudat Zion defines it as empty, substanceless things, which is the sense of the word's first meaning, 'nothingness'. Both commentators agree it is a prayer, not a boast.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative of כון, 'establish, make firm'. The image is of fixing steps on a base. Meiri glosses 'direct them to act according to your word'.
Wickedness or nothingness. Metzudat Zion defines it as 'a thing with no substance, that is, sins and iniquities'. The Targum renders it שקר, falsehood.

verses.translation_literal: Ransom me from the oppression of humankind, and I will keep your precepts.
verses.translation_dramatic: Buy me back from the hand that presses down, from the crush of people who would own my days, and I will keep every charge you have laid on me.
verses.directors_commentary:
פְּדֵנִי is the language of the market and the law court: 'ransom me', the word used of redeeming a slave or a firstborn. He speaks as a man whose time is being taken. Radak's reading is the practical one: free from pressure, and he will have leisure to keep the precepts. Rashi reads the 'oppression' as the inclination to evil that squeezes people from inside, and says other commentaries read it as the oppression done by a person. Both are available in the Hebrew.

עֹשֶׁק is extortion and exploitation, wealth taken by force or fraud, not just 'oppression' in a vague sense. KJV 'Deliver' is gentler than 'ransom'; ASV 'Redeem' keeps the price. The final clause is not 'so will I keep' (KJV) as a bargain but a simple 'and I will keep': the consecutive vav-plus-cohortative (וְאֶשְׁמְרָה) states purpose, 'that I may keep'.

philological_notes.note: 'Ransom, redeem': a payment-laden verb of release (slaves, firstborn, captives). It sets freedom as the condition of obedience.
Extortion, wrongful pressure on the weak, often economic. Rashi reads it as the evil inclination that oppresses, Ibn Ezra and Radak as human extortioners.

verses.translation_literal: Your face, make shine on your servant, and teach me your statutes.
verses.translation_dramatic: Turn your face toward me, LORD, and let it shine, as dawn comes over a servant standing at his master's door; and while it shines, teach me your statutes.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the Aaronic blessing (Num 6:25, 'the LORD make his face shine') turned into a petition. Radak and Metzudat David both read 'the light of your face' as favor and goodwill, and Ibn Ezra quotes Proverbs 16:15, 'in the light of a king's face is life'. A servant who stands before a king reads his face: a bright face means a granted request, a dark one a death sentence. Play it as someone watching a face.

The preposition is unusual: בְּעַבְדֶּךָ is 'in/on your servant', not 'toward' (as in Numbers). Malbim notices this and reads it as light inside the servant, an inner illumination that makes teaching possible; that is his reading, not a settled sense. KJV 'Make thy face to shine upon' hides the difference. 'Statutes' (חֻקִּים) are things 'cut' or 'inscribed', fixed decrees, not opinions; the verb is 'teach', so the servant is asking for a lesson, not a ruling.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative, 'cause to shine'. The face of God is shown as light: favor, as Radak and Ibn Ezra say.
'In/on your servant'. The prepositions in Num 6:25 and here differ; Malbim reads this one as inner light. His reading, not shared by the others in the packet.

verses.translation_literal: Streams of water have gone down, my eyes, because they did not keep your law.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rivers of water run down from my eyes, because your law is not kept.
verses.directors_commentary: Two things are left unsaid, and the actor must decide. First, the word order: 'streams of water have come down, my eyes', with the eyes held back to the end, as if the weeping arrives before its owner is named. Second, the subject of 'did not keep' is not stated. Most read it as the wicked: Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Metzudat David say the psalmist weeps for those who do not keep the law, and Meiri adds that he grieves over their ruin. But Radak, Ibn Ezra ('some say') and Meiri ('many interpret so') also read it as 'because my eyes did not keep your law': the eyes standing for the wandering gaze, as in 'do not go about after your hearts and your eyes' (Num 15:39). On that reading the weeping is repentance. Malbim sharpens it: though he once sought after his eyes (David, Bathsheba), he has wept streams and been forgiven. Play it with the question open. The KJV, 'Rivers of waters run down mine eyes, because they keep not thy law', turns the perfect into a present, calls 'peleg' a river where it is a divided channel, and silently chooses 'they' as the wicked. Metzudat Zion glosses פַּלְגֵי as water channels that 'divide and spread' to run each way: weeping that has found a course and does not stop. In a dry land such a stream is something you ration; here the eyes have it in plenty.

philological_notes.note: Channels or divided watercourses (cf. Ps 1:3), not great rivers. Metzudat Zion: named for their habit of dividing and running in different directions.

'They did not keep': the subject is unstated, either the wicked or the eyes. Radak, Ibn Ezra and Meiri give the second reading, with the eyes standing for the roving gaze. The verb is the same שמר used as the psalm's signature word for 'keep, guard'.

verses.translation_literal: Righteous are you, YHWH, and upright [are] your judgments.
verses.translation_dramatic: Righteous, LORD. That is what you are, and straight as a plumb line are every one of your judgments.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone turns. After tears, a flat declaration with no verb 'to be' in the Hebrew: צַדִּיק אַתָּה, 'righteous, you'. It is the language of a court that has heard the case and finds the Judge in the right; the psalmist is not asking for anything here. The stanza begins a run of eight verses each starting with צ, the Hebrew letter that opens צדיק and צדק, so the sound of 'tsedek' repeats on every line.

KJV and the others render וְיָשָׁר as 'and upright are thy judgments', correct but the adjective is singular, 'and straight (is) your judgment' for each one: Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all say 'each one of your judgments is upright'. Malbim adds a theological use: the delay of reward is itself just. The printed KJV letter-headings 'ZADDI' are not in the Hebrew verse but mark the stanza.

philological_notes.note: 'Straight, level, upright': a road-building word applied to law. It is singular, which is why the medieval commentators read 'each of your judgments is upright'.

verses.translation_literal: You commanded righteousness [in] your testimonies, and faithfulness exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: Righteousness is what you laid down in your testimonies, LORD, and faithfulness, faithfulness to the very edge of measure.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse has no verb for 'to be', and the Hebrew does not say that the testimonies are righteous; it says that God commanded righteousness, and faithfulness, in them. The testimonies are the vehicle, and what they carry is the character of the one who gave them. Actors should play this as a man laying down a claim in court, with the next verses as its proof: he is about to ask for help on the ground that this covenant document cannot lie.

The translations split. KJV (with Webster) turns the nouns into adjectives and inserts a relative clause: 'Thy testimonies that thou hast commanded are righteous and very faithful'. YLT also reads adjectivally: 'Righteous and exceeding faithful'. Only ASV keeps the noun shape: 'in righteousness And very faithfulness'. BBE goes further and drops 'faithfulness' for 'it is for ever'. The Hebrew word is אֱמוּנָה, the steadiness of someone who can be leaned on, and מְאֹד, 'very', hangs at the end of the line as an intensifier of a noun, which is why ASV's 'very faithfulness' sounds odd in English but is closer to the sound of the original. Malbim hears the first half as 'you commanded righteousness [in] your testimonies', reading the stories of the Torah as testimony that God repays each person justly.

philological_notes.note: 'You commanded', the verb of the commandment (mitzvah). Meiri glosses it as 'you decreed and fixed', as in 'he commanded and they were created'. The verb governs 'righteousness' directly, so the sense is closer to 'you ordained righteousness' than to 'you gave orders'.

Spelled עֵדֹתֶיךָ here, with the lemma עֵדָה (H5713B), as against עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ in verse 144 from עֵדוּת. Both mean 'testimonies', the covenant's witness to who God is and what he requires. Rashi notes the different vowel patterns of this word in verse 146.

verses.translation_literal: My zeal has cut me off, for my adversaries have forgotten your words.
verses.translation_dramatic: My own zeal is eating me from within, silencing me, because the ones who stand against me have forgotten what you said.
verses.directors_commentary:
קִנְאָה is the same word as 'jealousy', the passion of one who will not share what is his; it is used of God himself. The psalmist is jealous for God's honor, and the feeling nearly annihilates him: צִמְּתַתְנִי comes from a root meaning 'put an end to, destroy, silence'. Radak says it almost ended him, as he watched the forgetful prosper; Malbim, that the wicked's long success makes them say there is no providence.

KJV 'consumed' is a fair paraphrase, but the verb is stronger than 'use up': it is 'cut off' (Metzudat Zion cites the same root in Psalm 94:23). The adversaries are צָרַי, 'those who press on me', which sounds like the צַר 'distress' of verse 143, and with it the sound-play of the whole stanza: צ, צ, צ. 'Forgotten' is not mere absent-mindedness; in Hebrew it is neglect.

philological_notes.note: Perfect with an object suffix, 'it has put an end to me': a root of annihilation (compare Psalm 94:23, 'will cut them off'). Ibn Ezra reads it as 'almost'.
'My zeal/jealousy': the passion that will not tolerate rivals, here for God's honor. Metzudat Zion links it to anger, as in Deut 32:21.

verses.translation_literal: Refined [is] your word exceedingly, and your servant loves it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your word has been through the fire and come out clean, nothing left in it but the silver, and your servant loves it.
verses.directors_commentary:
צְרוּפָה is a metalworker's word: refined in the crucible until the slag, the סִיג, is burnt away. Metzudat Zion says so outright, 'borrowed from the refining of silver', and Ibn Ezra and Radak say there is no dross in it. Compare Psalm 12:7 and 18:31, where the same sound comes up. For an audience in a world that tested silver by fire, this is a guarantee of quality.

KJV 'very pure' loses the process; the participle names something that has been refined. KJV 'therefore thy servant loveth it' inserts a 'therefore' that the Hebrew does not have, only וְ 'and'. Where KJV makes love the conclusion of an argument, the Hebrew makes it a plain companion fact. Radak adds a note on ועבדך אהבה: the servant keeps it in mind while the others forget. The 'servant' speaks of himself in the third person, as in the court.

philological_notes.note: Passive participle, 'refined, smelted': a smelter's term (silver, gold). Metzudat Zion says the word is borrowed from the refining of silver.

verses.translation_literal: Small [am] I, and despised; your precepts I have not forgotten.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am small, and they look down on me, and still, your precepts I have not forgotten.
verses.directors_commentary:
צָעִיר is 'young, little, of low standing', the word for a younger son, and נִבְזֶה is 'held in contempt'. In a world of honor and shame, to be both is to be nobody. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'in the eyes of my enemies', quoting 'I am a worm and no man' (Ps 22:7); Rashi connects it with 'David was the youngest' (1 Sam 17:14), but that is a link made by the commentator, not a statement in this verse.

The contrast is the whole force: the verbs are in the perfect, 'I have not forgotten', set against the forgetting of the previous verse, where the enemies forgot. Radak makes the point: 'as they forgot'. KJV 'yet do not I forget' adds 'yet' and flips the tense to the present, but the Hebrew is simply 'not have I forgotten'. The pronoun is the long form אָנֹכִי, a little more weight than the simple one.

philological_notes.note: 'Small, young, insignificant', a younger-son word. Rashi links it to David the youngest; Ibn Ezra to the speaker's standing in his enemies' eyes.
Niphal participle, 'despised, treated as worthless'.

verses.translation_literal: Your righteousness [is] righteousness for ever, and your law [is] truth.
verses.translation_dramatic: What you call right is right for all time, and your law is truth itself.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is built on repetition: צִדְקָתְךָ צֶדֶק, 'your righteousness [is] righteousness'. Two forms of one root, the abstract and the plain: whatever God's justice does is what justice means, and it does not change. Radak reads 'for ever' as lasting with the world; Ibn Ezra offers the argument that, if God's righteousness never alters, then his law is the same. KJV 'an everlasting righteousness' is fair but makes the second צֶדֶק an adjective-like phrase and adds 'an'; 'the truth' adds an article not in the Hebrew.

אֱמֶת is truth as reliability, what holds weight. The pair 'righteousness' and 'truth' recall Psalm 119:138, 'righteousness' and 'faithfulness', and Malbim treats this as the point at which he speaks of the great saving acts, the Exodus and Sinai, as evidence.

philological_notes.note: A repeated root: 'your righteousness is righteousness'. The abstract and the plain noun side by side, an emphatic equation.
'Truth, reliability', from the same root as אֱמוּנָה in verse 138. The law is that on which one may lean.

verses.translation_literal: Distress and anguish have found me; your commandments [are] my delights.
verses.translation_dramatic: Trouble has tracked me down, and anguish with it; they have found me out, hemmed in on every side. And still your commandments are my delight, the one thing in all this that gladdens me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb is the hinge: distress and anguish do not merely strike, they 'find' the speaker, as hunters find prey or a creditor finds a debtor. The two nouns are a matched pair built on one sound, tsar and matsoq, both from the root for 'narrow' or 'tight'. The speaker is cornered in a narrow place, and the Hebrew makes the walls audible. Medieval readers split the pair: Malbim takes tsar as outer trouble and matsoq as inner torment of the soul, and sets the commandments as the answer to the inner one. That is his reading, not something the words state.

The verse ends on a startling word. Shaashuim is the delight of play, the word for a child who is a pleasure to its parents (Jer 31:20) and for the joy of Wisdom at creation (Prov 8:30). The KJV 'my delights' is faithful here and softens nothing, but 'trouble' and 'taken hold on' flatten the hunt in 'found me' and the tight place in tsar. So the contrast is between a narrow place and a playground: commandments are not a grim comfort but a pleasure. The Targum has parnuqi, 'my delight'.

philological_notes.note: A paired phrase of two near-synonyms from roots meaning 'narrow' and 'press', so 'distress and anguish' is a tight place with a second squeeze. Ibn Ezra links tsar to the straitness of the heart; Malbim distinguishes outer from inner trouble, which is his own division.
A plural noun with the suffix 'my': 'my delights', 'my playthings'. It names a delight of play or affection, stronger than ordinary pleasure.

verses.translation_literal: The righteousness of your testimonies [is] for ever; make me understand, and let me live.
verses.translation_dramatic: Right is every word you have witnessed, right for ever. Make me see it, LORD, make me understand, and then let me live.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first half can be read two ways. Construct: 'the righteousness of your testimonies is for ever' (KJV, Webster, BBE, the Targum 'the righteousness of your testimonies for ever', and the STEPBible tagging, which marks צֶדֶק as a construct form). Nominal: 'your testimonies are righteousness for ever' (ASV: 'Thy testimonies are righteous for ever'; Metzudat David also reads 'the testimonies said in righteousness'). The literal layer follows the construct because the form and the Targum point that way and because verses 138 and 142 carry the same pair. The sense is nearly the same either way, and the dramatic layer gives it a little of both. YLT's 'is to Cause me to understand' is a different grammatical reading that I did not follow.

The speaker's request is the center of the stanza: 'make me understand' (a causative, הֲבִינֵנִי), and then the cohortative 'and let me live', a request to be preserved. The older commentators take 'live' as the life of the world to come (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David); the plain sense is rescue from his enemies. Ibn Ezra notes that 'for ever' is placed to serve both halves, and the spelling with a vav, עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ, is a rare form.

philological_notes.note: Construct 'the righteousness of your testimonies' (as the Targum and the tagging) or noun predicate 'your testimonies are righteousness' (as ASV). The spelling with vav is the full form of the word, which Ibn Ezra discusses with the other vav-for-he spellings.
A causative imperative, 'make me understand', the same plea that recurs through the psalm, with the cohortative 'and let me live' as its purpose.

verses.translation_literal: I called with all [my] heart; answer me, YHWH! Your statutes I will keep.
verses.translation_dramatic: I cried out, and nothing in me held back. Answer me, LORD. Answer, and I will guard your statutes like a flame carried through wind.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Koph stanza opens, and every line of it starts with the letter ק. The first word, qara'ti, 'I called', sets the tone: the singer is shouting. Hebrew 'heart' (lev) is the whole inner person, mind and will together, not just feeling, so 'with all my heart' means nothing was held back. Play it as a man with no reserve left.

The KJV 'hear me' softens a sharper verb. ʿaneni is 'answer me', and the Hebrew does not ask only to be listened to but to get a reply. The KJV also renders 'statutes' with a Latinate word, though ḥuqqim are things cut or engraved, a ruler's fixed decree. The verb 'keep' (naṣar) is the guard's verb, to watch over something fragile. The singer promises vigilance as a payment of sorts. Radak reads this as a prayer to live in order to keep the decrees, not for life's own sake.

philological_notes.note: 'I will keep.' The verb naṣar means to watch or guard, as one guards a city or a vineyard. The cohortative ending -ah makes it a resolve ('let me guard') as much as a promise. It is a stronger word than the plain 'keep' of the KJV.
'Your statutes.' From a root meaning to cut or engrave, a decree set down once and for all.

verses.translation_literal: I called you; save me, and I will keep your testimonies.
verses.translation_dramatic: I called to you. Save me, and I will keep what you have testified.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is a pared-down echo of the last. The verb 'called' now has a direct object, 'you' (the suffix -kha), where v.145 had none: the cry has found its address. There is no 'O Lord' and no argument, only the verb, the plea and the promise. Radak notes the repetition of the idea in different words, 'to strengthen the request'. Play it quieter than v.145, an exhausted person's second try.

The KJV 'I cried unto thee' keeps the sense, but its 'I shall keep' reads as a prediction, while the Hebrew cohortative says 'let me keep' or 'I will keep'. It is a pledge. 'Testimonies' (ʿedot) are what God has solemnly attested, the covenant's witness, which is why the KJV's word is closer to the Hebrew than BBE's 'unchanging word'. Metzudat David adds that the singer will be free to keep them once the enemy's pressure lifts.

philological_notes.note: 'Your testimonies.' The word means what is attested or witnessed, the covenant's formal evidence. The root עוד means to return, repeat or bear witness, so these are the things God keeps repeating to Israel.

verses.translation_literal: I came early in the twilight and cried for help; for your word I have waited.
verses.translation_dramatic: I was awake before the light, in the grey hour before dawn, crying out. All I had to wait on was your word.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene moves to the hour before the sun. The verb qiddamti, 'I came early', means to get there first, to go before. The KJV's 'I prevented the dawning' is a trap for a modern reader: 'prevent' in 1611 meant 'come before', not 'stop', and today it reads as the opposite of what the Hebrew says. The singer beats the dawn, and gets there before anyone else is awake. Radak says David rose before all other people to pray.

nesheph is the half-light, here the dim hour before morning, though the word can mean evening twilight too. The verb ʾashawwe'ah is the cry of someone in need of rescue, a real shout for help, which is why BBE's 'cry for help' is accurate, and the KJV's bare 'cried' loses the edge. yiḥalti, 'I have waited', is also 'I have hoped': Hebrew has one word for waiting and hoping, because to wait was to hope. The singer's whole position is that he has nothing but a promise to wait for.

philological_notes.note: 'In the twilight.' It is the half-light at the end or beginning of the day. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'night' and cites Isa 21:4. Here it is the grey time before dawn.
'I have waited' or 'I have hoped'. The root joins the two ideas: waiting is hoping.

verses.translation_literal: My eyes came before the night-watches, to meditate on your saying.
verses.translation_dramatic: My eyes were open before the watchmen called the hour. I lay awake to turn your saying over and over.
verses.directors_commentary:
The same verb returns, qiddemu, 'they came before', but now the subject is the eyes, which act on their own: they open before the night is up. That is the picture of insomnia made into devotion. An actor should not play calm; these eyes will not stay shut.

The night was divided into watches, shifts of sentries on the city wall, with three in the Hebrew system (Judg 7:19 mentions the middle one), each about four hours. The commentators differ on which watch is meant. Rashi, citing the rabbis, has David rising in the first third of the night; Radak says he slept only the first part. In a world without clocks, the 'watch' was the only unit of night, and its call was how time was told. The KJV 'prevent' again means 'come before'. The KJV also has 'meditate in thy word', but laśiaḥ is a spoken word, to talk, murmur or muse aloud. Meditation here is murmured recitation, not silent thought. The word ʾimra is a 'saying', a spoken utterance, and gives the verse a spoken texture the KJV's 'word' blurs.

philological_notes.note: 'Night-watches.' The same root as 'keep' (shamar). A watch is a shift of guarding, and the night was counted in these shifts. The commentators disagree on how many there were and which one is meant.
'To meditate.' The root means to talk or murmur and also to muse, so it includes speech: reading the saying aloud under one's breath. Metzudat David glosses it as 'to occupy oneself with the Torah'.

verses.translation_literal: My voice, hear, according to your loyalty, YHWH; according to your judgment, give me life.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hear my voice, LORD, as your steadfast love has always heard. According to your justice, give me life.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse opens with 'my voice' before the verb, a cry rather than a request, and the name YHWH stands in the middle where it can serve both halves. KJV and Webster keep that placement partly; ASV moves 'O Jehovah' into the second clause. Actors should place the name as a hinge: the first line is spoken to him, the second is the demand.

The two grounds of the plea are חֶסֶד, covenant loyalty (KJV's 'lovingkindness' is Coverdale's coinage and is warmer than the legal sense), and מִשְׁפָּט, 'judgment' or 'ordinance'. Radak and Metzudat David both read the second as 'your way of acting', your custom of showing kindness; Meiri reads it as how God has dealt with him 'all the days'. KJV's 'quicken' is now archaic and means 'make alive'. The imperative חַיֵּנִי is a plea the psalm repeats (vv. 25, 37, 40, and 154, 156 in the next stanza), so this is not new but the habit of the whole poem. Notice also that this verse opens the stanza's closing movement with the letter ק, the sound of קוֹל, 'voice'.

philological_notes.note: 'According to your covenant loyalty'. The prefix כְ gives a standard: a reasoned plea, not a bare request. Radak reads 'do it according to your kindness, which you have done many times'.
A piel imperative, 'give me life, preserve me alive'. The plea is repeated across the psalm (vv. 25, 37, 40, 154, 156).

verses.translation_literal: They have drawn near, pursuers of wickedness; from your law they are far.
verses.translation_dramatic: They have come close, these who run after wickedness, close and still coming. And from your law they stand far away.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first verb carries no object, and that is the difficulty. Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David take it as near to wickedness: the pursuers have caught what they chased, and their distance from the Torah is the other side of that closeness. Radak says the two roads are opposites, so nearness to one is distance from the other. BBE reads it as near to me, the pursuers closing in on the speaker, which suits the verses before and after. Play it with the object left open, so the actor can lean on either reading.

The pair 'near' and 'far' sets up the next verse, where the same adjective, qarov, is turned on God. KJV 'follow after mischief' keeps the verb but weakens the noun: zimmah is a heavy word, used in Leviticus for sexual crime and for plotting, and Radak glosses it as abomination and evil deed. 'Mischief' sounds like a boy's prank. The pursuers (rodfei) are the same word that returns in v.157 as 'those who pursue me', so the speaker is hunted by hunters of zimmah.

philological_notes.note: Scheming, lewdness, a plan that crosses a moral line. In the Torah it names sexual crime and deliberate wickedness; here it is what the pursuers chase. Radak and Metzudat Zion gloss it as abomination and evil deed, and Metzudat Zion cites Leviticus 20. KJV 'mischief' is too light.
Pursuers, those who run after. The object is zimmah, so they chase wickedness; in v.157 the same participle takes a suffix and they chase the speaker.

verses.translation_literal: Near, you, YHWH, and all your commandments, truth.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you are near, LORD. You are near, and every command of yours is truth.
verses.directors_commentary:
Neither clause has a verb. The speaker sets 'near' first, then 'you', then the name, so the word that was used for the pursuers in v.150 now belongs to God before anything else is said. Then comes 'and all your commandments' and, last, 'truth', so the line ends on that word. English needs 'are', and KJV supplies it twice, which is fair, but the stress sits in the Hebrew order.

The commentators hear the answer to the pursuers. Radak and Meiri say God is near to all who call on him; Rashi says near even to those far off, if they turn back. Malbim reads it as a reply to people who thought God remote from the world and so thought no commandment could come from him. BBE 'teachings' for mitzvot loses the word 'commandments'. KJV is accurate here, apart from the 'are' it must add.

philological_notes.note: Truth, reliability, what holds when leaned on. It stands alone as the predicate: the commandments are not 'true' as a judgment but are truth itself. Metzudat David hears 'truth' as what pays out in reward.

verses.translation_literal: Of old I have known from your testimonies that for ever you have founded them.
verses.translation_dramatic: I learned it long ago, from your own testimonies: that you laid them down for ever, and set them on a foundation.
verses.directors_commentary:
Qedem means 'of old', 'from the first'; the speaker says either 'long ago I knew this' or 'at the start of my study I learned it'. KJV 'Concerning thy testimonies' turns the preposition min, 'from', into 'concerning' and loses the point that the testimonies themselves taught him. ASV 'known from' keeps it.

Radak gives two readings of the last clause. First: you made the testimonies a foundation for the world, and the more a man studies them the more he sees a ladder up to the knowledge of God; so the speaker saw this at the start of his study. Second: 'for ever' means the commandments have no fixed time, for they stand on justice and justice has no end. Meiri and Metzudat David take the second line. Malbim adds a third: against those who say God was near only in the days of the fathers, the testimonies are founded for ever, so what was once is always.

Yasad is the building word for a foundation, as for a house or temple. BBE 'your unchanging word is for ever' drops the builder and the verb.

philological_notes.note: 'Of old', 'from the beginning', also 'east'. Here a time word. Rashi reads it as 'before the thing came to be': God commanded before Israel took the land, so the speaker had the commands before the events.
You have founded them, laid their foundation. The verb is the building verb; the suffix 'them' refers back to the testimonies.

verses.translation_literal: See my affliction and rescue me, for your law I have not forgotten.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look at my affliction, LORD, and pull me out of it. I have not let go of your law. I could not forget it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Resh stanza begins, and with it a new, shorter plea: three words, 'see my affliction'. Notice what he asks. Not 'consider', the KJV's word, which sounds like a committee weighing a case, but 'see' (re'eh): look at me. God is asked to look at the wreck of this man and be moved by the sight.

ʿonyi, 'my affliction', is poverty, oppression and humbling all at once, and Metzudat David takes it as poverty. The verb ḥalleṣeni is a good one for the KJV to render as 'deliver', but its root means to pull out or draw off, as a sandal is drawn off (Metzudat Zion cites Deut 25), or a soldier is drawn out from the ranks. The picture is of being yanked free. The KJV 'I do not forget' is a present tense; the Hebrew perfect 'I have not forgotten' says it over the whole history of the suffering, and it is the ground of the plea: through all of this, I did not let go. Malbim adds that whoever keeps the Torah in poverty will keep it in wealth.

philological_notes.note: 'And rescue me.' The root means to draw or pull out, and is used for drawing off a sandal (Deut 25:9) or for a soldier drawn up for battle. Metzudat Zion glosses it with the sandal image, so it is more physical than 'deliver'.
'My affliction.' It names the state of being brought low, poverty, oppression and humbling together. Metzudat David reads it as poverty.

verses.translation_literal: Contend my contention and redeem me; according to your saying make me live.
verses.translation_dramatic: Take up my case and argue it for me. Buy me back. And as you have said, let me live.
verses.directors_commentary:
The courtroom comes in. rivah rivi is a figure of repetition, the verb and noun from the same root, 'contend my contention': the singer hands God his case file, and he wants God to be his advocate. The KJV 'plead my cause' keeps the legal sound, which is right, but it loses the doubled word. Keep the echo in performance: the verb and its object say the same thing twice, like a man repeating the case to a lawyer who must hear it plain.

The next verb is ge'aleni, 'redeem me', and the word has a family meaning. The go'el was the relative whose duty was to buy back a kinsman sold into debt, or to avenge him. So the singer calls God his next of kin: if he is sold, God will pay, and if he is wronged, God will answer for him. The KJV 'deliver' loses all of this. The prefix l- in la'imratekha, 'according to your saying', is read by Ibn Ezra and Radak as 'for the sake of', and Radak adds the singer is asking for life to keep the saying, not for pleasure. Malbim places the saying as the promise God made.

philological_notes.note: 'Contend my contention.' The verb and noun share a root, a legal term for taking up a lawsuit. God is asked to be advocate. Metzudat David: 'you will contend with those who contend with me'.
'And redeem me.' The go'el was the near kinsman who buys back a relative in debt or defends him (Lev 25:25, Ruth 4). The singer addresses God as his kinsman-redeemer.

verses.translation_literal: Far from the wicked, salvation, for your decrees they have not sought.
verses.translation_dramatic: Far from the wicked stands salvation. They have not looked for your decrees, and so it does not come near them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew puts 'far' first, as 'near' opened v.151, and ends on the cause: 'for your decrees they have not sought'. The verb darash is used of seeking out God, an oracle, a teacher; here the object is the decrees (huqqim), the laws that come without stated reasons. Malbim says the wicked may keep laws that reason explains, but not the decrees whose reason they cannot see, and so salvation is far from them.

The adjective raḥoq has the same root as raḥaqu in v.150, where the pursuers were far from the law. That is my own reading, but the sound carries it: they were far from the law, so salvation is far from them. Radak notes the grammar: raḥoq is masculine and yeshuah feminine, which he explains by saying the speaker means 'the matter of salvation'. KJV 'seek not' puts the Hebrew past tense into the present, and 'statutes' is fair for huqqim.

philological_notes.note: Far, distant. It has the same root as raḥaqu in v.150, so the distance of the wicked from the law comes back as the distance of salvation from them. This link is my own observation.
They sought, enquired after. The verb of going to a source for an answer. Radak ties it to the wicked having no merit by which to be delivered from trouble.

verses.translation_literal: Your compassions, many, YHWH; according to your judgments, make me live.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your compassions are many, LORD. Let your own justice decide it, and give me life.
verses.directors_commentary:
Raḥamim is the plural of 'womb' love: compassion felt in the body, as a mother feels it. KJV 'tender mercies' catches that. The plural is intensive and the adjective 'many' stands after it, so the line is a plain statement of fact, with no verb.

The second half asks for life 'according to your judgments', mishpatim, the word for the verdicts and rulings of God. Radak glosses it as 'your good ways', and Metzudat David as 'your way of having mercy on creatures'. Malbim reads it as a claim: since you are merciful, it is also right, by justice, that you grant me life by my merit. So mercy and justice are asked for together.

Radak connects the first half with the next verse: the speaker's pursuers are many (v.157, rabbim rodfai), so God's compassions, rabbim too, are more than they are. The same adjective, rabbim, stands in both. The verse returns to the refrain 'give me life', which the speaker sings at the end of vv.149, 154, 156 and 159; KJV 'quicken' is archaic for 'make live'.

philological_notes.note: Your compassions, from the root of rehem, 'womb'. The plural is of intensity. It is the love that comes from the inside.
According to your judgments: God's verdicts and rulings, his manner of judging. Radak glosses it as 'your good ways'; Metzudat David as 'your way of showing mercy to creatures'.

verses.translation_literal: Many [are] my pursuers and my foes; from your testimonies I have not turned aside.
verses.translation_dramatic: They are many, the ones who hunt me down, the ones who hem me in. Yet I have not stepped off the path of your testimonies — not by so much as a single pace.
