verses.directors_commentary:
The first half is all crowd and pressure: 'pursuers' (rodefai) is the language of a hunt, and 'foes' (tzarai) shares its root with 'tightness' — people who squeeze. Against that the speaker sets one fixed fact, in the perfect tense: I have not turned. Play it as steadiness, not boasting; he is stating where his feet are, with the pack at his heels.

The KJV 'decline from' is archaic (it means 'swerve away'); the Hebrew nata is the verb for a path bending sideways, and the same verb, in Ps 119, is the opposite of 'walking in' the law. Radak notes that the speaker did not seek the harm his enemies sought for him, which is the contrast the line draws between their pursuit and his steadiness.

philological_notes.note: To stretch out, bend, veer aside. Here the path image: leaving the road of the testimonies. Ibn Ezra stresses it is intransitive, like 'I have departed' (סרתי), not 'I bent something'.

verses.translation_literal: I have seen traitors, and I have quarrelled, because your saying they have not kept.
verses.translation_dramatic: I looked at the faithless, and I could not hold my tongue; I quarrelled with them. They did not keep your word.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verbs are in order: I saw, and I quarrelled. Bogedim are traitors, those who break faith, and the word reaches further than KJV 'transgressors', which turns a betrayal into a mere offence. They are faithless to a person, here to God's word (imrah, 'saying').

The second verb is the puzzle. The form is a rare reflexive from the root of 'quarrel'. Radak and Metzudat David read it that way: I picked a quarrel with them, and Radak adds that he quarrelled more over God's word than over what they did to himself. Metzudat Zion cites Psalm 95:10, 'forty years I loathed (aqut) that generation', for the related root. The other reading, which Meiri gives and Radak reports from his father, is loathing: 'I saw traitors prospering, and I was sick of life', after Job 10:1, 'my soul is weary of my life'. STEPBible and BBE ('with hate') follow that. KJV and YLT 'grieved' sit between the two.

The last word, asher, is 'that' or 'because'. Play the quarrel as zeal and keep the grief as colour behind it.

philological_notes.note: A reflexive form with two possible roots. Radak and Metzudat David take it as 'I quarrelled' (from qeṭatah, quarrel). Meiri's alternative, and Radak's report of his father's view, is 'I felt loathing', as in Job 10:1 and Psalm 95:10, which gives STEPBible's 'disgust'. Ibn Ezra relates it to 'my soul is weary' (Job 10:1).
Those who act treacherously, who break faith. Meiri says these are people from Israel's own side, who plotted against the speaker and broke God's covenant.

verses.translation_literal: See that your precepts I have loved, YHWH; according to your covenant loyalty make me live.
verses.translation_dramatic: See: I have loved your precepts, LORD. According to your steadfast love, give me life.
verses.directors_commentary:
The imperative 'see' (re'eh) answers 'I saw' in v.158: the speaker looked at the traitors, and now asks God to look at him. Ibn Ezra notes the match, and the asking for life 'according to chesed' also answers the quarrel of v.158. The clause is 'see that I have loved', not KJV 'consider how I love': ki is 'that', and the Hebrew states the fact and leaves God to weigh it. KJV and ASV 'how' makes it a question of degree.

The verb is in the past (aheveti), 'I have loved', a love already shown. Fiqqudim, 'precepts', are things appointed, charges given in trust. Radak hears the line as: see how much I love them, that I quarrel with the wicked for your sake and not mine. Metzudat David reads the love as the wish to do them, which God counts as deeds.

Chesed is covenant loyalty, the steadfast love that keeps a bond; KJV 'lovingkindness' is a Coverdale coinage and is close. The speaker asks for life by God's loyalty, where v.156 asked by his judgments.

philological_notes.note: Your precepts, the things you have appointed and entrusted. The word is found almost only in Psalm 119. It stresses the law as a charge laid on a person.
According to your covenant loyalty: the steadfast love that keeps a bond. The speaker appeals to God's own faithfulness, not to his merit.

verses.translation_literal: The head of your word [is] truth, and for ever [is] every judgment of your righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: The very head of your word is truth. And every judgment your righteousness has spoken stands — for ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the last verse of the Resh stanza and a pivot: the word 'head' (rosh) opens it, and the speaker stops running from enemies to steady himself on what does not move. The key word is ambiguous. Rosh can mean 'beginning' (KJV 'from the beginning', BBE 'from the first') or 'sum, total' (YLT, ASV 'the sum'); the Hebrew does not choose. Radak offers 'from the beginning of the world until now', while Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David hear the first words at Sinai, 'I am the LORD your God', as the head, with the later commandments proving it true.

Malbim notes a midrashic observation that the last letters of the first three words of Gen 1:1 spell 'emet' (truth); that is a rabbinic play, not the psalm's own point. The KJV 'righteous judgments' turns the genitive 'judgment of your righteousness' into an adjective and loses that the justice belongs to God's own character.

philological_notes.note: 'Head': beginning, sum, or chief point. The translations split between 'beginning' and 'sum'; the Hebrew holds both.

verses.translation_literal: Princes have pursued me for nothing, and from your word my heart has trembled.
verses.translation_dramatic: Princes — men with power and soldiers behind them — have hounded me, and for no reason at all. But it is your word that makes my heart tremble.
verses.directors_commentary:
The man who is hunted is not afraid of his hunters. The fear the speaker keeps for God's word is deliberately set against men of rank, the sarim, officers of the king. Radak places them in the reigns of Saul or Absalom; Meiri says Saul and his followers; these are the commentators' guesses, since the verse names nobody.

Two marks of the KJV's age: 'standeth in awe' tames the verb pachad, which is 'to tremble, be in dread', and 'persecuted' carries church-history baggage the Hebrew radaf ('chase') does not have. 'Chinnam' means 'for nothing, free of charge' and so 'without cause'. Malbim's image: one who faces a lion no longer fears a bee.

philological_notes.note: To tremble, be in dread. Stronger than 'stands in awe'; reverent fear, but bodily.
Free, for nothing; 'without cause', since they gain nothing and he has done nothing. Malbim adds: their pursuit also achieves nothing.

verses.translation_literal: Rejoicing [am] I over your saying, like one who finds great spoil.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I — I am glad. Glad over your saying, as glad as a man who comes upon a great heap of plunder.
verses.directors_commentary:
From fear to joy in one line. The simile is a soldier's, not a scholar's: shalal is the loot taken after a battle — silver, cloth, livestock, a year's wealth in an afternoon. Ibn Ezra reads it against the princes of the previous verse: he did not need to fear them, because he rejoices as if he had defeated them and carried off their plunder. That link is his, not the Hebrew's.

The KJV 'findeth' is accurate, but 'spoil' is now a word for ruin, not wealth; modern English wants 'plunder' or 'loot'. Note 'imrah' (saying, promise), a different word from the 'devar' of v. 160 and 161: Rashi explains it as the promise God made, or an obscure saying understood.

philological_notes.note: Booty taken in war. The comparison is to sudden military windfall.

verses.translation_literal: Falsehood I have hated, and I abhor [it]; your torah I have loved.
verses.translation_dramatic: Falsehood: that I hate. I hate it, and I turn from it with disgust. But your torah — that I love.
verses.directors_commentary:
The line is a balanced pair: two strong verbs of rejection, 'hated' (sane'ti) and 'abhor' (ta'ev), and one of love, with the objects set in front of the verbs for emphasis: falsehood, torah. The word sheker is not merely 'lying' (KJV): it covers deceit, empty claims and false worship, the opposite of the emet that headed v. 160. Malbim's reasoning is that whoever loves the truth must hate what opposes it.

'Torah' here is 'instruction', teaching; the KJV 'law' narrows it to the legal sense. In an acrostic whose lines each start with Shin, the stress falls on the first word: sheker, 'falsehood' — the speaker names the thing he hates before he names the thing he loves.

philological_notes.note: Falsehood, deceit, what is empty and misleading; broader than spoken lies.

verses.translation_literal: Seven [times] in the day I have praised you, for the judgments of your righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Seven times a day I lift my voice and praise you — for the judgments your righteousness has given.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Seven' is the number of fullness, and the older readers say so: Radak and Metzudat David take it as 'many times', not a count, like 'seven times the righteous falls and rises' (Prov 24:16). Rashi and Malbim, on the other hand, count: the recitations of the Shema with its blessings, or the three prayers of day and the night watches. The literal layer keeps 'seven' and leaves the choice to the reader.

The KJV 'because of' is fine; the Hebrew preposition al is the same as in v. 162 ('over your saying'), so praise and joy share one object-marker: both are poured out over something. The reason given is not blessings received but God's judgments, which in a hunted man's mouth means that justice is real.

philological_notes.note: Seven: a literal number or an idiom for completeness ('many times').

verses.translation_literal: Peace [is] great to [those who] love your Torah, and there is not to them a stumbling-block.
verses.translation_dramatic: Great peace, an abundance of it, rests on those who love your Torah — and in their path there is nothing to trip them.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the praise of v.164, the psalm turns from the speaker's own voice to a general truth about everyone who loves the Torah. Shalom is not the absence of noise but wholeness: a life that is unbroken and sound. The Hebrew says shalom rav, 'peace [is] much', with no verb, the way a proverb is spoken. Love of the Torah is the psalm's recurring note (vv.97, 113, 119, 127, 159, 163), and here it comes as a statement about the lovers, not a boast about the speaker.

The KJV's 'nothing shall offend them' is the weak point. 'Offend' once meant 'cause to stumble' (compare Matthew 18:6), but a modern reader hears 'hurt feelings'. The Hebrew is mikhshol, a physical stumbling-block lying in the road, the thing one trips over; the same root as 'stumble' (kashal). The KJV also turns a plain 'there is not to them' into a future ('shall'). The Hebrew has no verb at all, and so is a standing condition. Radak reads it as a lasting promise, 'those who love the Torah will never stumble', because their way is straight and they are content with the little that this world gives (Radak on Psalm 119:165). Malbim reads more strongly: peace from every mishap, and no sin coming into their hands (Malbim on Psalm 119:165). The Targum divides the promise across two worlds: peace in this world and no stumbling in the world to come.

philological_notes.note: A stumbling-block, anything that makes a traveller fall; from the root 'to stumble'. It can mean a literal obstacle or a moral snare. KJV 'offend' blurs it.
A poetic form of 'to them' (lahem), common in verse. It marks the line as elevated speech.

verses.translation_literal: I have waited for your salvation, YHWH, and your commandments I have done.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have waited for your salvation, LORD, waited — and all the while I have done what you commanded.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two short clauses, one waiting and one doing, and the order matters: the psalmist does not wait idly. Hope and obedience go together, and the verse places the commandments after the waiting only to show that the one did not stop the other. Radak adds that the doing was not for a reward: 'I did them as you commanded me', and knew that salvation would come regardless (Radak on Psalm 119:166). Metzudat David hears something more practical: the troubles of the enemy did not make his hands slack in the commandments (Metzudat David on Psalm 119:166).

The key verb is sibbarti. The KJV's 'hoped' is right in sense but the Hebrew is more tense: it is the root sever, 'to look expectantly', the posture of someone watching the road. Rashi glosses it 'I waited, hoped' (hoḥalti), and Metzudat Zion ties it to 'who hope in the LORD' in Psalm 146. The KJV also places 'Lord' at the opening; the Hebrew holds the divine name in the middle, as a pause in the breath. The word 'salvation' here is yeshu'ah, rescue; KJV is fine.

philological_notes.note: 'I have waited, hoped'. A verb of expectant looking, used again in Psalm 146:5 for 'whose hope is in the LORD'. Not the common 'to break' (same consonants, different root).

verses.translation_literal: My soul has kept your testimonies, and I love them exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: My very soul has kept your testimonies — and how I love them, how deeply I love them.
verses.directors_commentary:
Love is a recurring word in this stretch: 'I have loved' your commandments (v.159, 163), 'those who love your Torah' (v.165), and now 'I love them exceedingly'. Here it is joined to keeping: the soul keeps, and the speaker loves. Verse 168 then repeats the keeping ('I have kept'), so the pair reads as a frame around the love.

The subject is nafshi, 'my soul', literally 'my self, my throat, my appetite'. KJV 'soul' is fine but a modern reader hears something detached from the body; the Hebrew speaks of the whole living person. The verb is feminine ('she kept') to agree with nafshi. 'Testimonies' (edot) is one of the psalm's synonyms for the Torah, the things which testify to what God has done. Malbim reads them as the stories of the Torah that witness to providence, reward and punishment (Malbim on Psalm 119:167). Metzudat David reads the love as the point: the commandments were kept out of love and not only from fear of punishment (Metzudat David on Psalm 119:167). Radak says the soul reflected on them, and so came to love them (Radak on Psalm 119:167).

philological_notes.note: 'Your testimonies'; things that bear witness. Malbim takes them as the narratives of the Torah that bear witness to providence.
'My soul, my self'. In Hebrew it is the whole living being, and the verb after it is feminine.

verses.translation_literal: I have kept your precepts and your testimonies, for all my ways [are] before you.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have kept your precepts, your testimonies — for every road I walk lies open before your eyes.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse gathers two of the psalm's synonyms for the Torah, 'precepts' (piqqudim) and 'testimonies' (edot), in one breath. The reason it gives is the point of the verse: 'for all my ways are before you', literally 'opposite you', in your line of sight. It is not a boast of perfection; it is the awareness of being watched, and the willingness to be.

Rashi reads the clause as 'you know all my ways' (Rashi on Psalm 119:168). Ibn Ezra reads the reason as an obligation: I must keep them, because you see all that is in my heart and every deed (Ibn Ezra on Psalm 119:168). Radak and Meiri tie it to Proverbs 3:6, 'in all your ways know him', and to the saying in Avot that all one's deeds should be for the sake of heaven (Radak and Meiri on Psalm 119:168). The KJV 'before thee' is correct; the word negdekha can also mean 'in front of you' as an opponent or a counterpart, but here it is the gaze of one who sees.

philological_notes.note: 'Opposite you, in front of you, in your sight.' Rashi glosses the clause 'you know all my ways'.

verses.translation_literal: May my ringing cry draw near before your face, YHWH; according to your word make me understand.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let my cry rise and reach you, LORD. Let it come near, close enough to be heard. And when it has, give me understanding, as your own word has promised it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last stanza opens with taw, the final letter, and every one of its eight lines begins with it. The speaker is near the end of a long prayer and the voice should sound like it: no longer building arguments, just sending the cry up. Two verbs of nearness frame the stanza. In this verse the cry draws near (tikrav); in the next the plea comes (tavo').

The noun rinnah is not a quiet word. It is a ringing shout, sometimes of joy and sometimes of distress, so 'cry' is right but the actor should not whisper it. Ibn Ezra reads 'draw near' as a figure, since heaven is far from earth, and glosses rinnah as a loud voice. The Hebrew says 'before your face', where the KJV's 'before thee' flattens the picture of a petitioner standing in front of a king. The KJV also prints the heading 'TAU' inside the verse as if it were text, and puts the understanding clause last, as the Hebrew does, but softens the plain imperative 'make me understand' (havineni, causative) into 'give me understanding'. The causative is a request to be taught, as Radak takes it: that God give the insight to do what the word says.

philological_notes.note: A ringing cry: the root covers shouts of joy and cries for help. Ibn Ezra glosses it as a loud voice, quoting 'and the cry went up' (ותעבור הרנה). The same noun is the ancient word for a petition spoken aloud, not a silent wish.
Hiphil imperative with 'me': cause me to understand. The psalm asks for understanding again and again, so this is the last of those requests.

verses.translation_literal: May my plea for grace come before your face; according to your saying, deliver me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let my plea for mercy come in and stand before you. And then deliver me, LORD, as you said you would.
verses.directors_commentary:
The cry of verse 169 now becomes a petition, and the movement is one of entry: tavo' is the verb for coming into a presence, as a visitor comes into a court. The word tehinnah comes from the root of 'grace' (chen): it is a request for favor, made by someone with no claim except the other's kindness. 'Supplication' in the KJV is correct but stiff, and 'plea for grace' keeps the root audible.

The speaker asks for deliverance 'according to your saying' (imrah), meaning a particular promise. Metzudat David takes it as the promise made through Nathan the prophet, which fits the tradition that David wrote the psalm. Radak reads deliverance as rescue from the stumbling block of sin, not from an enemy, because the psalm names no foe in the verse. Both readings are open; the actor decides whether the danger is outside or inside. Note that imrah and davar (verse 169) are two different words that the KJV renders as 'word' both times. Hebrew has a different promise-word here, and the English loses the change.

philological_notes.note: A plea for favor, from the root of chen, 'grace'. The petitioner has no claim but the other's kindness.
A spoken saying or promise. Metzudat David ties it to a promise given through the prophet Nathan; Meiri reads 'according to your intention and will'.

verses.translation_literal: May my lips pour forth praise, for you teach me your decrees.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let my lips overflow with praise, like a spring that cannot be held back. For you are the one who teaches me your statutes.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns. After the pleas comes a vow, and the image is of water. The verb tabba'nah is from the root nava', to gush or well up, the same verb that describes a spring; in Psalm 19:3 'day to day pours out speech' uses its relative. Rashi simply says 'speak', but Radak and Meiri hear the spring: speech that does not stop. The actor should let the line run on.

The KJV, 'My lips shall utter praise, when thou hast taught me', makes two changes. It turns a wish ('let them pour forth') into a promise, and it turns ki ('for, because') into 'when'. Ibn Ezra and Radak do read a condition here, so the KJV has a Jewish precedent, but the plain sense is causal: the teaching is the reason for the praise, and it is going on now (the verb is imperfect and says 'you teach me'). 'Utter' is also a pale word for a verb that means to bubble over.

Malbim counts this as the seventh prayer of the psalm, matching 'seven times a day I praise you' (verse 164), and so the point at which the speaker already treats the request as granted.

philological_notes.note: From nava', to gush or bubble up, as a spring does. Rashi glosses it 'let them speak'; Radak and Meiri point to the spring that never stops flowing. Psalm 19:3 uses the related hiphil (yabbia') of speech.
Decrees, things cut or engraved. The word is used throughout the psalm for commands whose reason is not given; Malbim sets chukkim against commands whose reason can be seen.

verses.translation_literal: May my tongue answer your saying, for all your commandments are righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let my tongue ring out in answer to your word, for every command you have given is right.
verses.directors_commentary:
Lips poured out praise in verse 171; now the tongue answers. Malbim hears a step up: the lips make plain speech, the tongue speaks the considered, understood word. Whether or not that distinction holds, the line should grow louder. Rashi says that every form of the verb 'anah means a raised voice, and cites the Levites who 'answered and said' the curses from Mount Ebal (Deuteronomy 27:14). Metzudat David agrees: the tongue speaks 'in a raised voice, for these are just words.'

The KJV, 'My tongue shall speak of thy word', picks the weakest meaning and adds 'of'. The Hebrew has no preposition: the tongue answers the word itself, as a congregation answers a leader. YLT and the ASV's 'sing' follow the Masoretic note quoted by Radak and Meiri, which lists this as one of three places where ta'an means praise. The last clause is a bare noun phrase: 'all your commandments — righteousness'. Not 'are righteous' but 'are righteousness' itself, the standard by which right is measured. The KJV's 'are righteousness' is exact here, and the ASV copies it.

philological_notes.note: From 'anah, to answer or respond, always with a raised voice for Rashi; the Masorah, as Radak reports, counts three places where it is a verb of praise. The sense here is 'answer in song'.
Righteousness itself, not merely 'righteous': the predicate is a noun, and the commandments are said to be the thing itself.

verses.translation_literal: May your hand be to help me, for your precepts I have chosen.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let your hand be there to help me — for it is your precepts I have chosen.
verses.directors_commentary:
The hand of God in the Bible is usually power: the hand that brought Israel out of Egypt. Here it is asked to be at the psalmist's side as a helper. The reason given is choice: 'I have chosen your precepts' (bahareti). This is the first of two places in the psalm (with v.176, 'for I have not forgotten your commandments') where the psalmist gives his loyalty to the commandments as the ground of his appeal.

Ibn Ezra notes that 'the hand of the LORD', when it comes with the letter bet ('in'), is always for ill, and here there is no bet, so the hand is for help (Ibn Ezra on Psalm 119:173). Radak connects it to the previous verse: since I have explained your precepts, help me with them (Radak on Psalm 119:173). Malbim reads it as a request for direct help: not through messengers and intermediaries, but by your own hand (Malbim on Psalm 119:173). The Targum has 'my help' for the infinitive. KJV 'Let thine hand help me' is natural, but the Hebrew says 'may your hand be for helping me', a little more concrete.

philological_notes.note: 'I have chosen.' The verb of election, used of God choosing Israel; here the human chooses the precepts.
'Your hand', God's active power. Ibn Ezra observes that 'hand of the LORD' with the prefix bet is always for harm; without it, as here, it is for help.

verses.translation_literal: I have longed for your salvation, YHWH, and your Torah [is] my delights.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have ached for your salvation, LORD — and your Torah, your Torah is my delight.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse pairs longing and delight: the psalmist longs for rescue, yet already delights in the Torah. Verse 166 said 'I have waited for your salvation'; here the same phrase, 'for your salvation, YHWH', returns with a stronger verb, ta'avti, 'I have yearned', a word of appetite. Ibn Ezra compares it to a soul that 'longs and even faints' (Ibn Ezra on Psalm 119:174).

The closing word, sha'ashu'ai, is plural: 'my delights', not a single delight. It is a word of play, like a parent's play with a child; the same root appears in Jeremiah 31:20, 'Is Ephraim my dear son, a child of delights?'. The Targum has parnuqi, 'my delight'. KJV 'my delight' loses the plural but not the sense. Radak reads the salvation as that of the soul in the world to come, which is why the Torah is a delight, for it brings one there (Radak on Psalm 119:174). Metzudat David and Malbim read it differently: the longing is for relief from the enemy's pressure, so that the Torah can be studied without distraction (Metzudat David and Malbim on Psalm 119:174).

philological_notes.note: 'My delights', a plural of intensity; the same root is used in Jeremiah 31:20 for a beloved child. The Targum renders it parnuqi, 'my delight'.
'I have longed'; a rare verb of yearning, a word of appetite.

verses.translation_literal: May my soul live, and it will praise you, and your judgments will help me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let my soul live, so that it may praise you — and let your judgments stand beside me and help.
verses.directors_commentary:
The request for life comes with its purpose attached: 'let me live, and I will praise you'. This is the logic of the Psalms, where the dead do not praise (Psalm 115:17); life is wanted for the sake of praise. Radak reads it plainly: 'in this world I ask for life, in order that I may praise you', which means knowing the truth of your divinity (Radak on Psalm 119:175). Meiri agrees that it is a prayer for the life of the body, not for pleasure but for praise, and then also allows that it may mean the life of the soul (Meiri on Psalm 119:175).

The second clause shifts to 'your judgments', mishpatekha, which can be the rulings of the Torah or God's acts of justice. Radak calls them a ladder by which one climbs to the knowledge of God (Radak on Psalm 119:175). Metzudat David reads the judgments as those God passes on the psalmist's enemies, which rescue him from their hand so he is free to praise (Metzudat David on Psalm 119:175). The KJV 'let my soul live' is exact. Its 'and it shall praise thee' makes a certain future of what is, in Hebrew, a purpose clause: 'that it may praise'.

philological_notes.note: 'My soul, my life, my self'. Radak and Meiri take 'live' as life in this world, asked in order to praise; Meiri also allows the life of the soul.
'Your judgments': the rulings of the Torah, or God's acts of justice. Metzudat David takes it as the judgments God passes on enemies.

verses.translation_literal: I have gone astray like a sheep, lost; seek your servant, for your commandments I have not forgotten.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have wandered like a sheep, like a lost one. Come and search for your servant, LORD. For I have not forgotten your commands.
verses.directors_commentary:
The longest psalm ends not with triumph but with a confession and a request. It is one of the most surprising closing lines in the Psalter: after 175 verses of devotion, the speaker says he is lost. The picture is the shepherd's. A sheep that has strayed (se, a single animal of the flock) cannot find its way back alone, as Radak and Metzudat David both say, and waits until the shepherd searches. So the speaker's request, 'seek your servant', is the shepherd's work. Compare Ezekiel 34:16 ('I will seek the lost') and Isaiah 53:6.

The KJV's 'lost sheep' is fine, though 'sheep' has the participle 'oved ('perishing, lost') after it, and the sense of danger is stronger in Hebrew, where the verb can mean 'perish'. Its tense is also off: 'I do not forget' makes the last clause general, while the verb is a completed past, 'I have not forgotten', so the claim is about his whole history. Ibn Ezra puts the logic well: even as a lost sheep, the commandments were never lost from him. Malbim hears a more specific exile in 'astray', that of David fleeing from Saul, and asks that God bring him back to the land.

The actor should end small, quiet and unfinished. There is no 'amen'. The sentence ends with 'I have not forgotten', and the psalm lets that stand as the reason God should come.

philological_notes.note: A single sheep that is perishing or lost. The verb 'avad means both 'be lost' and 'perish', so the picture is of an animal in danger, not just one that has wandered off. Metzudat David and Radak both read the sheep as unable to return until the shepherd finds it.
Piel imperative: seek out, search for. It is the shepherd's task, and the speaker casts God as the shepherd who goes looking.
